#3374. Hands-on: Anker’s 10K MagGo 2 Pro offers fast 25W MagSafe charging with a kickstand

Anker’s new MagGo Pro 2 power bank offers active cooling, 25W MagSafe fast charging, 10,000mAh of capacity, and a smart display – all in one package. Anker touts it as the fastest and coolest wireless power bank on the market.

Thanks to the active cooling within this power bank, you’ll notice it doesn’t get as hot as other power banks on the market. This also helps it charge faster, since it doesn’t have to throttle as quickly to keep the temperature manageable.

As a result, you can charge an iPhone 17 Pro up to 50% in just 25 minutes with this battery bank. It also supports up to 45W of output via USB-C.

On the side of the power bank, you’ll notice a smart display. This display can show you the battery level, how quickly its charging an attached device (either wirelessly or with USB-C), the internal temperature of the battery bank, as well as the battery health. You can rotate between all of these options by pressing the power button.

This power bank also offers a kickstand, which I’ve found to be one of my favorite features on recent MagSafe battery banks. It makes it easy to just prop up your phone and watch a video, no matter the environment.

If you have an iPhone Duo, this power bank will extend past the bottom of the phone. If you rotate it and use the kickstand, there’s no issue propping up your phone and charging it.

Lastly, the MagGo Pro 2 comes in a bunch of fun colors, including a burgundy to match the new iPhone 18 Pro. It’s also available in silver, blue, and gray.

If the Anker MagGo Pro 2 Power Bank interests you, you can pick one up for $109.99 on Amazon.

Apple has finally released its very first touchscreen laptop—the MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display. I reviewed both the 14- and 16-inch models, and I can tell you that the tandem OLED is easily the best we’ve ever tested. That, along with a thinner and lighter design, blazing-fast M5 Pro/M5 Max performance, and epic battery life, makes it one of the best MacBooks available.

While the MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display is undoubtedly great, it’s proving to be one of Apple’s most divisive laptops. That’s not only based on what I’ve seen on social media, but also on what Tom’s Guide readers and followers have told us through polls and in the comments section of our TikTok videos.

To that end, I’ve scoured reactions to our MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display and selected highlights to give you a sense of what folks think.

From price and performance to features, here’s what Tom’s Guide readers and followers have to say about Apple’s new OLED MacBook Pro.

After the MacBook Pro with PROLED was announced and our initial hands-on with the laptop, we created a poll asking: Are you sold on the touchscreen MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR? with the four options you see above:

Based on a total 453 votes on our website, 144 votes went with “incredible tech, but $2,899 is way out of my budget,” followed up by 135 votes for “MacBooks don’t need a touchscreen — give me a standard M5/M6 laptop instead.”

“Touch, tandem OLED, and 2,000 nits make it worth the premium" received 131 votes, while “I want to see how third-party apps handle touch first” got 43 votes.

Sign up to the Tom's iGuide weekly newsletter with coverage on everything from product launches to software updates, this is your go-to source for the latest updates on all the best Apple content.

I can’t say I’m surprised by these results, as the MacBook Pro OLED is now the most expensive Apple laptop, with the 14-inch model with M5 Pro starting at $2,899 and the 16-inch model with M5 Max starting at $3,399. And naturally, adding additional RAM, storage, and upgrading to a nano-texture display all significantly boost the price.

The usefulness of a laptop touchscreen is something I discussed in my review. While the touchscreen itself is extremely responsive and intuitive, it’s a feature that some laptop users (such as myself) don’t always need. You can save $900 by purchasing the 14-inch MacBook Pro with M6, which starts at $1,999. Yes, that’s expensive too, but it’s still nearly $1,000 less than the starting price of the M5 Pro 14-inch PROLED.

That said, the tandem OLED touchscreen is worth it for some readers. Right now, it’s the brightest laptop display we’ve tested. It can even be much brighter than an OLED TV’s display. The screen is so vivid that others pale in comparison. If you can afford this laptop, I promise you won’t be disappointed by its mesmerizing display.

Many of the third-party apps I use daily, such as those from Google (Docs, Drive, Sheets), work perfectly, but there is still concern about how third-party apps handle touch. This is a fair concern, as developers have to optimize their apps for the touchscreen.

Given that it's still early days for the PROLED, issues could arise. This is something I plan to cover in greater detail if enough folks complain about their favorite apps not working as intended on Apple’s touchscreen laptops.

Commenters on our TikTok videos featuring the reveal of the MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display and our hands-on impressions are just as critical and skeptical about the MacBook Pro’s touchscreen.

User N7 Drones flatly says: “I see zero reason to have a touchscreen on my MacBook Pro!” While tk42121 says that “OLED is fine, but a touchscreen is worthless.” Another user under the handle of Reirei gives scorn and praise, saying that “Apple always late on tech but when they do it 10x better than others.”

I found the comment from Smooth Operator particularly interesting. “Why wouldn’t they do the screen flip to make it easier to touch the screen?” This is something I brought up regarding how comfortable it is to use a touchscreen laptop. A 2-in-1 convertible design would certainly make it easier for taking notes or drawing, though you’d also need Apple Pencil support—a feature the PROLED currently lacks.

While many comments on our TikTok videos weren’t the most positive, they weren’t all negative. For instance, krisnahafara said, “finally the logo [is] back.” Some other posts shared the same sentiment, though user Fernando Callo said: “Please, don't bring back the light-up logo to the rest of the lineup.” Guess they’re not a fan!

It shouldn’t be surprising that Apple’s first touchscreen laptop isn’t being universally praised.

While I think the MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display is the best laptop I’ve ever tested, its steep price point is hard to stomach for all but the most hardcore tech enthusiasts with deep pockets. I also think it’s fair to say that Apple is late to the touchscreen laptop party, even with the seamless integration of that technology.

This is an ongoing discussion, so let us know what you think about the MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display. Are you interested, or is the price keeping you away? Sound off below!

#3372. 'Mike Hammer' Star Stacy Keach Dead at 85

Tony Award nominee Stacy Keach has died at age 85.

Keach passed away Tuesday at his home in Poland ... according to his wife Małgosia Tomassi.

Tomassi said in a statement Keach died "after a long and difficult battle with a serious heart condition and heart failure."

Keach rose to fame in the '60s after getting his start on Broadway before pivoting to film in the '70s -- starring alongside Faye Dunaway in "Doc."

He is perhaps most known for his recurring television role as Mike Hammer in multiple TV series including "Mickey Spillane's Mike Hammer" and "The New Mike Hammer."

The prolific actor racked up more than 200 credits across movies and television during his six-decade career.

Stacy came from an accomplished family in Hollywood -- with his dad Stacy Keach Sr. being an iconic Western star and his brother James Keach being a filmmaker and actor.

#3371. Conor Oberst Will Play a Cave and a Haunted Hotel on His First Solo Tour Since 2019

Conor Oberst has announced a 2027 North American tour, which will mark his first solo headlining trek in eight years.

The 49-date “An Alleged Evening With Conor Oberst” tour will find the singer-songwriter traveling around the West Coast, Midwest, and the South. (While there aren’t any northeast dates on the itinerary now, more shows are expected to be announced.) The trek will kick off  Feb. 19 at Liberty Hall in Lawrence, Kansas, and will wrap with two nights, May 14 and 15, at the Stanley Hotel in Estes Park, Colorado.

While Oberst will primarily play theaters on the tour, there are some particularly unique shows on the schedule. The Stanley Hotel, for instance, is the famous haunted hotel that inspired The Shining. On April 22, Oberst will play La Rosa, a converted Benedictine monastery in Tucson, Arizona on April 22. And on March 19, Oberst will perform at the Caverns, a literal cave in Pelham, Tennessee.

Tickets for all shows will go on sale this Friday, Nov. 13, starting at 10 a.m. local time. Full information is available on Oberst’s website.

“An Alleged Evening With Conor Oberst” will be the singer-songwriter’s first solo headlining tour since 2019, when he was still promoting his most recent solo LP, 2017’s Salutations. (That year, he also toured extensively with Phoebe Bridgers as Better Oblivion Community Center.) After that, Oberst launched a run of residency-style shows in 2024, while also playing some shows with Bright Eyes. #3370. This Low-Profile Roborock Vacuum and Mop Is $500 Off Ahead of Black Friday

Pradershika Sharma is a tech deals writer for Lifehacker. She has a Master’s degree in English Literature, a B.Ed., and a TESOL certification. She has been writing professionally since 2018, creating product reviews, affiliate articles, and search ads for global clients while working with Rubix Agency and Cognizant. Previously, she spent a year teaching English at the junior high level.An avid reader since childhood, Pradershika's idea of extreme sports is staying up to read “just one more chapter.” She lives in India.

The Roborock Qrevo Edge 2 robot vacuum and mop is down to $799.99 from $1,299.99 in an early Black Friday deal, saving you $500 and bringing it to its lowest price to date, according to price trackers. Much of its appeal comes from a slim 3.1-inch profile that lets it reach under beds, sofas, and other low furniture where taller robot vacuums often can’t fit. It manages this with a feature Roborock calls RetractSense, which checks the clearance as the robot approaches a tight gap and lowers the laser navigation tower into the body, leaving a camera with a 100-degree field of view to guide it underneath.

Beyond its low profile, the Qrevo Edge 2 pairs 25,000Pa of suction with a split DuoDivide main brush that guides hair toward the suction opening, so long strands and pet fur are less likely to end up wound around the roller. Edges get extra attention too, since its FlexiArm Arc side brush reaches out into corners while its mop module swivels to get closer to walls, with the two mop pads spinning at 200 RPM as they work. It also adjusts its cleaning based on whether it encounters dry or wet dirt, boosting suction for dust and lifting its main brush over spills. For all that adaptability on the floor, getting between rooms can be trickier—the robot lacks an adjustable chassis to lift itself over obstacles, so it can struggle with thresholds higher than 0.8 inches.

Once a cleaning run wraps up, most of the upkeep happens at the dock, which washes and dries the mop pads and empties dust into a bag rated for up to 65 days. That said, its onboard water tank is relatively small at 2.3 fluid ounces, potentially requiring extra trips to the dock during larger mopping jobs. There's also no dedicated cleaning solution tank, meaning you'll have to add approved cleaning additives manually to the fresh water. The rest of the fine-tuning happens in the Roborock app, where you can set cleaning schedules, adjust suction power and water flow, and choose how the robot handles carpets.

In short, yes, Black Friday still offers discounts that can be rare throughout the rest of the year. If there’s something you want to buy, or you’re shopping for gifts, it’s a good time to look for discounts on what you need, especially tech sales, home improvement supplies, and fitness tech. Of course, if you need to save money, the best way to save is not to buy anything.

Black Friday sales officially begin Friday, Nov. 27, 2026, and run throughout “Cyber Week,” the five-day period that runs from Thanksgiving through Cyber Monday,  November 30, 2026. But Black Friday and Cyber Monday dates have expanded as retailers compete for customers. You can get the same Black Friday sales early, and we expect sales to wind down by Dec. 2, 2026.

Yes, Amazon has Black Friday sales, but prices aren’t always what they seem. Use a price tracker to make sure you’re getting the best deal, or refer to guides like our live blog that use price trackers for you. And if you have an Amazon Prime membership, make the most of it.

#3369. Indie App Spotlight: ‘CueFlip’ automatically turns the page for your sheet music

Welcome to Indie App Spotlight. This is a weekly 9to5Mac series where we showcase the latest apps in the indie app world. If you’re a developer and would like your app featured, get in contact.

If you find yourself playing an instrument with sheet music, flipping the page often requires you to stop playing to turn the page. CueFlip solves that. You can teach it how you play a song, then it can turn the page for you whilst listening.

CueFlip doesn’t just assume how it should turn the page, you can explicitly teach it how to. That starts with either a live rehearsal, or a recording you can share with it. Then, you mark the turns.

CueFlip also has a built in dictionary, where you can see certain notes on a page so you can learn how the composer meant to play them, rather than needing to guess them. Many times, these terms will be in other languages, but CueFlip offers built in translation with up to 13 languages. CueFlip covers over 20,000 terms, and it can pull terms from scanned scores as well.

Lastly, CueFlip has a neat little feature with Face ID. If you wink with your right eye, you can manually turn a page forward, and if you wink with your left eye, it’ll go backwards. Similarly, CueFlip also works with manual Bluetooth page turners in addition to the automatic turning, in case you need it.

Here’s why 15 year old classical guitarist Yuze Pan from Beijing decided to build CueFlip:

I play in the Primal Guitar Quartet, and page turns kept breaking up our rehearsals. Paper means taking a hand off the strings, a pedal or a wink is one more thing to remember in the middle of a phrase, and timed turns can’t follow a performer who speeds up and slows down. My first attempt, in 2025, didn’t work. In May 2026 I started again, this time by reading the research on audio alignment, and brought every new build to the quartet’s daily rehearsals.

CueFlip is available for free on the App Store for iPhone and iPad users running iOS and iPadOS 16.4 and later. The free version includes PDFs with annotations and automatic page turning for one score, whereas Pro unlocks unlimited page turning, the music dictionary, wink to turn pages, and much more for $4.99/month and $29.99/year.

The Barista Express is one of our highest-rated all-in-one espresso machines for a reason

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

If I were buying my first espresso machine, I would probably get one with a built-in grinder. Actually, my first-ever home espresso machine — the De'Longhi La Specialista Opera — had a built-in grinder. I recommend that new home baristas think about a bean-to-cup for a few reasons: it's less kitchen clutter and less confusing for newbies.

I always recommend the Breville Barista Express — this bean-to-cup is one of our highest-rated all-in-one espresso machines thanks to its reliability, PID controller, powerful steam wand, and ease of use. It's definitely one of the best espresso machines on the market — even in 2026. Yes, this machine first released in 2011, which just goes to show how great it is.

Right now, the Barista Express is $499 at Amazon — the same price as Breville's Bambino Plus (with no grinder), so if you think about it, you're technically getting that grinder for free. Although you can get cheaper grinders and espresso machines, I would personally grab this bean-to-cup.

At $499, the Breville Barista Express is the same price as Breville's bestselling Bambino Plus — which means you get the Express's grinder technically for free. This model, like other Brevilles, has a PID controller (water temperature controller) and a powerful steam wand.

Let's do some coffee math. I'm going to work out how mcuh it would cost me to buy an espresso machine and a separate grinder versus how much the Breville Barista Express costs. Spoiler alert: you can get a machine + separate grinder for less than $499.

Breville Barista Express, $499 (right now)

As you can see, the cheapest grinder I'd recommend for espresso is the Casabrews Tornado. While I only gave this a 3-star rating in my review due to its somewhat inconsistent grind, my parents got this grinder and love it. I think if you're a more casual coffee drinker, this will be more than enough.

I also recommend the Breville Dose Control Pro, which has a lot of haters online, but it's a perfectly fine grinder for $149. It's more uniform than the Casabrews model and even has a light-up screen.

There's also the Baratza Encore ESP and Baratza Encore ESP Pro. Baratza is actually owned by Breville, and Breville uses these grinders in its espresso machines, so your Barista Express has a Baratza grinder built in. I'd recommend the ESP over the ESP Pro as the latter is a little too pricey for my liking.

Now, these examples are all the cheapest you can get. Unfortunately, decent espresso machines and coffee grinders don't really go below $150 each, so the cheapest you're looking at is $300.

If you're looking for an easy, one-way ticket to coffeeville, the Barista Express on sale is your best bet. I would be wary about buying it full price ($699), but right now, at just $499, it's a no-brainer.

I don't flat-out recommend buying an espresso machine with a built-in grinder if you want to "nerd out" over coffee. You might be better off with a standalone grinder in that case as you'll be able to customize the grind better. However, then you need more space for two products and more time to get used to two products.

Don't even get me started on four-figure automatic machines like the Philips 8000 Series — I'd skip them in a heartbeat.

Which kind of barista are you? Are you a coffee nerd, or do you want the easiest machine possible? If you're the latter, go for the Barista Express. If you're the former, check out the Breville Bambino Plus and one of the best coffee grinders.

#3365. Chromagraph Camera is exactly the camera app I’ve been looking for on iPhone

Last week, movie director Rian Johnson announced a surprise new camera app for iPhone that reimagines what a smartphone photo should look like. Many people would agree that Apple’s iPhone photos are a tad bit overprocessed.

iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone Duo introduced a new film texture option, but in my view, it’s a bit too exaggerated. Chromagraph Camera, on the other hand, feels pretty perfect.

Attempts have been made to improve iPhone photos for years, but they all feel a little bit too heavy, in my view. Most camera apps for iPhone require you to dial settings in. While that can be appropriate for certain settings, I ultimately want my iPhone to just be a point and shoot experience. If I wanted the perfect photo, I’d be using my camera.

That said, iPhone photos just don’t look super excellent out of the box. It’s not a limitation of hardware. If you take a RAW iPhone photo and edit it yourself, you can actually get surprisingly good results. Apple’s camera app just has poor defaults.

When Apple introduced the film grain feature on iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone Duo, I was actually quite interested in it. It was certainly my favorite camera feature of the phone when I briefly tried out the iPhone 18 Pro. For some reason though, the film look just feels a bit exaggerated on iPhone Duo.

Apps like Adobe’s Project Indigo have gotten really close in terms of look, but the fact that there’s so much time spent post-processing means it’s often inconvenient. I’ve also had a few instances of losing photos because the app closed in the background while it was still processing the photo.

When Chromagraph Camera was announced, I was quite interested. I paid the $12.99, and I’ve been happy with the results. I tweeted some of my sample photos when I just got the app, and it’s been well worth it.

$12.99 may be a higher starting price, but if you really want an iPhone camera app that just takes good looking photos without a lot of hassle, it works really well.

The 75-inch Hisense U6SF Pro has dropped to $747.97 from $1,399.99 ahead of Amazon’s Black Friday sale—bringing it to its lowest price to date, according to price trackers. For a budget set, the U6 Pro gets a lot right when it comes to picture quality—its high peak brightness helps it hold up during a sunny afternoon in a living room with big windows, so a daytime football game or cooking show won’t look washed out, while its excellent contrast and effective local dimming keep dark scenes looking deep when you settle in for a movie at night. When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

I don't know about you, but I am constantly hitting my token usage limits at the worst times. And it seems like whichever model I use, I get stuck much sooner than anticipated. Although AI coding assistants promise to take the hard work out of programming, it seems like the catch is that paying $20 a month doesn't mean you can keep coding for as long as you want. Unlike ChatGPT's unlimited free chatting, coding limitations are actually pretty strict.

Because I was so tired of hitting the wall, I decided to compare which subscription offers better value, particularly for someone who codes regularly but doesn't want to pay $200 a month.

Rather than burn through two subscriptions with unexpected coding challenges, I compared the companies' published usage policies, pricing and available independent research.

What I found is that neither company guarantees a fixed number of coding tasks for $20, and a major change coming to ChatGPT could make that decision even more important. Here's a closer look.

On paper, the subscriptions look very similar. ChatGPT Plus costs $20 per month and includes Codex alongside the regular ChatGPT experience. Claude Pro also costs $20 per month and provides access to Claude Code alongside Claude's chatbot.

Both subscriptions impose 5-hour usage limits and weekly allowances. The key difference is how those allowances work and how clearly users can estimate their remaining usage.

OpenAI publishes estimated message ranges for Codex models, while Anthropic explains that Claude's limits depend on factors including conversation length, model selection and task complexity. In other words, Anthropic remains completely vague about how and when you'll hit your limit.

Sign up to the Tom's AI Guide weekly newsletter summing up all the biggest AI news you need to know. Plus, analysis from our AI editors and tips on how to use the latest AI tools!

Neither 5-hour limit means that much time of uninterrupted coding. You can use up your allowance before the window ends, which I have done nearly every day since subscribing.

One advantage Codex has is that OpenAI publishes estimated usage ranges for different models. I have found the company's current usage documentation helpful. Knowing what to expect is at least a starting point. From this, I have surmised that ChatGPT Plus users can expect approximately 5 to 45 local messages using GPT-6 Astra within a 5-hour window. Knowing this has helped me manage my token budget much better. For example, switching to GPT-6.1 Sol increases that estimated range to 15 to 160 messages, while GPT-6 Luna has an estimated range of 350 to 3,000 messages. Clearly, this is an enormous difference depending on which model you choose.

There are caveats, of course. These aren't guaranteed message counts, and a complex task involving multiple steps can consume considerably more usage than a simple request. Cloud tasks may also use more allowance than local messages.

Still, publishing these ranges gives users a better starting point when deciding which model to use.

Claude Code operates under a similar system, but Anthropic doesn't provide an equivalent universal table of guaranteed coding tasks for its $20 Pro subscription.

Instead, it explains that usage depends on the model, conversation length, features and complexity of the work. That makes it difficult — nearly impossible — to predict exactly how far $20 will take you with either platform.

There's another factor worth considering: how many tokens the assistants consume while completing tasks. A Zapier comparison cites a February 2026 benchmark involving a Figma-to-code task.

What matters is how much useful work gets completed before the subscription limit is reached. I find myself hitting a limit much sooner with Claude Code.

According to the comparison, Claude Code consumed approximately 6.2 million tokens while Codex used 1.5 million, a difference of more than four times.

However, Claude Code reportedly produced a more thorough result. That matters because lower token consumption doesn't automatically mean better value if the output requires more work afterward.

More recent data also reinforces how differently developers use these tools. An analysis from whoburnedmore published recently examined reported usage across an opt-in group of 229 developers over 30 days.

Claude Code accounted for 57% of observed tokens, compared with 35% for Codex CLI.

But it's good to note that this wasn't a controlled test of identical coding tasks, and the sample wasn't representative of all developers. It shows how much the participating developers used each tool, not which assistant is more efficient.

The takeaway is that token counts alone aren't enough to declare a winner. What matters is how much useful work gets completed before the subscription limit is reached. In my experience, I find myself hitting a limit much sooner with Claude Code.

Here's something anyone considering either subscription should understand. With Claude Pro, usage is shared across Claude's chatbot and Claude Code. This means, if you've been spending the morning researching, analyzing documents or working through a long conversation in Claude, that activity can reduce the allowance available for coding.

Anthropic confirms that usage across its supported Claude interfaces contributes to the same limits.

Codex has a similar consideration, although the structure is changing. Currently, Codex and ChatGPT Work share an allowance, with five-hour and weekly limits applying to Plus users.

But OpenAI says that starting in December 2026, Plus, Pro and Business subscriptions will move toward a shared ChatGPT and Codex usage allowance.

The company says usage will be measured in tokens, with consumption depending on the model and task. Instant chat won't draw from that allowance.

Neither subscription necessarily leaves you without options when you run out of included usage. It's all too tempting to pay for additional usage credits, which switch eligible requests to pay-as-you-go pricing after the subscription allowance is exhausted. But hopefully by understanding what you get, you won't have to now.

The important point is that paying $20 doesn't guarantee unlimited coding with either tool.

If you routinely work on complex applications, large repositories or lengthy agent-driven tasks, you should expect to encounter limits sooner than someone who only occasionally asks for a bug fix.

After comparing the published policies and my own usage, I'd give Codex the edge for users who want more visibility into their usage, particularly because OpenAI provides estimated message ranges for its different models.

Claude Code remains a compelling choice, especially for users who prefer its workflow or consistently get better results from Claude's models. Personally, I find it the more effective option the majority of the time for my projects. But if your biggest concern is paying for an assistant that suddenly tells you to come back later, both products require some planning.

For occasional coding, either $20 subscription could be enough. For more intensive work, the models you select, the complexity of your projects and your other AI activity can have a major impact on how quickly those limits disappear.

#3361. ChatGPT's New GIF Generator Is Fun, but Won't Replace Us Humans (Yet)

Khamosh Pathak is a freelance tech journalist with over 13 years of experience writing online. An accounting graduate, he turned his interest in writing and technology into a career. He holds a specialization in user experience design from ISDI Parsons in Mumbai, where he sought to deepen his understanding of UX, consumer devices, and interplay between software and technology.

Khamosh has written thousands of how-tos and guides on every major platform (iOS, macOS, Android, and Windows). He got started writing how-tos and guides for Guiding Tech, where he also published several e-books. His work has also been seen at MakeUseOf, How-To Geek, and PCMag. He is truly passionate about brewing good coffee.

When it comes to generating AI images, both Gemini and ChatGPT do a passable job. In most cases, the results will look AI-generated, but they likely won’t have glaring spelling issues or missing limbs. Now, OpenAI is trying something new, introducing GIF support for ChatGPT. It's the company's first "moving images" feature since OpenAI shut down Sora, and while you can generate hyper-realistic videos in Gemini, this new ChatGPT feature is trying to fill in the gap, in a small way.

OpenAI is pitching the new feature as an animation tool, not exactly as a way to create looping videos—though that’s how I ended up using it. You give ChatGPT a prompt, as detailed as you can make it, and the chatbot produces a GIF in just a few seconds. You can start with your own drawings or images, too. ChatGPT uses sketches as the base for animations, though it can turn any still image into animated GIFs. Like other AI editing tools, you can edit it if ChatGPT didn't quite get it right: You can ask ChatGPT to make the GIF longer or shorter, remove certain objects, change the style, slow down transitions, among other edits.

AI art can be quite sterile, but I was surprised by how adding motion and animation to the mix makes generating images a lot more fun. Unlike traditional GIFs, which usually pull from existing video clips, you can turn anything you want into a GIF, which is especially cool if you're using your own art. In my testing, I found this to be the most rewarding part. It’s not always possible to one-shot a GIF with a single prompt. But after a few rounds of edits, I ended up creating some GIFs that I actually wanted to share in my WhatsApp groups.

That being said, I think human-made GIFs are still the gold standard here. For example, I asked ChatGPT to generate a video of someone brewing a pour-over, with a gooseneck kettle, showing the coffee blooming process. It did okay, but it’s nothing like actually making a pour-over. The kettle doesn’t move in circles, the water doesn’t rise evenly, there are no bubbles, and the steam is all over the place.

Compare that to the GIF below, which comes from a royalty-free video. Even though it’s a compressed, low-quality, and noisy GIF, it still shows the movement of the pour, the water rising, and even the bubbles. The details captured by a real video just aren’t there in ChatGPT GIFs. If that’s what you’re expecting, you will be disappointed. But I don't think that's the point of this feature anyway.

I found that ChatGPT excels when you’re making something fun, and you don’t look into the details too much. It pulled off a loop of a cat playing with a ball, and it was great at making a festive GIF for Diwali. It even made a GIF based on a photo. I asked it to create a fun promotional GIF for my JBL Bluetooth speakers, and it did the job quite well. At first, the transitions were too jarring, and the movement just made no sense. After some editing, though, I got it to a decent place.

Still, the main issue with ChatGPT GIFs is that complex movement and transitions aren’t nailed down. A hand shifts position weirdly between frames, and colors and objects appear out of nowhere. But if you can get over these issues, you can make some fun, lighthearted GIFs and memes to share with your friends on Instagram or WhatsApp.

#3360. Apple aiming to make Siri ‘more like an agent’ as soon as next year: report

Apple finally shipped its long awaited personalized Siri with iOS 27. The company lived up to its promises, and delivered on its hefty goals that it set out back in 2024.

That said, Siri still lacks in terms of proactively taking actions for you, a feature that many AI companies are actively working towards. Apple might come around on that next year, per Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman. The company is also experimenting with a new engineering pipeline that might make faster development possible.

In recent months, companies like Meta and SpaceXSI have gone all-in on new agentic AI interfaces that can carry out tasks for you. Muse and Grok Bot are agents that have their own virtual machines and can proactively handle tasks in the background for you, then deliver results.

Apple has a lot of potential to deliver in this space, especially given all of the frameworks they’ve built up over the years, like App Intents. With Apple, you hypothetically wouldn’t need to depend on as much computer-use ability, making certain tasks a lot less expensive.

According to Mark Gurman in his Power On newsletter, Apple could debut its own proactive version of Siri as soon as next year:

Dots, Muse and Grok can keep track of goals, determine what needs to happen next and continue pursuing objectives without the user initiating every individual step. Apple ultimately wants to go in this direction, I’m told, and I believe the company could make Siri more like an agent as early as next year — not that it has much of a choice, given current consumer and market demands.

It remains to be seen what Apple will ultimately ship here, but with the right execution, Apple certainly has high potential to compete in this space.

A major part of better execution is having a better process. According to Gurman, Apple is also giving engineers more time to code and explore, rather than spend as much time integrating features within the operating system.

Typically, each of these stages is four weeks. With the first cycle of iOS 28 development, Apple is allotting 6 weeks to coding and 2 weeks to integration. This change was likely driven by the massive advances in agentic coding tools in the past couple years:

For this cycle, though, Apple has done things differently for the M1 milestone. Instead of the normal split between two four-week efforts, Apple engineers were tasked with six weeks of coding, exploration and feature development, and then only two weeks of convergence. Employees say they like the change, indicating that it creates more time for coming up with ideas and exploring them before needing to lock things in.

This is Streamalikes, where you can find a curated list of recommendations to stream based on what you already like.

Following the dramatic conclusion of Cyberpunk: Edgerunners way back in 2022, the show has returned for a new season set in the megalopolis of Night City with a standalone story and a new cast of characters (by necessity).

Though the aesthetic and themes of cyberpunk have their roots in American science fiction of the 1970s and '80s, anime and manga of the '90s and beyond embraced the form and took it to entirely new places—so much so that a Japanese/Polish co-production of an adaptation of a video game from a Polish designer has taken its cues from a couple of decades' worth of great anime and cerebral sci-fi. Which is to say, if you're looking for more heady sci-fi series, these 10 are a good place to start.

An iconic, effortlessly cool genre classic, Cowboy Bebop is one of the undisputed GOATs of anime, blending western, noir, and crime genres and setting the resultant mash to a killer soundtrack of old-school jazz (which serves much the same purpose as Cyberpunk's propulsive electronic grooves). The title's "cowboys" are bounty hunters in a near-future in which humans have been forced to colonize the solar system after Earth became uninhabitable. Different settings, but both shows offer up ragtag crews with highly dubious fates. Former hitman Spike Spiegel leads his crew on one nearly disastrous mission after another, their standalone adventures all building to a thoroughly memorable climax. Stream Cowboy Bebop on Crunchyroll or buy it from Prime Video.

This one's set in 22nd-century Japan, with a slick Blade Runner-esque aesthetic and a setup reminiscent of Minority Report. Here, technology exists to measure intentions, so crimes can be stopped before they’ve occurred, at which point the “criminals” are placed into psychological treatment (à la A Clockwork Orange)—or subject to summary execution because their threat potential is too high. That ability to predict behavior bleeds over into every aspect of life: careers and even relationships are determined in large part by the same systems that sniff out criminal intent. Obviously, this is all perfectly fine, and there’s no potential for abuse or miscalculation whatsoever...though there are a couple of warning signs. The first involves a new Enforcer who becomes a potential murderer himself when he miscalculates the extent of a criminal’s potential to do wrong, and, even more significantly, the existence of a criminal mastermind who is somehow invisible to the tech, even as his criminal actions grow more and more elaborate. Stream Psycho-Pass on Prime Video and Crunchyroll.

Created by Tim Miller and with director David Fincher as an executive producer, this animated anthology series is a grab bag of wildly diverse offerings: Each episode is produced by a different international studio, with the only link between them being one of the three words in the show's title. One episode deals with robotic gladiator fights in dystopian London, another finds us under the threat of sentient yogurt, yet another finds an ambitious cat learning to make use of a family's robot helper. Its format dictates that no two episodes are going to have the same premise, but it shares with Cyberpunk an edgy sensibility and stories set in an apocalyptic future, albeit with a dark sense of humor—its four seasons offer up a mix of tech, sex, violence, and gorgeous animation. Stream Love, Death & Robots on Netflix.

One of several completely standalone spinoffs of the wildly influential 1995 film (itself based on the beloved manga series), Stand Alone Complex requires no prior knowledge. The style is largely the draw, as the series luxuriates in its fictional Nihama City setting, a world unto itself in a future Japan in which cybernetic people hack directly into the internet. Our sympathies are more with the authorities—in this case, Public Security Section 9, a cybercrime and antiterrorism police unit—than the cyber criminals, but the show approaches some of the same themes as Edgerunners with legit punk style. Stream Ghost in the Shell: Stand Alone Complex on Tubi and The Criterion Channel.

In this adaptation of the Richard K. Morgan cyberpunk classic of the same name, Joel Kinnaman and Anthony Mackie (yes, both of them) star as Takeshi "Tak" Kovacs. In this future megacity setting, human consciousness can be transferred between bodies. The tech is widely available, but only the wealthy can afford the backups and protections that make it a form of virtual immortality. Kovacs is a former soldier turned mercenary, revived from a backup after 200 years by Laurens Bancroft (James Purefoy), one of the wealthiest men alive. His motives for bringing the man back are shrouded in mystery, but he's giving Tak a chance to solve a very cold case: his own murder. Stream Altered Carbon on Netflix.

Another popular (and Emmy-winning) game adaptation, Arcane is based on League of Legends, a top-down actioner involving online opponents shooting lasers across a map. It doesn't sound like fodder for a show this impressive, but here we are. The League of Legends lore forms the backdrop for the show, but the pull is in the narrative involving two sisters caught up in the growing conflict between a utopian city and its oppressed underclass, without whom it couldn’t exist. The painted animation style is truly something special—not a stylistic match for Cyberpunk, but the two shows both go far above and beyond to create striking visual worlds. Stream Arcane on Netflix.

Vash the Stampede is a hunted outcast with a dark history that slowly comes to light over the course of the series. He’s got a reputation as a human wrecking ball, bringing destruction wherever he goes, and seemingly just for fun—but in reality he’s far more respectful of life than his pursuers. Still, cities evacuate at the mere possibility of his arrival, and a huge bounty sits on his head (no matter that the bounty hunters do far more damage than Vash). He and his friends—actually a couple of insurance agents—find themselves in a series of misadventures on the planet Gunsmoke, building to a final showdown that caps the series with finality. Visually, it’s probably one of the defining ‘90s shōnen-style action series, with elegantly choreographed gunfights that never get old. Tonally similar, Trigun also shares with Cyberpunk 2 the work of legendary composer Tsuneo Imahori, his music being crucial to both shows. Stream Trigun on Crunchyroll or buy it from Prime Video.

Another from animation studio Trigger, Darling in the Franxx leans heavily into the mecha sub-genre, set in a post-apocalypse where children are bred and indoctrinated into piloting the title's massive Franxx to defend the remnants of humanity. Adults are pretty much immortal, so the kids simply don't have any other utility. Two of these teens begin to develop romantic feelings for each other, potentially complicating their usefulness to society and leading to an explosive, bittersweet finale. Stream Darling in the Franxx on Crunchyroll or buy it from Prime Video.

What starts out as a relatively straightforward action show about space bounty hunters (the title's “Killjoys”) develops surprising depth over the course of its five seasons. As officially sanctioned Killjoys, the trio at the show’s heart (Hannah John-Kamen, Aaron Ashmore, and Luke Macfarlane) are bound to remain politically neutral at any cost. Initially, that’s a way to get them right into the heat of a fight, but as they develop ties of friendship and family in an exploited community, they come to understand the high cost of unchecked wealth and greed, and the ways in which neutrality always benefits the oppressors. The show’s creators make exceptionally good use of a limited budget and offer up some impressive queer rep along the way, a rarity in pop sci-fi. Stream Killjoys on Tubi or buy it from Prime Video and Apple TV.

Another great cyberpunk metropolis: here it's Kansai, an increasingly lawless city run by elite criminals known as Akudama. An ordinary girl, quite inadvertently, becomes caught up in a major planned heist and is forced to fake credentials as a master swindler in order to stay alive. Like Cyberpunk, the show tackles anti-authoritarian themes among a diverse crew of outsiders. Stream Akudama Drive on Cunrchyroll or buy it from Prime Video.

#3357. Report: John Ternus pushing Craig Federighi to speed up Apple software engineering

In the past few years, a major Apple story (especially in the age of AI) has been that the company isn’t moving fast enough in the space to keep up with competitors. According to Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman, new Apple CEO John Ternus is reportedly pushing on software chief Craig Federighi to ‘accelerate’ Apple’s roadmap for software.

At the moment, there’s no indication that Apple’s well known software SVP Craig Federighi will be leaving the company. In fact, Craig has made it a very low priority of his to develop a succession plan in any sense, per Mark Gurman. That said, Ternus still wants to see change in how Craig Federighi thinks about Apple’s software strategy:

In recent weeks, Ternus held a closed-door meeting with Craig Federighi, who became Apple’s AI czar following last year’s dismissal of its former AI leader. Desiring more and frustrated by what he sees as a reluctance to embrace AI with the same urgency as competitors, Ternus pushed his software chief to accelerate the company’s road map and move quickly beyond merely making necessary improvements to Siri.

A large part of Federighi’s approach has been how hands-on he is, resulting in his viewpoint shaping how Apple’s software development goes to a large extent. That’s left team members feeling that they have ‘limited influence’ over what happens:

Federighi is known for taking an especially hands-on role in meetings and major decisions, with some employees describing a management style that can leave little room for competing ideas to gain traction. He is also known for vigorously debating opposing viewpoints, using his command of technical details and ability to argue his position to push back against proposals he disagrees with. That approach has at times frustrated members of the software engineering and design teams, some of whom believe they have limited influence over the direction of products.

Another part is that Federighi reportedly only plans for a 12-18 month timeframe, versus the years-long roadmaps used in hardware engineering. These are some of the gaps that Apple may want to bridge in the coming years.

Separately, Vision Pro and Siri AI leader Mike Rockwell is still seriously considering stepping down. He’s currently vice president of Siri engineering:

The management concerns go beyond Federighi. Mike Rockwell, who created the Vision Pro headset in addition to leading the development of Siri AI, continues to seriously consider stepping down. That could mean leaving his role as vice president of Siri engineering — or Apple altogether — next year. Such a move would be a major blow, given his role in bringing the new Siri to market after an embarrassing two-year delay.

In the same report, Gurman also reported that Apple is experimenting with a new development pipeline, giving engineers 50% more time to code and explore more, and spend less time on integration, as coding agents have improved.

It remains to be seen what else might change at Apple to enable faster development timelines, though it seems likely that Craig Federighi may have to release his ‘firm grip’ on the software engineering org, and instead allow some other leaders to blossom and act on their own accord.

The Amazon Alexa Photo Frame uses AI to smartly curate your huge collection of pictures, and present them in an orderly fashion. However, it's best for those who have an Amazon Prime subscription.

Why you can trust Tom's Guide Our writers and editors spend hours analyzing and reviewing products, services, and apps to help find what's best for you. Find out more about how we test, analyze, and rate.

I never thought a gadget would make me want to cry — least of all one from Amazon.

After unboxing and setting up the Alexa Photo Frame, one of the first images it displayed was a black-and-white picture of my father, who has been deceased for 16 years, feeding a squirrel.

I remember having the photo stored digitally somewhere, but it’s been several years since I last saw it. But the Alexa Photo Frame pulled it up, and juxtaposed it next to another picture of a squirrel clinging to a screen door. The Photo Frame also wasted no time digging up scores of photos of our family cat, who also died around the same time as my dad.

It was a very emotional first few minutes with this device.

But the Alexa Photo Frame also went on to deliver photos of my child playing, vacations and other happy occasions, which brought back more pleasant emotions.

While I have plenty of criticisms of AI and its use, this is one instance where I feel like it delivers something positive, and makes this one of the best photo frames I’ve ever used.

This might be stating the obvious, but if you want to get the most out of the Alexa Photo Frame, you’re going to need either an Alexa+ ($19/month) or an Amazon Prime subscription ($149/year), so you can use Amazon’s AI to its fullest.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

The Alexa Photo Frame uses Amazon’s AI in one of the smartest ways yet. It combs through your entire library of images, and then pulls them up based on criteria such as the time of year, themes, objects, and events.

So, during the fall, you might be served pictures of pumpkins and leaves falling; in the summer, it might be photos of you at the beach.

While the Alexa Photo Frame only works in landscape mode, it does a clever thing with all the portrait photos in your library. If, for instance, you have photos of your child blowing out birthday candles over the years, it might put two of those images side by side, to show you the changes over the years. The photos of my dad and the squirrel was one example; another was two pictures of my kid potty training.

Or, if you want to go the more direct route, you can also ask Alexa to “show me photos of cats and kids,” and it will create a curated slideshow of all those images from your library.

Alexa+ isn’t perfect; when I asked it to create a slideshow of my daughter, a number of the pictures were of old ladies and some other random kids. However, it’s smart enough so that when one of these images showed up, I said “Alexa, that’s not my daughter,” and it went back through and edited the collection so those mismatched photos were no longer there.

Of course, the Photo Frame can act as a smart speaker. You definitely wouldn’t want to use it to play music, but you can use Alexa+ on it as you would any other Amazon smart speaker. And, should you not want it to listen, you can press the microphone mute button on the back.

Another trick with the Alexa Photo Frame is that you can attach short audio files to pictures, so if you’re gifting it to your parents, you can add a photo of your kids around a Christmas tree, with a voice note wishing them happy holidays. You have to tap the photo on the screen to hear the note, so it’s a nice extra, but I’m not sure how much it will be used.

Specs-wise, the Alexa Photo Frame isn’t the most impressive when compared to the best digital photo frames. The $229 Aura Aspen, for example, has a 12-inch screen with a much higher resolution of 1600 x 1200, and can be set up in portrait or landscape mode. The Lexar Pexar has an even crisper 2000 x 1200 display, and costs even less, at $179. And, the Alexa Photo Frame can’t play videos, which also make up a good portion of my phone’s library.

But neither makes curating all your photos as effortless — or as ingenious — as what Amazon does with Alexa+. For me, it’s solved the biggest issue I’ve had with digital photo frames and my massive photo library. How do I rediscover those old photos, and how do I make them show up on my photo frame without spending hours combing through everything?

#3355. Five Smartwatch Heart Rate Zone Hacks Every Runner Should Know

If you've spent any time in or around running culture over the last few years, you've undoubtedly encountered someone preaching the gospel of Zone 2 cardio. Legend has it that easy, conversational effort cardio—also known as cardio that takes your heart rate into "Zone 2"—is the secret to unlocking everything from a bigger aerobic engine to faster race times and even a longer life.

To train by heart rate, you aim to keep your heart rate in the "zone" that gives you the desired workout. The catch is that Zone 2 is easy to get wrong, especially since no one can agree on what it actually means.  Your smartwatch can show you your heart rate, but many recreational runners will still drift into a “gray zone” that's too fast to be truly easy, and too slow to give them a real workout. If you're struggling to hit Zone 2 consistently, there are a few smartwatch hacks that can help.

Pace can be a distraction during easy runs, especially considering all the different variables that affect your effort, like hills, humidity, and general fatigue. A 9:30 mile might be Zone 2 on a flat, cool day and Zone 4 on a hot, hilly one.

Dig into your watch's activity settings (on Garmin, it's Activity > Data Screens; on Apple Watch, the Workout app's metrics layout; on Coros, Polar, and Suunto, similar menus) and put live heart rate zone front and center, ideally as a zone number or colored gauge rather than just a raw bpm figure (though this assumes these zones are accurate—more on that below).

Create an alert when your heart rate goes above or below a target range, delivered as a vibration pattern, a beep, or both. Set the alert for the upper boundary of Zone 2, and you've essentially hired a mini coach who taps you on the wrist whenever you get overzealous. Whenever you hear or feel that buzz, you’ll know you need to ease into a slower jog until your heart rate settles.

Instead of free-running and checking your numbers afterward, build structured workouts that carry the targets for you. In Garmin Connect, TrainingPeaks, Apple's Custom Workout feature, Coros Training Hub, or similar platforms, you can create sessions like "10-minute warm-up in Zone 1, 40 minutes in Zone 2, 5-minute cooldown" and sync them straight to your watch.

During the run, your watch displays the current step, the target range, and whether you're above, below, or in the pocket. Many will automatically advance between intervals and alert you when it's time to shift gears.

Heart rate-based intervals, like 4 x 4 minutes in Zone 4 with Zone 1 recovery, where you don't have to do mental math or check the clock.

Progressive long runs that start in Zone 2 and finish in Zone 3.

Hill repeats, where pace is meaningless but effort matters.

Most watches calculate default zones using a generic formula like 220 minus your age, which can be off by 10 to 20 beats for any given individual. If your zones are wrong, your Zone 2 training isn't Zone 2 training.

Here’s how to fix your watch’s heart rate zones:

Find your true max heart rate. The informal way is to just notice what number you see on your watch when you can no longer speak comfortably; the more formal way is this treadmill test. You can also look through your recent hard efforts, like races, hill repeats, or all-out intervals, and see the highest sustained heart rate you've recorded.

Use lactate threshold heart rate instead. Many watches can estimate this automatically after a few hard efforts, and zones built from threshold tend to be more personalized than ones built from max.

Customize the boundaries. Dive into the heart rate zone settings and input your own numbers. Some runners prefer the "MAF" method (180 minus age, with adjustments) for aerobic base building, and most watches let you set that as a custom range.

Recheck every few months. Fitness changes, and so do your zones.

A screen crowded with cadence, vertical oscillation, ground contact time, running power, and lap pace is a recipe for second-guessing.

Create a dedicated Zone 2 data screen with just two or three fields: current heart rate zone, elapsed time, and maybe distance. Turn off auto-scroll so it doesn't flip to a screen full of numbers you don't need. If your watch supports multiple activity profiles, make a separate "Easy Run" profile with this stripped-down layout and keep a different profile for tempo days and races.

A chest strap (or a forearm or upper-arm optical band) is generally more accurate and responsive than the wrist-based sensor on your watch. For heart rate training, where a few beats can mean the difference between Zone 2 and Zone 3, I recommend buying one. This COOSPO heart rate monitor is one of my favorites, and it's only $31.99.

The bottom line: Your smartwatch can make heart rate training far easier, but only if you set it up to support you rather than overwhelm you.

#3354. macOS 27.3 could change how you grant AI agents Full Disk Access, here’s how

In its blog post, Apple announced that apps will require “very explicit user action” to have Full Disk Access on your Mac. At the time of the announcement, Apple didn’t make it super clear what that would actually mean. Now, we have an idea of what’s to come.

Code sifter pdfu posted on X that Apple will be getting rid of a clever loophole that developers could use to make it easier for users to enable Full Disk Access. In current versions of macOS, if an app requests a file that would require Full Disk Access, the system denies the request and logs the app as an option in the Settings app for enabling Full Disk Access.

At that point, developers often prompt users to open that section of the Settings app and flip the toggle.

Starting as soon as macOS 27.3, apps that request files outside of the permission scope will no longer get logged, and as a result, won’t show up as an option for quickly toggling Full Disk Access, per leaker pdfu.

macOS 27.3 starts implementing changes to Full Disk Access (FDA). Here’s what ‘very explicit user action’ may mean.When an app tries to read a protected file without FDA, macOS doesn’t prompt the user to grant permission. Instead, it automatically denies access and records that… https://t.co/zjUuEh7EIb

At the moment, developers can still request users to drag an app icon to the Settings panel to enable Full Disk Access, even once the feature flag for the aforementioned change is enabled. To me, it still doesn’t quite feel like you’ll need “very explicit user action” to enable Full Disk Access, but it’s possible this will change in the future. This is all still in development.

All in all, I’m not fully convinced that this solves the core problem. Developers are requesting Full Disk Access because they’d like to tap into things like iMessage, and there hasn’t been a better way of doing so. As long as that demand is there, users will likely still have to enable Full Disk Access and risk all sorts of other data, just so they can share their texts with an agent.

Granted, pdfu also mentions the idea of Private Folders, which could potentially allow users to grant scoped access to just the iMessage database folder. It’s unclear if that’ll be possible since there’s little detail on how Private Folders will work. If that’s the case, then hopefully Full Disk Access can stop being the default permission you have to provide for any personal data.

#3352. These Early Black Friday Ring Camera Deals Start at $24.99

If you’re browsing home security options, Ring has one of the best early Black Friday deals that should be on your radar. Right now, you can add an indoor camera and another one at your front door for less than $65. The Ring Indoor Cam 2K is 58% off at $24.99 (originally $59.99), while the Ring Battery Doorbell 2K is 60% off at $39.99 (originally $99.99)—both at their lowest-ever price.

Both offer features like 2K video and two-way talk, but the indoor cam is the simpler purchase if you mainly want to check on a pet or kids and see what’s happening near an entrance. It plugs into an outlet, so there’s no battery to recharge, and its low-light color video helps preserve detail when lights are off or dimmed. However, since it’s a fixed-view camera, keep in mind that you’ll need to position it carefully.

The Battery Doorbell is the better pick if alerting you to visitors, deliveries, and potential intruders is your priority. It has a 140-degree horizontal and vertical field of view that provides head-to-toe framing, plus up to 6x zoom for better detail. You can install it without wiring, though you’ll need to recharge its built-in battery. It also requires a 2.4GHz wifi network.

The main catch with both devices is the ongoing subscription cost: Live viewing, two-way talk, and basic real-time notifications all work without a subscription, but reviewing saved footage requires a paid plan, starting at $4.99 per month or $49.99 annually for one device; coverage for multiple devices at one location starts at $9.99 monthly or $99.99 annually.

At these prices, the Ring Indoor Cam 2K is perfect for occasional live check-ins, while the Ring Battery Doorbell 2K is better suited to monitoring your front entrance. Buying both makes sense if you already have a Ring plan that covers extra devices.

#3349. Apple Won't Make a Small Phone so This Company Is Stepping In

Big smartphones have long been the norm. It seems many, if not most, of us prefer our smartphones to be akin to tiny tablets. Even Apple's smallest iPhone isn't that small, with a 6.1-inch display. (Compare that to the 5.4-inch iPhone mini it used to sell.) But just because a lot of us like it that way doesn't mean all of us do.

Despite what companies like Apple would lead you to believe, there are plenty of people out there who want their smartphones to be smaller. For some, the iPhone mini was perfect, featuring a design that most could use comfortably with one hand. While the sales might not have been steady enough for Apple to continue producing the mini line, anecdotally, I know quite a few people who would happily keep using iPhones this small, if only Apple would make more of them. Perhaps you know people like this too; maybe you're one of them.

While the rumor mill does not suggest that Apple plans to make a new iPhone mini, that doesn't mean the dream of the tiny smartphone is dead. Enter "Enough Phone," a new device with a humble goal: to create a "small, modern smartphone that's enough."

Enough Phone really does seem small. The company says its upcoming device is 133mm by 64mm, and less than 12mm thick. That's the equivalent of 5.24 inches by 2.52 inches, and less than 0.47 inches thick. It's remarkably similar to the iPhone 13 mini, at 5.18 by 2.53 inches, and 0.3 inches thick. While the Enough Phone might be a tad larger overall, and perhaps noticeably thicker, it's still reminiscent of that "mini" footprint.

The Enough Phone's 5.3-inch display isn't particularly modern, however. While we don't know the display type, we do know that it has a resolution of 1520 x 720, which may look less sharp to anyone coming from the 2340 x 1080 resolution of the iPhone 13 mini. I'd wager that most people interested in a device like this aren't looking for an ultra-sharp OLED display anyway, but it's worth noting here.

As for the Enough Phone's other specs, the company says it plans to pack in a 2.4GHz MediaTek Dimensity 7500 chip with 8GB of RAM, 128GB of built-in storage, though you can expand that with a microSD card (something you don't see on many smartphones these days). The current plan is to ship with a single 50MP Sony IMX766 rear camera, and a 32MP selfie cam, which would be amongst the highest-resolution front-facing cameras on any smartphone. It supports 5G, Wi-Fi 6, and eSIM, with the option to use a physical SIM as well.

Enough is also aiming to make its smartphone more repairable than the competition. While smartphone OEMs have made slight improvements to repairability in recent years, few phones are made to be opened up by the user, and their components replaced. While Enough Phone isn't fully modular, it is designed with easy-to-open screws, and comes with a fully replaceable 3,500 mAh battery. Combined with promised software support through 2032, Enough says this device "should last you into the next decade."

Now, all of these specs are targets, as the phone is currently in the prototype stage. Enough says that final details may change "slightly" during testing. I would at least hope that the dimensions, particularly the screen size, remain the same by launch. What will likely stay the same, however, are the ringtones: Enough says they hired composer Brian Squillance of LAANDS to produce the jingles for its phone, which is a neat touch.

Unfortunately for Apple fans, however, Enough Phone isn't an iPhone. That said, it doesn't have to be an Android phone, either. While you can buy the phone with Android 17 installed, you can also choose to run OdysseyOS, a minimalist "de-Googled" operating system made by SLEKE. Enough says OdysseyOS is meant for "intentional phone use," which might appeal to anyone looking for a phone that's "dumb" as well as small.

Of course, neither operating system is iOS. Unfortunately for Apple users, the only true iPhone options here are to continue using an old iPhone mini, which Apple does still support, or to opt for an iPhone 17e, the smallest iPhone the company currently makes. It's pretty easy to find a used and refurbished iPhone 13 mini for reasonable price; but while they can still run the latest version of iOS, you won't be able to take advantage of all of Apple's newest features. Plus, while there's no telling how long Apple plans to support the 13 line for, it won't support it forever—by iOS 28 or iOS 29, your phone might lose support entirely.

If the promise of a modern mini smartphone entices you, you can back the Enough Phone on Kickstarter today. While the company's $399 "Super Early Bird" reward is already sold out, as of this article, the "Early Bird" reward is still up. That reward costs $449, and includes a glass screen protector pre-installed, a protective case, a USB-C cable, a USB-C to 3.5mm headphone adapter, a hex screwdriver, and green "Founders' Edition" backplate screws. Enough says that the retail price for its phone will be $599 after the campaign, so you can save $150 by backing the phone today—if you're serious about small phones. The Enough Phone is slated for a May 2027 launch.

#3348. Apple staff accused of signing up customers to subscriptions without consent; company responds

Repair technician turned consumer rights advocate Louis Rossmann recently accused Apple store staff of signing up customers to the company’s services subscriptions without their consent.

Apple has not yet commented, but has taken two steps indicating that the company takes the accusations seriously …

Rossmann is a repair technician who specializes in component-level logic board repairs and data recovery. He later became a key figure in advocating for right-to-repair legislation, which Apple initially opposed and later backed.

In a recent video, he claimed that some Apple store staff were signing up customers to trials of paid services subscriptions without their informed consent. Targets set by Apple are said to have encouraged the practice.

Customers accepting the offer of a personalized shopping experience could be shown the free trials of Apple services available to them based on their recent purchases. For example, buying an iPhone currently entitles you to a free three-month subscription to Apple TV. However, these trials automatically start debiting your payment method if you don’t cancel them before they end.

Staff were instructed to show these offers to customers and were allegedly set a 40% sign-up target, which Apple tracked as a performance metric. Crucially, the offers are shown on the employee’s device rather than on the customer’s phone. A store member told Rossman that some staff were hitting the Accept button without properly obtaining consent from customers in order to hit their target.

When I asked whether they’d seen a specialist press Agree with their own eyes, they answered “Yes, I saw some specialists press on behalf of the customer. So, they are hitting agree. They are signing the customer up to something without actually having the customer click okay, hit okay, or provide express consent.”

The store member also claimed that staff were describing the offer as a gift, which further disguised the fact that it would turn into a paid recurring subscription unless canceled.

At the time of writing, Apple has not responded directly to the accusations, but in a follow-up video yesterday Rossman cites a staff member describing the company’s response.

He says a memo was read out in the morning meeting stating that only customers could press the Accept button, and internal systems indicate Apple is no longer grading staff on the signup metric.

We have reached out to Apple for comment and will update with any response.

The new legal action from plaintiff Dinora Cabria Amaya follows two other similar lawsuits that were filed against Jenner last April. While the new 20-page complaint obtained by Rolling Stone doesn’t accuse Jenner of first-hand mistreatment, it suggests the reality star played a role in decisions regarding scheduling, supervision, and allegedly unlawful wage practices.

Cabria Amaya, who started working for Jenner in March 2025, claims she was denied overtime and subjected to a hostile work environment. She also claims she suffered multiple workplace injuries that were mishandled. On Sept. 4, 2025, for example, Cabria Amaya says she was cleaning a laundry room when an unsecured can of pepper spray allegedly discharged directly into her face and eyes, causing “severe burning and vision problems” that she reported to her supervisor via text.

“Sorry to interrupt you, I had an accident at work, someone left pepper spray and took off safety,” she wrote in the message, according to the lawsuit. Her manager allegedly responded, “thanks for letting us know.” Cabria Amaya says she was asked to fill out a report and give it to Jenner’s security before visiting a doctor. She later received no accommodations when she reported experiencing “significant eye pain, blurred vision, headaches, burning, irritation, and sensitivity” that affected her performance, her lawsuit filed in Los Angeles County Superior Court by attorney Della Shaker claims.

“The more plaintiff complained that she was hurt, the harder defendants made her job,” the lawsuit states. Cabria Amaya and her lawyer claim she was sometimes “confined in a room because defendant Jenner did not want to see her,” and that her “repeated reports of ongoing pain” were never taken seriously or accommodated. Instagram has a number of protections for the accounts of teenagers, but it’s very common for teens to lie about their age in order to circumvent them. Back in May, the company said it would be using AI-powered age estimation to address the problem.

The company said it would use the tool to block users aged below 13, and to ensure that those in the 13 to 17 range had limited accounts. Teen accounts have age-appropriate feeds, limitations on who can interact with them, and default time management tools – though things didn’t get off to the best of starts when a 12-year-old kid fooled it by using an eyebrow pencil to draw a fake moustache.

Meta today says that it is rolling out the (hopefully now eyebrow pencil-proof) tech globally.

We use AI technology to find people we suspect to be teens, even if they use an adult birthday, and place them in Teen Account protections. Since first introducing this technology, we’ve been placing more teens in age-appropriate protections and are encouraged by the results. Based on that success, today we’re expanding this technology globally.

The company goes on to say that parents in the US will receive a notification sometime this month, with a link to a video and an article about the system.

This month, parents in the United States will begin to see an in-feed video on Instagram explaining our approach to ensuring their teens are in age-appropriate protections. The video will link to an article, written by Larry Magid, internet safety advocate and President and CEO of ConnectSafely, detailing our multi-layered age assurance approach, which includes keeping children under 13 off our platforms, providing age appropriate experiences for teens, and informing parents about ways they can partner with us to ensure their teens provide the correct age online.

If you don’t want to wait, you can read the article here.

#3344. Atomically Thin Materials Significantly Shrink Qubits

MIT researchers use 2D materials for capacitors in quantum circuits in an effort to scale processors

Superconducting quantum processor and its microwave packaging.

Quantum computing is a devilishly complex technology, with many technical hurdles impacting its development. Of these challenges two critical issues stand out: miniaturization and qubit quality.

IBM has adopted the superconducting qubit road map of reaching a 1,121-qubit processor by 2023, leading to the expectation that 1,000 qubits with today’s qubit form factor is feasible. However, current approaches will require very large chips (50 millimeters on a side, or larger) at the scale of small wafers, or the use of chiplets on multichip modules. While this approach will work, the aim is to attain a better path toward scalability.

Now researchers at MIT have been able to both reduce the size of the qubits and done so in a way that reduces the interference that occurs between neighboring qubits. The MIT researchers have increased the number of superconducting qubits that can be added onto a device by a factor of 100.

“We are addressing both qubit miniaturization and quality,” said William Oliver, the director for the Center for Quantum Engineering at MIT. “Unlike conventional transistor scaling, where only the number really matters, for qubits, large numbers are not sufficient, they must also be high-performance. Sacrificing performance for qubit number is not a useful trade in quantum computing. They must go hand in hand.”

The key to this big increase in qubit density and reduction of interference comes down to the use of two-dimensional materials, in particular the 2D insulator hexagonal boron nitride (hBN). The MIT researchers demonstrated that a few atomic monolayers of hBN can be stacked to form the insulator in the capacitors of a superconducting qubit.

Just like other capacitors, the capacitors in these superconducting circuits take the form of a sandwich in which an insulator material is sandwiched between two metal plates. The big difference for these capacitors is that the superconducting circuits can operate only at extremely low temperatures—less than 0.02 degrees above absolute zero (-273.15 °C).

Superconducting qubits are measured at temperatures as low as 20 millikelvin in a dilution refrigerator.Nathan Fiske/MIT

In that environment, insulating materials that are available for the job, such as PE-CVD silicon oxide or silicon nitride, have quite a few defects that are too lossy for quantum computing applications. To get around these material shortcomings, most superconducting circuits use what are called coplanar capacitors. In these capacitors, the plates are positioned laterally to one another, rather than on top of one another.

As a result, the intrinsic silicon substrate below the plates and to a smaller degree the vacuum above the plates serve as the capacitor dielectric. Intrinsic silicon is chemically pure and therefore has few defects, and the large size dilutes the electric field at the plate interfaces, all of which leads to a low-loss capacitor. The lateral size of each plate in this open-face design ends up being quite large (typically 100 by 100 micrometers) in order to achieve the required capacitance.

In an effort to move away from the large lateral configuration, the MIT researchers embarked on a search for an insulator that has very few defects and is compatible with superconducting capacitor plates.

“We chose to study hBN because it is the most widely used insulator in 2D material research due to its cleanliness and chemical inertness,” said colead author Joel Wang, a research scientist in the Engineering Quantum Systems group of the MIT Research Laboratory for Electronics.

On either side of the hBN, the MIT researchers used the 2D superconducting material, niobium diselenide. One of the trickiest aspects of fabricating the capacitors was working with the niobium diselenide, which oxidizes in seconds when exposed to air, according to Wang. This necessitates that the assembly of the capacitor occur in a glove box filled with argon gas.

While this would seemingly complicate the scaling up of the production of these capacitors, Wang doesn’t regard this as a limiting factor.

“What determines the quality factor of the capacitor are the two interfaces between the two materials,” said Wang. “Once the sandwich is made, the two interfaces are “sealed” and we don’t see any noticeable degradation over time when exposed to the atmosphere.”

This lack of degradation is because around 90 percent of the electric field is contained within the sandwich structure, so the oxidation of the outer surface of the niobium diselenide does not play a significant role anymore. This ultimately makes the capacitor footprint much smaller, and it accounts for the reduction in cross talk between the neighboring qubits.

“The main challenge for scaling up the fabrication will be the wafer-scale growth of hBN and 2D superconductors like [niobium diselenide], and how one can do wafer-scale stacking of these films,” added Wang.

Wang believes that this research has shown 2D hBN to be a good insulator candidate for superconducting qubits. He says that the groundwork the MIT team has done will serve as a road map for using other hybrid 2D materials to build superconducting circuits.

Dexter Johnson is a contributing editor at IEEE Spectrum, with a focus on nanotechnology.
