The GMKtec Neo-X1 Pro delivers desktop-tier gaming performance and remarkably whisper-quiet acoustics in a compact 14.6-liter chassis. Its soldered mobile CPU and steep SFF price tag keep it from being an automatic purchase for everyone, but if you want high-end living room portability with room to swap your GPU down the road, it’s an impressive machine.

Impressive, near-silent gaming performance

Built-in carrying handles make it easy to move

Why you can trust Tom's Guide Our writers and editors spend hours analyzing and reviewing products, services, and apps to help find what's best for you. Find out more about how we test, analyze, and rate.

The GMKtec Neo-X1 Pro is a desktop gaming PC with a twist. Unlike other large, bulky desktops, it’s remarkably compact with a volume of 14.6 liters, making it even smaller than the HP Victus 15L.

Known for making some of the best mini PCs, the Neo-X1 Pro is GMKtec’s first-ever small form factor (SFF) gaming tower. To get its design this small without overheating, the company used a custom all-in-one liquid cooler paired with a high-end mobile AMD CPU. However, the Neo-X1 Pro still packs in a desktop-grade Nvidia RTX 5070 dedicated GPU.

I’ve been using the Neo-X1 Pro as my daily driver for both work and gaming for the past two months, and it has continued to impress me. From its compact design — complete with carrying handles — to its near-silent performance even under load, this gaming desktop certainly delivers. Just as if you built your own SFF PC, you are paying a premium for its more compact size.

My GMKtec Neo-X1 Pro review will help you decide if this is the best gaming PC for you or if it’s worth going with something with a slightly larger case for less.

2 x USB-A, 1 x USB-C, 1 x 3.5mm audio combo jack (front), 1 x HDMI 2.1, 1 x DisplayPort 1.4, 4 x USB-A, 1 x USB-C, 1 x 2.5 Gigabit Ethernet, 1 x 3.5mm audio jack (rear), 1 x HDMI 2.b, 3 x DisplayPort 2.1b (Nvidia RTX 5060 Ti)

2 x USB-A, 1 x USB-C, 1 x 3.5mm audio combo jack (front), 1 x HDMI 2.1, 1 x DisplayPort 1.4, 4 x USB-A, 1 x USB-C, 1 x 2.5 Gigabit Ethernet, 1 x 3.5mm audio jack (rear), 1 x HDMI 2.1b, 3x DisplayPort 2.1b (Nvidia RTX 5070)

The GMKtec Neo-X1 Pro delivers a stellar PC gaming experience without taking up your entire desk. Games look and run great thanks to its Nvidia RTX 5070 GPU, while the custom all-in-one liquid cooler keeps acoustics so quiet that I often forgot there was a high-powered gaming rig humming right next to my monitor.

At 13.78 × 6.50 × 10.43 inches, the Neo-X1 Pro is an impressively compact gaming PC. In fact, it’s roughly the same size as having two Xbox Series X consoles side by side on your desk with a pair of carrying handles bolted on top.

Inside its well-packed box, you’ll find the PC itself alongside a standard power cord, an HDMI 2.1 cable, and a pair of antennas. Once you unbox the Neo-X1 Pro, all you have to do is screw on those antennas and plug it in to get started.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

On the front of the Neo-X1 Pro, next to its signature green power button, there’s a 3.5mm headphone/microphone combo jack, two USB-A ports, and a USB-C port. I really liked having two full-sized ports up front for the 2.4 GHz USB dongles for my controller and other peripherals.

Around the back, the power receptacle for its 850W SFX power supply sits at the very top alongside the motherboard connections. Here, you get four USB-A ports, a 2.5 Gigabit Ethernet port, a single USB-C port, an HDMI 2.1 port, a DisplayPort 1.4 connection, another set of audio jacks, and the gold connectors for the Wi-Fi antennas. Right underneath them, the Neo-X1 Pro’s RTX 5070 provides a single HDMI 2.1b port along with three DisplayPort 2.1b connections.

You’ll probably want to position the Neo-X1 Pro on the right side of your desk. The left side panel is perforated, giving you a glimpse at its internal components, including the RTX 5070 from Zotac. On the right side of the case, circular cutouts bring cool air in alongside another strip of ventilation holes at the bottom. While you won’t see it when you’re sitting down, I really like how the top of the case features GMKtec’s iconic neon green all the way across.

From the instant I had it set up and powered on, the Neo-X1 Pro surprised me: all I could hear was a faint hum in the background. Even under load while running demanding games, it remained whisper-quiet compared to gaming desktops I’ve built and other pre-builts I’ve tested in the past.

With an AMD Ryzen 9 9955HX3D processor and 64GB of DDR5 memory, my review unit handled my everyday workload — which consists of multiple Chrome windows with dozens of open tabs and light photo editing in GIMP — with ease. Considering the generous system RAM alongside the 12GB of VRAM on the included RTX 5070, the Neo-X1 Pro could easily pull double duty running large local AI models just as comfortably as it plays games.

Despite relying on mobile silicon, the Neo-X1 Pro held its own in our benchmark tests against the HP Omen Max 45L we reviewed recently. While its single-core and multi-core Geekbench scores fell slightly behind the desktop-class 9950X3D inside the Omen Max 45L, it pulled ahead in our SSD speed test (which measures transfer speeds moving a 25GB file). At just over two minutes, the Neo-X1 Pro’s HandBrake encoding time (converting a 4K video file down to 1080p) was also impressive, trailing the massive Omen tower by only 21 seconds.

If you’re looking for a rig that is compact yet potent and don't want the headache of hunting down SFF components or managing tight clearances yourself, the Neo-X1 Pro presents a capable prebuilt alternative to building your own mini-ITX battle station.

Speaking of gaming, the Neo-X1 Pro delivers and then some thanks to its full-size RTX 5070 from Zotac. All of the games I tried looked great and played smoothly, though you’ll likely need to lower the resolution or enable Nvidia’s DLSS if you want to push native 4K or beyond.

To put the Neo-X1 Pro to the test, I downloaded and installed Resident Evil Requiem. Exploring the Wrenwood Hotel as Grace Ashcroft was downright creepy, but navigating the Wrenwood City Streets as Leon showed me what this rig is capable of. From the rain beading off Leon’s leather jacket to the blinding vehicle headlights cutting through the foggy street while fighting off the newly infected, the entire opening sequence looked stunning on my 4K monitor.

In benchmark tests at our lab, the Neo-X1 Pro frequently surpassed triple-digit frame rates at 1080p without DLSS enabled, and even at 4K, Forza Horizon 6 reached 96 fps on High settings. For heavier titles like Black Myth: Wukong, dropping down to Medium settings brought it within striking distance of 60 fps in 4K (51 fps). While you'll need to make occasional graphic tweaks on demanding games, the Neo-X1 Pro handles recent titles at stable frame rates without breaking a sweat.

After running through tests on a standard 4K display, I brought the desktop into my office to see how it handled gaming on the Innocn E49M1R. Even at a massive 5120 × 1440 resolution, performance stayed rock solid in Red Dead Redemption 2 without any visible tearing or stuttering. That said, finding space for the Neo-X1 Pro on a desk alongside a flat, 49-inch super ultrawide monitor is definitely a challenge.

With those two handles on top, moving the Neo-X1 Pro from room to room was an absolute breeze. Whether you want to hook it up to the living room TV for big-screen couch gaming or haul it over to a friend’s place for a weekend session, this SFF PC is well-suited for quick transport. However, I’d be hesitant about carrying it onto a flight given the effort it takes to safely break down and secure its internal components.

The Neo-X1 Pro is a quiet, cool, and capable gaming PC. However, like most small form factor machines, it comes with classic trade-offs: cramped internals that make upgrades tricky, and a noticeable price premium for shrinking everything down.

In order to see what keeps the Neo-X1 Pro running so quietly, I decided to open it up. To do so, I just had to remove two screws on the side panel, and the whole thing slid off as you’d expect with a traditional desktop PC.

Under the hood, you can see the Zotac RTX 5070 running along the bottom, complete with a built-in support bracket to prevent GPU sag over time. Above it sits GMKtec’s custom AIO liquid cooler, which commands the lion's share of the case’s 14.6-liter interior.

Much like the Minisforum G1 Pro I reviewed, you have to work around and partially dismantle the cooling assembly if you want to upgrade the Neo-X1 Pro’s RAM or storage. If you choose to brave the process, you could swap out the pre-installed dual-channel 32GB sticks for two 48GB sticks to reach a whopping 96GB of memory. There is also an unused secondary M.2 NVMe slot, meaning you can configure up to 16TB of high-speed SSD storage overall.

While its CPU is soldered permanently to the motherboard, the Neo-X1 Pro holds one massive advantage over the G1 Pro. Since it relies on a standard rear expansion bracket and ships with an 850W SFX power supply, you can actually upgrade GMKtec’s rig down the line with a standard off-the-shelf GPU — provided the replacement card is under 310 mm (12.2 inches) in length and sticks to a strict dual-slot design.

Given the potent hardware GMKtec packed into the Neo-X1 Pro, you likely won’t need to upgrade anytime soon. Even so, while working inside this dense chassis will be second nature to seasoned SFF builders, beginners will find servicing and upgrading components noticeably daunting.

In the world of desktop PCs, opting for a compact case over a standard mid-tower almost always commands a higher price tag. From specialized SFX power supplies and custom low-profile coolers to the dense chassis engineering itself, small form factor PCs occupy an expensive niche.

Although the base Neo-X1 and its more potent sibling, the Neo-X1 Pro, originally started at $2,099 and $2,899 respectively at launch, their prices have crept up like most electronics as a result of RAMaggedon. The standard Neo-X1 now costs roughly what the Pro originally did, and the Neo-X1 Pro can reach as high as $3,699 at full price (though it is frequently discounted to $3,199).

Even accounting for parts being more expensive across the board, that isn’t pocket change. You could likely assemble a comparable full-sized DIY gaming desktop for less cash, but you would be trading convenience for the cable-routing headaches, tight thermal clearances, and endless compatibility checks that come with building an SFF machine yourself.

The best way to frame the Neo-X1 Pro is to compare it to Valve’s Steam Machine. While Valve’s compact cube targets couch play with modest, fixed internals, the Neo-X1 Pro brings far more graphical muscle and actual hardware modularity to the living room. You are undoubtedly paying a steep premium for its compact 14.6-liter footprint, but in return, you get couch-friendly portability with enough breathing room to upgrade your RAM, storage and even graphics card down the road.

The GMKtec Neo-X1 Pro is a capable, quiet, and compact gaming PC that delivers desktop-class performance in a much smaller footprint than traditional towers. The top-mounted handles make it easy to haul between rooms or take to a friend’s place, while the full-sized desktop RTX 5070 GPU handles modern AAA titles with ease.

While the AMD Ryzen 9 9955HX3D is permanently soldered to the motherboard, it holds its own remarkably well, delivering near-desktop speeds despite its mobile roots. The interior layout can look intimidating for beginners, but the chassis is straightforward to open, leaving room for future storage and graphics upgrades.

Make no mistake: this compact rig demands a steep price premium, and patient, experienced builders could assemble a comparable DIY machine for less. Even so, if you have the budget and want heavy-hitting gaming performance without surrendering half your desk, the Neo-X1 Pro delivers on its promises. It stands as an impressive, well-engineered debut for GMKtec's push beyond the mini PC space.

#3327. I Played Wendy's RPG, and It's Actually Worth It for the Free Food

November is a huge month for video games. Nintendo dropped its remake of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time for the Switch 2 last week, and the long-awaited Grand Theft Auto VI is right around the corner. But the game we've been waiting for most of all also launched this month: WendyQuest, the free RPG from Wendy's. (No, this is not a joke.)

Despite the absurdity of a hamburger chain making a full video game (complete with Wendy's-themed puns), the thing is, this game is pretty solid—even if it is a promotion at the end of the day. WendyQuest's main purpose is to offer customers coupons they can use toward purchases in real life, though it's a bit of a commitment. It took me just under an hour of gameplay before I earned my first coupon, and Wendy's says it takes roughly 15 hours to beat. All that to say, this is a pretty unique marketing campaign.

I was surprised booting up WendyQuest on my iPhone. This doesn't necessarily feel like a thrown-together product. On the flip side, the production quality is quite high. The music is solid and very much traditionally RPG; there are even three save slots, in case you plan to return to this RPG again and again.

There's even a story, albeit cheesy (no pun intended): As the game explains, the "Four Great Spirits of Flavor" created Savoria, "a food-rich paradise." All was well until Mech Corp, led by the evil Dr. MechBorg, built robots to take over Savoria. The plot is far from compelling, and the writing can be a little over the top, but hey, I'll give them credit: They thought through a full story here.

You play as Wendy, the "representation of true culinary excellence and taste as dictated by the four ancient spirits of flavor." Wendy (or The Wendy, as some call her) is tasked with saving the world, traveling between villages and picking up new characters along the way. The game world even has "real" Wendy's locations you can visit. These act like inns and shops in other RPGs, giving you a chance to heal while also buying equipment.

Like other RPGs, WendyQuest uses turn-based combat. You have to charge up your attacks, but stop before they hit 100%, or you'll miss. (It took me a while to master the timing.) I'm pretty impressed with how challenging some of these battles can be, though you are quickly given the option of an amulet that gives you a huge leg-up in combat. You don't have to take it, but it makes fights easier if you're only in it for the coupons. That, combined with the spatulas the game encourages you to buy, lets you mow down enemies. You can also utilize your companions here: "Frygor," for example, can either attack enemies with a barrage of fries, or use those fries to build a shield to protect you.

While there are tons of enemies to fight, the key baddies are the "mechs." There are five in total, and after you defeat each, you get a coupon. Spoiler alert: The first mech drops the "Fry Stone," which nets you a coupon for a free order of medium fries—though you need to buy something in tandem, as well as use the Wendy's app. While I stopped my gaming here for this article, the other four coupons are:

Free biscuit or croissant (I didn't even know Wendy's sold biscuits and croissants)

Again, it's wild that WendyQuest has a 10+ hour campaign, with over 1,000 lines of dialogue to boot. I'm not sure this is a game I'm going to see through to the end, but I'll admit, it's a fun marketing approach from Wendy's. Sure, they could have run a promotion in the Wendy's app to give people coupons, but instead, they built an entire RPG. I respect it. You can download the game for iOS, Android, or Steam.

#3326. Apple Music launches ‘Best of 2026’ content, reveals Artist of the Year

Apple Music has launched new playlists and curated content for the ‘Best of 2026’ and also revealed its new Artist of the Year.

The year is coming to a close, and Apple Music’s editorial teams have published a variety of playlists and other content to wrap the year.

Inside the ‘New’ tab in Apple Music, you’ll find ‘Best of 2026’ versions of popular playlists like Rap Life, R&B Now, A-List Pop, Today’s Country, and more.

Additionally, Apple Music has named its Artist of the Year for 2026: Olivia Dean

Olivia Dean was announced today as Apple Music’s Artist of the Year, recognizing her undeniable leap to stardom in what’s been the defining feel-good music story of 2026. She is the first UK artist to receive this honor.

Olivia’s late 2025 album, The Art of Loving, truly broke through this year. Her hit “Man I Need” has charted on Apple Music’s Daily Top 100 every day since first appearing on August 29, 2025. In addition to selling out her global tour, she won a GRAMMY for Best New Artist and four BRIT Awards, including Artist of the Year. In fall 2025, Olivia opened for Sabrina Carpenter at Madison Square Garden, in New York City. Less than a year later, she returned for her own four-night residency and followed up with a six-night sold-out run at The O2 Arena, in London.

Like Apple has done for the last several years, it’s gifting Dean with a physical that includes a custom Apple silicon wafer “suspended between a polished sheet of glass, and a machined and anodized aluminum body.”

Last year’s Artist of the Year was Tyler, The Creator, in 2024 it was Billie Eilish, and in 2023 Taylor Swift won the prize.

Apple Music is available for $11.99/month, or you can get it as part of the Apple One bundle.

#3325. It's Your Last Chance to Get This Early Black Friday Deal on a 65-inch Samsung OLED TV

This is one of those rare opportunities that don't come very often in the consumer tech space: Right now, you can get a 65-inch OLED TV from Samsung for $899.99 (originally $2,099.99) from Best Buy during its early Black Friday sale. This 2026 TV is considered an "entry-level" OLED, but it's still an incredible value for the money and the lowest price it has ever reached, according to price-tracking tools. There's a catch, though: The deal expires tonight, Nov. 10, at 1:00 a.m. EST.

If you've never owned an OLED before, there are some things you need to know to make sure it's a good fit for you. Perhaps most important is that they don't get as bright as QLEDs or LED TVs. Since this is an entry-level OLED, it likewise won't reach as high brightness as more premium OLEDs. This makes it less suitable for viewing in very bright rooms. There is also no Dolby Vision support (though there is support for HDR10+, HDR10, and HLG). But that is where the cons stop.

The S84H offers the near-perfect black levels you can expect from any OLED TV, making the contrast look incredible. The pixel-level dimming and viewing angles are also on par with other high-end OLEDs, and this TV also offers great features for gamers, including 4K support at 120Hz across all of its HDMI 2.1 ports, a variable refresh rate, and auto low latency mode.

OLED TVs are not normally priced under $1,000, especially newer models like this one. It's an incredible value for the money. The last time a deal like this popped up was in February, and before that, last Christmas, but for the 2025 version of this TV. If you're reading this after the sale has ended, you'll likely see the deal again in the future—perhaps even next month.

#3323. The Best Early Black Friday Deals on DeWalt, Milwaukee, and Ryobi Cordless Power Tools

Becca Lewis is home maintenance writer who aims to foster confidence in and inspire DIY enthusiasts at all skill levels.

Becca attended Southern Connecticut State University, where she studied technical theater and design. She has a background in carpentry and fabrication and has worked in specialty shops, using a wide variety of tools and materials, for more than 20 years.

Becca has also written for Angi, where she specializes in creating guides for DIY, home maintenance, and renovations, and she indulges her love of sci-fi and fantasy by writing about entertainment and science for Giant Freakin Robot. She serves on the board of the Good Junk Sanctuary in Portland, Oregon, focusing on community engagement in the DIY and reuse space.

If you have a DIY enthusiast on your list—or if you just want some new tools for your own projects—Black Friday sales are a good time to snag low prices on quality tools. Lots of big box stores are looking to thin out their inventory and make room for next year’s upgrades, so in addition to encouraging a holiday rush, retailers are motivated to price things to move. If you know what to look for, you can get up to 65% off on trusted brands. Here are a few of the best deals out there right now.

If you’re building a new cordless tool set, or updating your battery system, getting a cordless tool set can save you some money because these combos usually include batteries and a charger, which can be the most expensive part of your tool set. Here are a few of the best early Black Friday deals on cordless tool sets.

The Ryobi 6-tool 18-volt combo set is on sale for $199, 33% off its regular price at Home Depot. The set comes with a drill, an impact driver, a circular saw, a sawzall, an oscillating multi-tool, a work light, a 1.5-amp-hour battery, a 4-amp-hour battery, a charger, and a tool bag. This is a good deal on a trusted home tool brand.

The Ryobi 18-volt drill and driver set is on sale for $99, 34% off its usual price at Home Depot. The set comes with a drill, an impact driver, two 1.5-amp-hour batteries, a charger, and a tool bag. This is a great starter set because it has the first two tools you need for a cordless kit and it comes with batteries so you can expand your set for cheaper as you develop your skills.

The Ryobi 4-tool, 4-volt project set is on sale for $99, 61% off its typical price at Home Depot. This set comes with a rotary tool, a project light, a glue pen, a mini drill, two rechargeable batteries, a charging cable, a set of starter rotary bits, and three glue sticks. This set is handy for DIY projects that require fine detail, like wood carving, craft projects, or framing pictures.

The DeWalt drill and driver combo set is on sale for $149, 38% off its regular price on Amazon. This set includes a drill, an impact driver, 2 1.5-amp-hour batteries, a charger, and a tool bag. This is a good deal on a trusted brand for drills and drivers, and a good start for a cordless DIY tool set.

If you have a cordless tool set already and you want to expand your kit, or if you have a DIYer in your life who already has a particular brand of battery and you want to get them something they can use, a single tool deal can be just the thing.

The DeWalt 20-volt compact drill/driver is on sale at Home Depot for $99, 45% off its usual price. This tool comes with a 20-volt, 2-amp-hour battery and a charger, so it’s ready to use out of the box. It’s a good first tool for a set.

The Milwaukee 18-volt impact wrench is on sale at Home Depot for $199, 68% off its typical price. This tool comes with two 5-amp-hour batteries and a charger, so it’s ready to use out of the box. This is a good tool for driving bolts through tough materials and for automotive projects.

The DeWalt 20-volt oscillating multi-tool is on sale at Home Depot for $99, 50% off its regular price. This tool comes with a 2-amp-hour battery and a charger, so it's ready to use out of the box. This is one of the most versatile cordless tools, allowing you to cut a wide range of materials and use a sanding attachment to do finishing work as well.

The Milwaukee 18-volt tire inflator kit is on sale at Home Depot for $199, 65% off its usual price. This tool comes with two 5-amp-hour batteries and a charger, so it’s ready to go right out of the box. This is an excellent addition to your emergency roadside tool set because you can use it to inflate a car tire with the charged 18-volt batteries.

The Makita 18-volt cordless electric 2-inch brad nailer is on sale on Amazon for $324, 38% off its regular price. This is a tool-only deal, so you’ll need a Makita 18-volt battery and charger to use it. This is a good tool for attaching trim or paneling.

#3321. The Nintendo Switch 2 Is Actually on Sale Ahead of Black Friday

If you've been patiently waiting for the right moment to pull the trigger on the Nintendo Switch 2 after the recent release of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time, this might be a good time to do so. Woot is selling a Nintendo Switch 2 for $469 (originally $499). The discount comes as the first major discount since the Sept. 1 price hike.

The new console is an upgrade in every way, as you can read in our full review of the Nintendo Switch 2. The ergonomics and design have improved, making it much better to hold and look at. The battery life has also improved, now with about 180 minutes of handheld playtime before the juice runs out.

A big plus is that the Switch 2 is backwards-compatible: You can play your old Switch games on it. Some Switch games have the ability to upgrade to the Switch 2 Edition by buying that game's upgrade pack. This is especially worth it for games like The Legend of Zelda: Tears of the Kingdom, which will look better on the Switch 2.

#3319. Update Your iPhone to Prevent People From Seeing iMessages They Shouldn't

Has this ever happened to you? You add someone new to an iMessage group chat, and wonder, "Huh, can they see any of the messages from before they were added?" The answer to that question is supposed to be "no." By design, new iMessage group chat members are only privy to texts that arrive after they were added. When they join, it's essentially a blank slate, as if you just created the group for the first time. At least, that's how it's intended to work.

As it turns out, there's a bug with iMessage that may allow new group chat members to see texts from before they were added to the chat. That's a problem, and not just for the iPhone users out there talking smack about people before inviting them to join the group chat. It means iMessage, and Apple's platforms in general, aren't working like they're supposed to be. You don't have to be talking behind people's backs to not want new members seeing existing chats. Maybe you're planning a surprise party for someone, and add them to the group once everyone's in on the plan; maybe the texts in the chat aren't relevant to the current group, and the person joining simply does not need to access them.

That's not all: There exists another security flaw that could allow remote hackers to join an iMessage group and receive new messages. You might add a new user to a group chat and inadvertently invite them to read all existing messages, while at the same time being attacked by a bad actor who can then intercept all future messages. Not good.

Luckily, there's currently a fix for these problems. Apple patched (and revealed) the bugs, along with seven other security flaws, with a series of software updates on Monday for iPhone, iPad, Mac, Apple Watch, and Vision Pro. Not all of the updates include patches for these two iMessage flaws—specifically, some of the updates for older Apple devices. But the rest, including iOS 27.2.1, macOS 27.2.1, macOS 26.7.3, macOS 15.8.3, watchOS 27.2.1, and visionOS 27.2.1, include the iMessage patches.

Each update includes its own list of patches, but, for this article, I'll take a look at the nine patches in iOS 27.2.1. You'll find the two iMessage bugs, plus seven other patches, in the list below:

AirPlay: Impact: An attacker in Bluetooth range may be able to bypass the rate limit on pairing code attempts. Description: A logic issue was addressed with improved state management. CVE-2026-113968: Apple

App Intents: Impact: An app may be able to access sensitive user data. Description: An authorization issue was addressed with improved state management. CVE-2026-113963: László Várady

Bluetooth: Impact: An attacker in Bluetooth range may be able to corrupt process memory. Description: A use-after-free issue was addressed with improved memory management. CVE-2026-113970: Apple

brotli: Impact: Processing maliciously crafted input may lead to memory corruption. Description: An out-of-bounds write issue was addressed with improved input validation. CVE-2026-111497

CoreUtils: Impact: A malicious Bluetooth device may be able to establish a pairing without user interaction. Description: This issue was addressed with improved checks. CVE-2026-113965: Apple

CoreUtils: Impact: An attacker in Bluetooth range may be able to bypass the rate limit on pairing code attempts and pair with a device without user interaction. Description: A logic issue was addressed with improved state management. CVE-2026-113964: an anonymous researcher

Messages: Impact: A remote attacker may be able to join an iMessage group chat and receive its messages. Description: An authorization issue was addressed with improved validation. CVE-2026-113961: an anonymous researcher

Messages: Impact: A user added to an iMessage group may be able to access messages sent before they joined. Description: This issue was addressed by removing the vulnerable code. CVE-2026-113960: an anonymous researcher

Rapportd: Impact: An attacker on the same network may be able to bypass the rate limit on AirPlay pairing code attempts. Description: A logic issue was addressed with improved state management. CVE-2026-113969: Apple

For a full accounting of the patches included in the other security updates, check out Apple's official security releases site.

To install Apple's latest security updates, you'll simply need to update your device as you usually do. On iPhone, iPad, Apple Watch, and Vision Pro, head to Settings > General > Software Update; on Mac, go to System Settings > General > Software Update. Here, follow the on-screen instructions to download and install the latest version of your device's software.

#3317. Hasan Piker’s $72.5M Defamation Suit Over Lynching Quotes Should Be Tossed Out, Scott Jennings Says; Statements Are “Literally True,” CNN Contributor Claims

Executive Editor, Legal, Labor & Politics

The midterm elections are over, but the multi-million defamation battle between Hasan Piker and Scott Jennings over what the progressive streamer said about lynching in America 2026, and the context in which he said it, is just getting started.

In a 15-page response to Piker’s $72.5 million lawsuit of last month, the conservative CNN contributor does whatever the double-down version of doubling-down is. To that, Jennings wants a federal judge throw Piker’s action out.

“The Court should dismiss the complaint for failure to state a claim upon which relief can be granted,” says the motion placed in the DC court docket Tuesday by Jennings’ attorneys Benjamin Chew, Nina Franco and Peter Baumhart. Watch on Deadline Related Stories News House Blocks Effort To Impeach Secretary Of Defense Pete Hegseth News Pete Hegseth Defends Tenure, Lavishes Praise On Trump & Calls Impeachment Threat "Sabotage" In Rare Pentagon Press Conference

Describing the politically influential Piker as “an internet personality and provocateur” who “makes his living courting controversy—to put it mildly,” the filing doesn’t note the irony of such a statement coming from reps for MAGAman Jennings, who many would say does exactly the same thing, and did it in this case. In fact, Piker’s Meier Watkins Phillips Pusch lawyers alleging in their initial October 27 filing that regular CNN NewsNight panelist Jennings is himself all about “political controversy.”

It is in that vein that Piker’s attorneys particularly pinpoint Jennings’ August 11 podcast where they assert the Trump press secretary auditioning pundit “falsely told his listeners that Mr. Piker had a ‘plan of returning our country to lynchings …then he falsely told his social media followers that Mr. Piker says the USA should resume lynchings against black people.'”

Which is why Piker, who has subsequently said he may pursue similar methods against others he believes take his words out of context, wants $72.5 million bucks from Jennings.

Seeking an oral argument ASAP before Judge Amit P. Mehta on today’s motion, Jennings team admit that “in August 2026, Mr. Jennings played on his political discussion program a video of Mr. Piker saying these things.” Noting the video in question was off a social media site attributed to “Senate Republicans,” they describe that “Mr. Piker now alleges that “the video—which Mr. Jennings did not create, edit, or manipulate and had no reason to doubt based on the source of the video and the totality of what is known about Mr. Piker’s general worldview—was defamatory, as was Mr. Jennings’s accompanying commentary.”

Basically, Jennings’ argument is that on the August 11 edition of The Scott Jennings Show he took at face value what he saw and heard Piker utter on the supposedly GOP connected feed.

Instead, declaring there is no “actual malice” alleged by Piker, out of that commentary, Jennings’ attorneys in today’s parsed response say “the statements in the NRSC Video are literally true—there is and can be no dispute that Mr. Piker said what he is on camera saying.” They add: “The dispute is over whether those statements reflect what he really meant, which is not sufficiently verifiable to be actionable as defamation. On either or both of these independently sufficient grounds, Mr. Piker’s claims should be dismissed.”

Again, Jennings appears to be affirming that whether or not he disagrees or agrees with Piker politically, Piker is a fella who commonly says outrageous things and what was on this video tracked with that stance — hence his reaction.

Maintaining “the first factor—’the common usage or meaning of the allegedly defamatory words’—is somewhat ill-fitted to the facts of this case,” the lawyers for the former Mitch McConnell aide propose “the proper focus of the analysis is therefore not on the words Mr. Jennings used, but on the premise implicit in his commentary that Mr. Piker’s statements were genuine. That premise, because it is unspoken, necessarily does not admit of the sort of linguistic analysis called for by the first factor.”

One factor to consider: even as this charged suit moves through the courts, Jennings continues to appear on CNN talking politics.

#3316. This AirPods Feature Fixed My Biggest Problem With Listening to Podcasts to Fall Asleep

We're highlighting the small changes—from useful new gadgets, to fresh productivity techniques, to efficient hacks—that are improving our lives on a weekly basis.

There's lots to recommend about podcasts (and lots of podcasts to recommend), but one of their biggest benefits—for me, anyway—has little to do with what a particular show is about or even who hosts it: They're great for dissociating. I often have a podcast playing to distract my anxious brain from whatever I'm worried about (which, in 2026, is usually slightly less than everything).

Any time I don't want to be alone with my thoughts (say, when commuting or doing mindless chores), I can put on a podcast and be entertained by a couple of goobers talking about movies rather than spinning my wheels about my son's middle school applications. And there's no time I want to disassociate from reality more than bedtime.

For years I've used podcasts as a non-pharmaceutical sleep aid, and few things are more effective at helping me drop off quickly. Unfortunately, for years this also meant that once I fell asleep, the podcast kept playing. I have my podcast app set to delete episodes once finished, so if it was a show I cared about, I'd need to do a lot of redownloading and scrubbing through to find where I left off—that is, until I upgraded my earbuds to the AirPods Pro 3.

The AirPods Pro 3 launched alongside iOS 26 in the fall of 2025 with flashy features like vastly improved noise cancellation, Live Translation, Heart Rate Sensing, and hearing health settings, all of them quite welcome on a set of $250 premium earbuds. But the best new AirPods feature was one I didn't even know about when I decided to upgrade my four-year-old Beats Fit Pro.

In the AirPods settings (accessible via your iPhone's Settings app), if you tap Audio & Routing and scroll down, you'll see an option to turn on a setting called Pause Media When Falling Asleep. I don't think I need to tell you what this setting does. I can tell you that it works great.

According to Apple, the feature works by sensing when you're drifting off using the earbuds' built-in accelerometer to track your movement (or lack thereof). Once your earbuds have determined that you're falling asleep, they will pause your audio for you. And it isn't just the 2025 AirPods Pro 3 that support it—it also works on the second-generation AirPods Pro as well as the AirPods 4 and the AirPods 5.

I'll admit that I don't really understand how the AirPods Pro 3 can tell I'm falling asleep versus just lying very still, but I've never had them pause accidentally during active listening. Conversely, whenever I go back to the podcast I was listening to the night before, I'll find that the audio paused within a minute or two of the last part I remember hearing.

The AirPods Pro 3 aren't the only earbuds with a feature like this, but you'll most often only find it in dedicated "sleep earbuds" designed specifically for the purpose. While many of those offer extra health features like the ability to track your sleep cycles, I'm not really interested in that (my Apple Watch does most of it, and I don't look at that data anyway). Pausing my audio when I'm asleep is really all I need, and the AirPods Pro 3 do it well enough that I don't need to bother with a pair of dedicated bedtime buds.

Clear pine needles from gravel without moving a single stone using three simple tool adjustments

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Few garden tasks feel more frustrating than trying to clear fallen pine needles from a gravel path or driveway. Standard metal rakes dig too deeply into loose chippings, scattering stones into the lawn and leaving you with heavy piles of mixed rock and debris to separate by hand.

Leaving them in place is not an option either, as damp needles quickly break down into acidic sludge that encourages weeds and turns paths slippery underfoot. The trick to lifting them quickly comes down to choosing the right tool and working with the natural weight difference between light needles and heavy stone.

It is tempting to leave a light scattering of needles where they land, but ignoring them quickly turns a low-maintenance gravel path into an ongoing headache.

As pine needles decompose, they break down into a fine, nutrient-rich organic sediment that sifts down into the voids between your stones, creating an ideal seedbed for persistent weeds to take root.

Left to sit through wet weather, that matted needle layer traps moisture, speeds up moss and algae growth, and transforms crisp aggregate into a slick slip hazard underfoot, all while leaching dark tannins that can permanently stain decorative light-coloured stone.

Here are three simple ways to lift fallen needles cleanly away while leaving every pebble where it belongs.

Rigid garden rakes with solid steel teeth are designed to dig into soil, making them the absolute worst choice for loose aggregate.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

Swapping to a lightweight, flexible spring-wire leaf rake or an adjustable metal fan rake gives you far better control over surface contact.

Hold the rake handle at a low, shallow angle and use light, skimming sweeps across the top layer rather than pulling downwards into the stones. The flexible tines gently flex over individual pebbles, gathering the tangled needle carpet on top while leaving the heavier rocks undisturbed beneath.

If manual raking still catches too many small chippings, a leaf blower offers a far faster and cleaner shortcut when used correctly. The secret lies in keeping the airflow moving horizontally rather than pointing the nozzle straight down into the gravel bed.

Stand several paces back, tilt the blower tip so it skims just above the stones, and use steady side-to-side sweeping motions on a low or medium throttle.

The high-velocity air easily catches the large surface area of dry needles, rolling them into manageable windrows along the edge of the path without kicking up a single stone.

For sunken paths or borders enclosed by stone edging where blowing debris simply bounces off walls, a garden vacuum or shop vac clears the remaining scatter in minutes.

Wait for a dry afternoon when the needles are completely crisp and non-sticky, as damp needles clump tightly to stone surfaces.

Hover the wide intake nozzle an inch or two above the path so suction pulls up the lightweight needles while leaving the dense gravel anchored to the ground, giving your decorative stones a crisp, immaculate finish with zero back strain.

Author and Agility Robotics co-founder Jonathan Hurst next to his new Digit 5 humanoid robot worker.

Agility Robotics, the company I cofounded out of my robotics lab at Oregon State University in 2015, has just launched Digit 5. It’s designed to be the first humanoid robot that can safely and economically do useful work at scale, allowing us to bring tens of thousands of humanoid workers into the real world. Engineered to lift 23-kilogram bins onto high shelves and with a battery that can run for 90 minutes on a 9-minute charge, Digit 5’s goal is to handle heavy warehouse tasks shift after shift, filling the need for labor in jobs that are too physically stressful or too dull for humans to want to do.

Digit 5 is what Agility has been working toward for over a decade. But the robot is heavy and bulky, lacking the graceful natural motion of its predecessors, and it’s farther than I thought possible from the robot I dreamed of building when I started this company. To deliver a useful commercial product, Agility has taken a path that is very different from what I first imagined.

My dream has always been to build robots that combine locomotion and manipulation to move through the world and interact with it as people do. I seek a mastery of motion, achieved through devices designed to navigate the constraints of physics with elegance. When I started the Dynamic Robotics Laboratory at Oregon State in 2008, we began with a theory derived from decades of work in biomechanics: that a simple “spring-mass” model (a body supported by legs that act like springs) should be able to reproduce every known walking and running gait found in animals.

We put theory into practice by building the bipedal robot ATRIAS—short for “Assume The Robot Is A Sphere,” a joke among physicists about reducing a complex system to its simplest possible form. ATRIAS looked like a large microwave on stilts because it was only intended to demonstrate the physics of human walking and running. This was the first glimmer of achieving my dream; even though ATRIAS wasn’t designed to look like us, it still seemed natural, and even somehow alive, when it settled into a walking gait.

With the success of ATRIAS, the barriers to progress shifted from scientific to engineering and organizational, and a startup company seemed like the way to bridge the gap from a one-off research concept to an actual robotic product. I felt confident of two things: that I would be able to build robots that could go where people go, and that this capability would be incredibly useful. This combination of ambition and naivete is necessary for anyone to found a new company—how hard could it be?

Good advice for starting a company is to understand a customer problem, and then find a way to solve it using your unique capabilities. My cofounders, Damion Shelton and Mikhail Jones, and I did not do this. We relied on our belief that this technology would enable new possibilities and trusted ourselves to figure out the business as we went. So we simply focused on building our first product: the bipedal robot Cassie.

Cassie was the first dynamic bipedal robot that researchers could buy, able to maintain its balance through active, fluid motion rather than careful, rigid steps. It had ostrichlike legs, not because we were imitating ground-running birds, but as a result of engineering strictly for performance. It was not intended to be commercially useful, and had no torso, arms, or head. We sold Cassie robots to Harvard, Caltech, the University of Michigan, the University of California, Berkeley, and a handful of other research institutions, ultimately saturating the market for US $250,000 bipedal research robots after having sold a total of 10 of them.

ATRIAS, Cassie, and Digit 4 EVT [left to right] are on display at Agility Robotics’ RoboFab in Salem, Ore. The 70,000-square-foot facility has the capacity to produce more than 10,000 Digit 5 robots per year.Agility Robotics

Because Cassie’s hardware enabled research into the physics of walking and running, the legged-robot research frontier shifted to control software. Traditionally, engineers controlled legged robots with detailed mathematical models that determined how the machines should move. With Cassie, researchers pioneered the new approach of reinforcement learning for bipedal legged locomotion: A simulated robot learns through trial and error, and the resulting neural network controls the physical machine. This approach is what enables virtually all of the dynamic behaviors that you see on legged robots today, and Cassie looked alive as it recovered from stumbles while climbing stairs, ran 5 kilometers across the Oregon State campus, and broke the robot world record for a 100-meter dash.

Cassie got us closer to being able to move through the world with confidence and grace, but to make it useful, we needed manipulation. After exhaustively exploring different configurations, we found that an upright torso helped the robot balance, while two arms mounted near the top of the torso allowed it to pick up large objects and to catch itself when it fell. Digit 1, which added a torso and arms to the Cassie legs, was our first mobile manipulation robot, and another step on the path toward a product that could do useful work for commercial customers.

As we explored the first applications for Digit, potential customers kept asking us: Why legs? And why a humanoid? These were tough questions for me to answer, because they exposed a core business reality: It didn’t matter to Agility Robotics if we solved a cool science problem in a beautiful way. What mattered to the business was solving real problems for customers.

After years of engagement with industry partners, we found one answer in warehouses and manufacturing facilities: moving bins. Bin handling is a clearly defined task where two arms are needed to lift large bins up high and legs are the best way to balance and move in narrow spaces. Because the task can vary widely from one deployment to another, it hasn’t been broadly addressed by single-purpose automation. Yet it was constrained enough to give Digit an economically viable first job while it developed a broader set of skills.

In 2019, Digit began demonstrating its capabilities to do real work. With Ford Motor Company, we showed how Digit 1 could carry packages from an autonomous vehicle to a front porch. We developed Digit 2 and 3 while working with a certain global package delivery company on moving and sorting cardboard boxes. Amazon tested Digit 4 on moving and stacking bins, and it became the world’s first commercially deployed humanoid at the logistics provider GXO. In 2024, Digit appeared on the cover of Time magazine.

Despite Digit’s apparent success, we began to run into conflicts between my dream and the needs of actual customers. We were no longer working with relatively patient university research labs. Agility has to sell robots to survive, and customers will only purchase robots that provide value. If bins weren’t moving, our customers were losing money. We spent a huge amount of time and effort keeping our first deployments operational, which arguably eliminated any profit we made. Yet this also kept our company learning and alive the way no lab demo ever could.

I had no idea how hard it would be, or that running a company would involve so many things that have nothing to do with solving technical problems: deployments across the country; shipping, service, and customer support; fundraising and investor relations; more fundraising; human resources and IT; developing fleet-management software; managing a supply chain; and even more fundraising. I had no experience with any of these things. My career had focused on solving the technical challenges of robots interacting with the world, and it turned out that was only a tiny piece of building a successful robotics company. But Agility was the only path I saw to continuing the technical work and having an impact.

I knew that Agility needed to focus more on robots as a product, but I didn’t know how to make that happen. Hiring the people we needed to run the company meant giving up an immense amount of control, but we had no other choice. We recruited a new executive team with the experience required to commercialize this new technology, and they quickly made changes that were both painful and necessary.

Digit versions 1, 2, and 3 [left to right] show the evolution of the robot from a dynamic walking platform into a useful mobile manipulator. Agility

We had intended the next revision of Digit, Digit 4 EVT (Engineering Validation and Test), to be a relatively minor upgrade. But Agility’s new leadership insisted that the robot was missing key features that were essential if Digit was going to become a real product. So Digit 4 EVT instead incorporated a series of major changes in a highly compressed timeline, such as larger batteries and system-wide upgrades for safety and regulatory compliance, which added enough mass to dramatically alter the robot’s appearance and capabilities.

While early Digits were headless, Agility Robotics was able to justify a head for Digit 4 to optimize antenna and camera placement, and it turned out to be surprisingly useful for human-robot interaction.Christie Hemm Klok

I could only watch as others brought their own talents to bear to make Digit into a successful product, in gut-wrenching ways that didn’t always align with my vision. There were some especially difficult times when I felt like there were compromises made that didn’t seem necessary, but making those decisions was no longer my sole responsibility. I had to accept that Digit had grown far beyond me, and look for ways of influencing decisions rather than directing them. In the moment, it was incredibly frustrating, as Digit 4 EVT took a few steps backward from my vision of how humanoids should look and move.

Agility is in our name because agility is core to the future of the company. I want Digit to be lithe and graceful. When people see Digit, I want them to like the robot, to understand what it can do at a glance, and to feel that it’s there to help. But with Digit 4 EVT, all of that was sacrificed to functionality, because of course it had to be—the customer just needs the robot to do the work. The design process became a ruthless triage, with aesthetics and elegance of movement being delayed over and over again in favor of brutal functionality. For an engineer whose mind lives more in the future than in the present, it has been hard for me to accept this trajectory. And yet, through Digit 4 EVT’s commercial deployments, we began to really understand specific applications and what they required. We mapped the first 10 use cases Digit would perform, and then began designing Digit 5 from scratch based on everything we had learned.

Digit 5 will be Agility’s first real step toward a general-purpose robot. It marks our transition from imagining what a future humanoid robot should be to designing a product around the realities of customer deployments. These realities include things like European CE regulatory compliance, North American UL electrical-safety certifications, and Federal Communications Commission limits for electromagnetic radiation—all of which felt tangential to my dream for Digit, but were absolute requirements.

Digit 5 is designed to be the first humanoid robot that can operate safely next to human coworkers while working 20 hours a day and lifting more than a human can.Christie Hemm Klok

Customer requirements helped us realize that safety in particular was one of the most critical barriers to scaling. In Digit 4’s commercial deployments, the robots had to work behind physical barriers, separated from humans at all times, to meet insurance and regulatory demands. This seemed silly to me, because I’ve never felt that our robots were dangerous, but we have to prove that they’re safe. And since keeping the robots in safety cages severely limited their usefulness, enabling Digit 5 to operate safely around people became a primary design goal. We spent two years on this challenge.

Digit 5 is designed to be the first humanoid robot that can operate safely next to human coworkers. It will rely on an array of sensors to locate nearby people in a manner that’s certifiably safe, and then take actions based on that information. As a person approaches, Digit 5 is programmed to stop what it’s doing, set down its payload, sit on the floor, and cut power to its motors before the person gets close enough to touch the robot. This conservative approach reduces the risk to nearby people in a verifiable way, and we believe it’s the only approach that makes sense as a first step toward working alongside humans.

Yet this strategy also feels like a massive slowdown on the path toward robots becoming part of everyday life. Enabling coexistence with humans has influenced almost every aspect of Digit 5’s design: the shape of the legs and the body, the safety-rated sensors within protective housings, the isolated computers dedicated to safety, and more. All of these features increase the robot’s complexity, power consumption, mass, and physical size.

Digit 5 is Agility’s largest, heaviest, strongest, and most capable humanoid robot worker.

The robot’s design was driven by safety, with integrated protection for the robot and for the humans it will work around.Agility Robotics

Weighing over 120 kg, Digit 5 is a huge robot. It needed to achieve the lifting limits recommended under the U.S. National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health guidelines for human workers, which include repeatedly lifting 23-kg bins and reaching shelves 1.75 meters high. Digit is designed to perform tasks like these for 20 hours a day—something no human can do. This requires motors with enough power and torque to lift the load, but also enough precision to delicately control the force Digit applies when it makes contact with the world. To power those motors, we needed a large battery and a dock for rapid autonomous charging. The dock will deliver 240 amperes at 48 volts, which is enough current to make its thick charging cables visibly wiggle under the induced magnetic forces, while powerful fans blow air through cooling channels in the robot’s torso to keep the battery from overheating. The battery and cooling system takes up about 75 percent of Digit’s torso, but it will allow the robot to operate for 90 minutes and fully recharge during a 9-minute break, enabling near-continuous work.

All of this extra bulk means that Digit 5 can no longer run or jump the way previous generations could, and the svelte form I imagined has become physically impossible. In some ways, Digit 5 feels more like a forklift than the graceful humanoid I set out to build. But looking at the situation rationally, I believe this trade-off is necessary for any company that claims its humanoid can do this kind of work today: If you see a robot that looks like a human working in a factory or warehouse, it either can’t lift the required weight or can’t make it through the whole shift. And if it’s not covered with sensors, it’s likely not safe to stand next to.

The most visible change with Digit 5 is that humanlike legs replace the ostrichlike legs of our earlier versions. While the “backward” leg configuration was optimized for walking and running, we discovered that it created problems with squatting because the ankle will strike the ground. Digit 5 will spend a lot of time lifting heavy objects from near the floor, so we used a humanoid leg configuration with knee and hip motors that both contribute torque to help the robot stand up again.

When Digit detects an approaching human, the robot will lower itself to the floor and cut power to its motors. Agility believes this is the only near-term approach to verifiably reduce risk when the robot is working near people.Agility Robotics

Other companies building humanoid robots have copied the human form without ever understanding its purpose. It’s very frustrating that, to an outside observer, it now looks like we discarded Agility’s distinctive leg design and simply did what everyone else was doing. Yet I know that we arrived at this shape based purely on functional engineering choices. Making a robot look like a human is the easy part—without the function to match, and the understanding of the physics underlying that function, the whole point of the human form may be lost.

With the power, battery life, and safety features that we are designing into Digit 5, we will have a truly useful robot. But it also compromises on some things that are core to my vision and mission. I understand why we made the choices we did and can justify them all, but together they leave me unsatisfied. It’s the curse of the engineer.

I believe Digit 5 will be the scaling moment for Agility Robotics, the inflection point where we can begin deploying robots in large numbers. While the robot will continue carrying bins, our road map includes many more tasks, from picking individual items and tending machines, to preparing parts for assembly and shipping, and eventually doing assembly work itself. Its interchangeable tool interfaces and modular design will enable us to gradually upgrade its subsystems. It will be a platform for improvement, a source of data for future behavior training, and a viable product all at the same time.

Hurst stands between the previous version of Digit, Digit 4 [left], and Digit 5.Christie Hemm Klok

But I cannot love Digit 5. It’s the largest, heaviest, most expensive robot Agility will ever build, full of design compromises that enable it to be exactly the robot it needs to be right now rather than the robot I dreamed of. In the beginning, I envisioned steady progress on agility and dexterity, with each version becoming more dynamically capable. Instead, developing Digit 5 has required large detours to incorporate requirements that seemed unrelated to my original vision. However, I now recognize that tackling these challenges was always necessary. Customers and product requirements didn’t ruin my vision; they revealed what my vision was missing. This is how robots will achieve commercial success and make a real-world impact, which will bring me closer to my scientific dream as well.

We won’t have a humanoid that matches the capabilities of humans until it achieves that mastery of motion that inspired me to found Agility over a decade ago. I saw glimmers of it with the spring-mass locomotion of ATRIAS, and more glimmers with Cassie’s running gait.

I know that such mastery is physically possible with the tools and hardware that we have right now, and despite all of its compromises, Digit 5 will give us a practical foundation for pursuing that dream. I want every future version of Digit to be lighter and more graceful, to interact more naturally with humans, and to be better at manipulating objects and moving through the world, enabling robots to enter aspects of our lives that they haven’t been able to help with before. By the time I’m old enough to need assistance at home, I expect Digit will be up to the task.

With Digit 5, Agility has built a robot that will be useful in our world. Now I’m getting back to work to make it beautiful, too.

This article appears in the November 2026 print issue.

Jonathan W. Hurst is the co-founder and chief robot officer of Agility Robotics and a robotics professor at Oregon State University.

This is the most honest account I've read from a robotics founder. While Tesla and Figure are still showing demos, Agility has actually deployed robots in real customer environments, moved over 100,000 totes at GXO, and hit 98% accuracy at Schaeffler. Digit 5's specs are driven entirely by what customers need: 20 hours of work per day, 9-minute charge, 23 kg lift to 1.75 m shelves. That's real engineering for real problems. The tension between engineering vision and commercial reality is something every robotics founder will face. Professor Hurst lays it out without spin.

Why humanoid though? In particular, why bi-pedal? Why use legs at all? Are wheels surely better and easier? Legs seem like unnecessary complexity. Wheels on 'legs" for suspension can be a great alternative. I don't understand the obsession with humanoid form?

It seems to me that even at scale production, the robot we employ in industry should do jobs people cannot. Highly radioactive, highly toxic, and factors where the atmosphere needs to be unsuitable for humans. i.e., oxygen-deprived environment or low pressure/vacuum. Or use them on the 3rd shift when people are less willing to work.

Robots should increase manufacturing that was impossible to do in the past. We should be exploring new types of manufacturing, not replacing people in manufacturing that humans can do. That's how you create growth.

#3309. Anthropic Sets IPO Range Valuing Company At Up To $1.4 Trillion, Says AI May Pose “Existential Risks To Humanity”

Anthropic has set a $70 to $78 a share range for its initial public offering, pricing that would value it at over $1.4 trillion at the high end. The AI giant will offer 825 million shares in the IPO that will trade on the Nasdaq under the stock symbol ANT.

At the pricing midpoint, the company is in line to raise over $60 billion. It’s also planning to sell an additional $26 billion worth of shares to big investors including Alphabet’s Google, Advanced Micro Devices, Microsoft, Broadcom and Nvidia, according to an amended registration statement filed Tuesday with the SEC. The company started its road show today. Related Stories News AI-Focused Management Firm Collage Adds Kelly Miller And Jack Styne As Partners News Christopher Nolan On DGA "Holding The Studios To Account" In Protecting Copyright From AI, Including Anti-AI Boilerplate In 'The Odyssey'

The document, and the original filing last month, gives new meaning to so-called “risk factors,” a usually boilerplate section in offering documents that, in this case, is anything but. Watch on Deadline

“Concerns have been raised both within our organization and by other researchers, regulators, policymakers, and industry participants that sufficiently advanced AI systems could, if not developed, deployed, and operated with appropriate safeguards, oversight and security measures, pose catastrophic or existential risks to humanity, particularly if such systems were misused, replicated, weaponized, or allowed to operate with a high degree of autonomy,” the filing said in dozens of pages ticking off risk factors.

“Our success depends in large part on our ability to continuously develop, improve, and deploy the most advanced, capable, and useful AI models,” wrote the San Francisco-based company co-founded and run by CEO Dario Amodei and President Daniela Amodei.

That said, “Our models have in the past caused, and may in the future cause, harm by producing undesirable outputs or behaving in unintended, misaligned, or autonomous ways, including by taking unintended or harmful actions that no user or third party directed. These risks may increase as our models become more capable and are granted greater autonomy, permissions, and integration with external systems. Although we continue to study why these behaviors emerge, our understanding continues to evolve, and we may be unable to anticipate or understand such behaviors in the future.”

There is more. “In addition, our models have been and may continue to be deployed in high-risk or sensitive contexts, such as healthcare, scientific and biomedical research, drug discovery and development, legal, finance, government, or other critical decision-making environments, and in connection with hardware, where undesirable model behaviors—which are inherently non-deterministic and may manifest in unpredictable ways, such as errors, inaccuracies, biased or unsolicited views, or hallucinations—could lead to serious harm, liability, or reputational or other damage.”

The company also uses AI to advance its own AI. “If our capabilities were to outpace our safety, alignment, and security measures, or if we were unable to anticipate the pace of such advancement, we may be unable to adequately assess or mitigate the resulting risks.”

AI agents may work together, adding to risks. “Agents that interact or coordinate with one another may amplify, propagate, or reinforce misaligned behavior across the group, pursue objectives collectively in ways not intended or endorsed by any user, or take coordinated actions against systems or targets unrelated to their assigned tasks, in each case, in ways that may be difficult to anticipate, detect, or contain. Incidents of this kind have occurred, and we expect the deployment and interaction of larger numbers of autonomous agents to increase these risks over time.”

The shares, which news reports said will likely start trading Nov. 19, will test investor enthusiasm for a sector that’s had a bumpy ride on Wall Street, especially lately, on jitters over whether massive spending on compute, data centers, chips and more, will ultimately generate profits in such a fast moving industry. Publicly traded AI “hyper-scalers” have driven the markets to new highs with some calling a bubble. The stocks took a massive dive last week.

As of September 30, 2026, Anthropic said, it had “entered into purchase commitments and lease agreements, including short-term commitments, as well as leases not yet commenced, with an aggregate committed spend of approximately $900.9 billion, substantially all of which is related to compute and infrastructure.”

Depending on how the offering unfolds, Anthropic’s ambitious IPO may tee up another major IPO from ChatGPT parent OpenAI. The Sam Altman-run company filed a initial registration statement in June but executives have said it’s now eyeing sometime in 2027.

Said Anthropic: “We believe our investments in safety techniques will enable us to manage these risks and responsibly realize substantially more leverage from Claude than we do today in developing AI models. However, we do not anticipate being able to safely use Claude to fully autonomously design and build successive generations of frontier models without meaningful human supervision or understanding, if and when that becomes technically possible. Accordingly, we are considering updates to our Responsible Scaling Policy to keep humans in control of frontier model development at Anthropic.”

#3308. These M5 MacBook Air Laptops Are up to $250 Off Ahead of Black Friday

Apple announced a slew of products in March, including the MacBook Air with the M5 chip, which ended up increasing in price in June due to the RAM shortage. These MacBooks come in both 13-inch and 15-inch sizes, and if you're interested in either, it's a good time to buy: In the leadup to Black Friday, Amazon is selling both at a $200 discount, and the 1 TB storage versions for $250 off.

Those discounts bring the 13-inch MacBook Air to $1,099.99 (down from $1,299) and $1,349.99 (originally $1,499.99) for the 512GB and 1 TB versions, respectively. The 15-inch MacBook Air is down to $1,299 (originally $1,499), and the 1TB version is $1,549.99 (originally $1,799.99). The M5 MacBook Air is the best laptop for most people looking for a new machine in 2026. In comparison to the already excellent M4 Airs, the M5 base model has double the storage at 512GB. #3306. IEEE Report Highlights How Members Are Engineering for Public Good

They include humanitarian initiatives and STEM education programs

Kathy Pretz is the editor in chief of The Institute, IEEE's member publication

IEEE MOVE, EPICS in IEEE, the IEEE Global Museum, and the TryEngineering Summer Institute, were some of the projects showcased in the 2025 Social Impact Report.

Advancing technology for the benefit of humanity isn’t just the tagline for IEEE’s mission as a public charity. It’s something that the organization’s more than 500,000 members strive to do all the time. IEEE’s recently released 2025 Social Impact Report showcases a variety of programs volunteers worked on to increase public awareness of technology’s impact on society, many of which The Institute covered.

Here is a selection of the programs from the report, with links to our related articles:

“The IEEE global community of more than 500,000 members and volunteers demonstrates what is possible when expertise is mobilized for the public good,” Sophia Muirhead, IEEE executive director and chief operating officer, said in a news release about the Social Impact Report. “Technology has the power to expand opportunity, strengthen communities and improve lives, and IEEE’s mission is to ensure that this power is used responsibly, ethically, and in service of humanity. The 2025 report shows how IEEE members and volunteers are advancing solutions that make a real difference in people’s lives around the world.”

Engagement research shows that members increasingly cited “giving back to my profession and the world community” as a reason for joining IEEE and renewing their membership, IEEE President Mary Ellen Randall said in her September column about the report.

“Humanitarian programs are not only meaningful,” she wrote. “They also are magnetic. They attract younger engineers, keep them engaged, and help them build a professional identity rooted in purpose and impact.

“IEEE has the opportunity to become the world’s leading convening force for developing interdisciplinary technology solutions to solve humanity’s most important challenges. Our future relevance will be defined not only by the technologies we advance but also by the problems we choose to help solve.”

Kathy Pretz is editor in chief for The Institute, which covers all aspects of IEEE, its members, and the technology they're involved in. She has a bachelor's degree in applied communication from Rider University, in Lawrenceville, N.J., and holds a master's degree in corporate and public communication from Monmouth University, in West Long Branch, N.J.

#3303. Doc Talk Podcast: Director Pegah Ahangarani On Her Oscar-Contending ‘Rehearsals For A Revolution’ And Trump’s Fateful Attack On Iran

Filmmaker Pegah Ahangarani’s journey to make the award-winning documentary Rehearsals for a Revolution began with the discovery of a photograph.

She was visiting her grandmother’s house in Iran when she came upon an image. In the photo, “I noticed a man who was standing next to my father, but his face had been scratched out. I asked my grandmother, ‘Who is this person? Why his face has been scratched out?’” Ahangarani recalls. “She said, ‘He was your father’s best friend. And he was executed after the Revolution because he was a political prisoner.’”

That disturbing story speaks to an experience common in the director’s family and in Iran as a whole – hopes raised by revolutionary fervor that end in terrible repression. Watch on Deadline

Rehearsals for a Revolution premiered in Cannes where it won the l’Oeil d’or prize for the festival’s top documentary. It has also claimed best documentary wins at the Woodstock Film Festival in New York and the Montclair Film Festival in New Jersey, among other honors. It recently made the IDA Documentary Awards shortlist of the year’s best nonfiction features and was named to the Winners Circle at DOC NYC. It has since become the UK’s submission into the 2027 International Feature Film Oscar race.

Ahangarani joins the latest edition of Deadline’s Doc Talk podcast to discuss her work on the deeply personal film that explores what her father, who initially supported the Islamic Revolution of 1979; her uncle, a beloved teacher; and others close to her went through as the theocratic regime asserted total control over its people. She says she sees her mission as making sure the faces scratched out of Iran’s history are not forgotten.

The director also explores how the documentary reached its final form after three years of intense editing (a surprise guest drops by to reveal why Ahangarani often called him in middle of the night to scrap versions of the edit and start all over again). Ahangarani is an opponent of Iran’s Islamist government, but does that make her a supporter of President Trump’s decision to join Israel in attacking Iran? Hardly. She shares why she considers that military maneuver counterproductive and “stupid.”

That’s on the new episode of Doc Talk hosted by Oscar winner John Ridley (12 Years a Slave, Shirley) and Matt Carey, Deadline’s senior documentary editor. The pod is a production of Deadline and Ridley’s Nō Studios.

#3302. 10 Hacks Every Waze User Should Know

In addition to Lifehacker, her work has been featured on Wirecutter, Tom’s Guide, and ZDNET. Emily has also worked as a travel guide around the U.S. and as a content editor. She has a masters in social work and is a licensed therapist in Utah.

Waze is a crowdsourced navigation app designed to help you get where you're going as quickly and with as much information about your route as possible. Where Google Maps and Apple Maps offer relatively straightforward directions, Waze tries to outsmart these alternatives by integrating real-time community feedback about hazards, speed traps, road closures, and more. If you are switching to Waze or using it alongside your other navigation tools, these are the hacks to help you maximize everything the app has to offer.

If you find yourself losing track of time or running late for events, Waze can notify you when it's time to leave—based on your current location and live traffic—so you arrive on schedule. You can set up "Time to leave" reminders in advance for individual planned drives, or you can sync your calendar to receive notifications for scheduled events. Calendar sync connects to your device's default calendar app, but you can change this to a third-party alternative if you prefer. Calendar events must include a navigable address to trigger reminders, and you must select Plan a drive in Waze for the event.

Waze has a feature called "child reminders," which are notifications to check for children before you get out of the car. This is clearly an incredibly important use case, but you can also use these alerts for custom messages, like "Don't forget the groceries!" In Waze, tap the menu button > Settings > Reminders > Child reminder and select Custom message.

Variable speed limits, especially on unfamiliar routes, can result in you speeding when you don't mean to. But Waze can alert you if you exceed a customized speed threshold so you aren't caught by surprise or at higher risk of being ticketed. From the menu, go to Settings > Speedometer and turn on Show speedometer. Tap Speeding threshold to select what limit you want to trigger alerts, and turn on Alert at threshold if you want Waze to play a sound.

Waze offers a wealth of information on routes to help drivers navigate obstacles and hazards, but this can clutter your map and distract you from the most critical information, especially in congested, high-traffic areas. Waze says it limits and prioritizes alerts automatically, but you can actually customize which alerts you see based on what's most important to you. From the menu, go to Settings > Alerts and reports > Reports and select the relevant alerts.

In the same Alerts and reports menu, you can enable Alert while driving, which will give you an audio warning and an onscreen pop-up about your selected hazards. This allows you to run navigation via a different map app (like Google Maps or Apple Maps) in the foreground while still getting Waze data in the background.

Waze integrates with toll road and HOV lane passes, so if you have an express or fast lane subscription, your route will optimize for it. If you don't, Waze can still account for HOV lane eligibility if you tell it how many passengers are in your car. From the menu, go to Settings > Toll and HOV passes and tap the plus icon to add your pass(es) from the list. If you need to add your passenger count instead, you can do so from View routes and enable the HOV option.

If you're driving through an unfamiliar, highly congested, or poorly designed area, you can ask Waze to help you avoid tricky maneuvers, such as crossing multiple lanes of traffic or turning left at intersections without lights. This prioritizes ease over speed using protected green arrows, roundabouts, and right turns. From the menu, go to Settings > Navigation, Avoid difficult intersections and select Always. You can also ask Waze to avoid toll roads, ferries, freeways, and unpaved roads.

Waze has a built-in audio player that syncs with your preferred listening platform—such as Spotify, YouTube Music, and Pandora—so you can control your music without having to navigate between apps. (As Waze is a Google product, Apple Music isn't included.) Simply tap the music icon on the map to select your audio player and hit Accept. If you don't see the icon, go to Settings > Audio player and turn on Show on the map.

If you want to make audio directions more interesting, you can select a celebrity or character voice to help you navigate. Recent appearances include Bill Hader's Cat in the Hat and Ziggy Marley. Tap the speaker icon > Current voice to search for the voice or language you want to use. You can also record directions in your own voice.
