On November 4, just a few days back, we achieved a major reimbursement milestone when the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services or CMS reverted earlier proposed non payment decision and established separate Medicare hospital outpatient payment for diagnostic QT scan examination effective January 1, 2027.

Under the final 2027 Medicare rules CMS assigned our dedicated CPT billing code 1.08 thousandT to ambulatory payment classification 5520. With payment status indicator s. Importantly, CMS recognized that physician ordered QT scan examination addressing specific diagnostic findings qualify under Medicare's existing diagnostic ultrasound coverage framework. Together with the October 1 implementation of our dedicated CPT billing code, this decision removes a significant reimbursement uncertainty and establishes a clear Medicare hospital outpatient payment pathway for medically necessary diagnostic QT scan examination. This is a very meaningful commercial milestone for QT imaging. Hospitals now have both a dedicated billing code and an established Medicare payment classification strengthening the business case for adopting our breast imaging technology.

Our focus is now on translating this progress into scanner installations and clinical adoption. We have developed a comprehensive coding and billing guide to support hospitals and imaging providers. While continuing our engagement with Medicare and commercial payers expanding the clinic and economic evidence needed for broader coverage. Medicare payment applies to medically necessary physician order examination rather than routine screening. We will continue pursuing additional reimbursement opportunities related to our SaaS platform and AI software improvements. An essential part of our commercial execution is ensuring that imaging centers and hospitals have access to breast radiologists properly trained to interpret the QT scan. We have initiated a structured training program with 2 established radiology groups under the leadership of Dr.

Mary Yamashita. These relationships will expand our clinical reading capacity and support the adoption of Breast Acoustic CT imaging modality across our growing installed base. Approximately 13,000 women have now been imaged using QT Imaging Breast Acoustic CT technology. Making a significant milestone in clinical adoption and reinforcing the growing real world foundation for advancing quantitative breast imaging. Equally important, our multisite repeatability reproducibility research demonstrated less than 1% variability in speed of sound measurements under the conditions studied. This finding support the operator independent nature of our automated imaging modality, a significant advantage over conventional handheld ultrasound, where image acquisition and measurements are highly dependent on operator technique and experience.

Our payer strategy builds on the newly established Medicare reimbursement pathway for medically necessary diagnostic scan examinations and focuses on the following clinical application. 1, diagnostic evaluation of women with dense breasts who require additional imaging following mammography. Diagnostic evaluation of high risk women, particularly those who face barriers to breast MRI. 2, quantitative monitoring of response to adjuvant cancer therapy and 3, beyond these applications, we see a significant opportunity to improve participation in the breast cancer screening. More than 30 percent of eligible women are not up to date with recommended screening. Our radiation free, compression-free technology has the potential to help bring these women back into the standard of care.

Although routine screening is not currently covered under Medicare. We will work diligently to generate the clinical evidence to pursue the necessary regulatory approvals and expand reimbursement pathway to make QTscan accessible to more women particularly those who face barriers to conventional breast imaging. We are aligning our clinical research programs with these priorities, working with our clinical partners to demonstrate QT scans incremental diagnostic value, potential to reduce unnecessary biopsies, ability to provide quantitative biomarkers for treatment monitoring. Our objective is to generate the clinical and economic evidence needed to expand payer coverage strengthen physician adoption and accelerate broader patient access. Third, technology and operational scale. We are building an integrated breast imaging platform, not simply a manufacturing scanner.

Our breast acoustic CT technology provides radiation free compression free 3D imaging and quantitative information derived from the acoustic properties of breast tissue. The QTI Olea Viewer supports clinical interpretation while QTI precision pathway is our cloud platform for image processing and quantitative analysis. We continue to advance our reconstruction software, improve reflection quality and streamline radiologist workflows. These investments are designed to strengthen clinical performance and support the scalability of our technology. We strengthened our scientific leadership in July with the appointment of Dr. Julia Albright as chief science officer. Her role is to connect our research, product development and clinical evidence priorities.

We also completed the relocation of our headquarters and manufacturing operations to a new approximately 22 thousand-square-foot facility in Petaluma, California. Under the leadership of our Chief Operating Officer, Steve Choate. This expansion more than doubles our available space and has approximately doubled our scanner manufacturing capacity. While significantly reducing our lease cost per square foot. The new facility allows us to streamline production workflows, improve operational efficiency and strengthen quality control as manufacturing volumes increase. Importantly, this investment positions QT Imaging to support growing demand in the U. S. And the international markets as we scale our commercial operations in 2027 and beyond. Execution at scale depends on quality.

In July, we completed our first routine FDA inspection with 0 Form FDA 483 observations. This is an important result for our team and the systems we have put in place. Fourth, international expansion and financial discipline. In July, we have received regulatory registration from Israel's Ministry of Health enabling commercialization in the market. We are working toward a scanner placement and clinical collaboration with Rambam Healthcare Campus focused on women with hereditary breast cancer risk. Our international expansion a major milestone with our first commercial order, in the Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) region, secured with American Hospital Dubai through our distribution partner Al Naghi Medical.

American Hospital Dubai was the first healthcare institution in The Middle East to join the Mayo Clinic Care Network. Operate the multidisciplinary breast institute integrating advanced imaging breast surgery, oncology, pathology and high risk patient care. Beyond this first commercial order, we intend to work closely with American Hospital Dubai and Al Naghi Medical on joint marketing initiatives physician education and clinical research evaluating the performance patient acceptance and quantitative tissue measurement. The clinical need in The UAE is significant. A 2023 study found that only 23 percent of surveyed women had undergone mammography, while separate research reported a median breast cancer diagnosis age of 48. While 50% presenting with locally advanced or metastatic disease.

Women die of breast cancer in UAE 12 years earlier than in the United Arab Emirates. We also received regulatory approval for our Breast Acoustic CT scanner in Bahrain and Qatar. Further expanding our authorized market presence in the Gulf region. Together with our first commercial order from American Hospital Dubai, this milestone strengthens our foundation for commercial expansion across the GCC. The Middle East conflict and the disruption affected regional logistics has delayed anticipated shipments to our customers and distribution partners in Saudi Arabia and The UAE. We are maintaining and further developing those relationships but we cannot responsibly commit to a shipment date while conditions remain uncertain.

Beyond these commercial and operational milestones, October was also an important opportunity to reinforce why we are building this company. On October 2, we had the honor of ringing the NASDAQ closing bell to mark Breast Cancer Awareness Month. Just days after World Breast Cancer Day. I emphasize the principle at the heart of QT imaging. For decades, women have been asked to adapt to breast imaging technology We believe technology should adapt to women. Patient comfort matters because adherence to screening matters. And women with dense breast deserve better imaging options. Our vision is a future of breast imaging that is multimodal, quantitative and personalized. The Nasdaq ceremony celebrated how far we have come.

But our responsibility now is to bring this technology to more physicians more communities, and more women around the world. #3237. Graphon Labs raises $35m to give AI agents a memory that lasts

Graphon Labs says its graph-based memory tops rival systems on three benchmarks. The 20-person company counts HP and the San Francisco 49ers among its users.

Graphon Labs co-founders, from left: Deepak Mishra, chief operating officer; Arbaaz Khan, chief executive; and Clark Zhang, chief technology officer.

Graphon Labs, a San Francisco startup that builds memory for AI agents, has raised $35m. RRE Ventures led the Series A. HP, Energy Impact Partners, Hitachi Ventures and Gaia VC also invested, Graphon said on Tuesday. The round brings its total funding to $43.3m, less than six months after it left stealth with an $8.3m seed round.

The 20-person company will spend the money mainly on engineers and researchers, plus some sales staff. Chief executive Arbaaz Khan gave those details to Shubhangi Goel of Business Insider, which reported the round first.

Khan compares common AI search to tearing the pages out of a book and digging through the scraps for an answer.

“You’ve basically lost all that information because each piece is living on its own,” he told Business Insider.

AI agents can write code and carry out tasks. But they can lose track of past conversations and changing company data. Graphon says common methods can lose context, relationships and timing as data grows. One example is retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), which feeds a model snippets of stored text.

Graphon’s system is built on graphons, a mathematical framework for very large graphs. Khan and co-founder Clark Zhang built graph-based memory for robots during their PhDs, Khan wrote in a blog post. The software maps the links between a company’s documents, videos and images, including where information came from and when it changed.

“You can basically point your Claude or GPT or whatever to Graphon,” Khan told Business Insider.

Graphon says it scored 93.9% on LoCoMo, a test of memory over long conversations. It used 58% fewer tokens than loading the whole conversation into the model. On ATM-Bench, a University of Cambridge benchmark across video, audio, images and text, it scored 81.7%. That is 5 points ahead of the next system on the public leaderboard.

Graphon says the San Francisco 49ers, Hitachi and other large companies use its software. HP also uses it, Business Insider reported. Costa Kladianos, the 49ers’ executive vice president of technology, said the team is exploring how to use it. One example is finding new sponsorship deals. Hitachi Rail said its evaluation “shows promise” in its industrial setting.

The company has three products: Graphon Enterprise, a developer platform, and on-device memory for phones, laptops, cameras and wearables. Khan told Business Insider that Graphon will stay focused on enterprise customers before moving further into devices and consumer products.

The biggest AI companies are also adding memory to their assistants. In August, Anthropic merged Claude’s memory across chat and Cowork. In October, Apple’s iOS 27.2 gave Siri memory.

#3236. Another report backs OLED iPad Air early next year

Following the recent update to the iPad mini, we’re expecting the iPad Air to be next in line to be upgraded to an OLED screen.

Previous reports have gradually narrowed down the launch to early 2027, and a new supply chain report echoes this …

OLED screens were initially exclusive to the iPad Pro. That finally changed last month when Apple gave the iPad mini its biggest update in years. The new model is thinner and lighter and powered by an A20 Pro chip, while the headline news is the new OLED screen.

The iPad Air got a chip update earlier this year, but nothing else. An upgrade to OLED is expected next year, with recent reports suggesting that it will be in the first half of 2027. That’s now backed by a new supply chain report by DigiTimes.

Given past timings, the smart money would be on the OLED iPad Air being announced in March. With the precedent set by the latest iPad mini, we can likely expect the new iPad Air to have similar specs, which means sticking with Touch ID and a 60Hz display.

#3235. Multiphysics Modeling for Next-Generation Electromagnetic Manufacturing Technologies



Advances in sensing, manufacturing, computational resources, and data-driven methods are enabling new approaches to electromagnetic sensing, non-destructive evaluation, and advanced materials processing. This webinar will demonstrate how the COMSOL Multiphysics software supports predictive modeling by coupling electromagnetic fields with thermal, chemical, mechanical, and transport phenomena across multiple length and time scales.

The first application we will show focuses on eddy-current thermometry for reconstructing three-dimensional temperature fields in metal plates. Temperature-dependent electrical conductivity alters induced currents and magnetic fields, enabling volumetric thermal inference. COMSOL simulations of defects and laser-induced transient heating will support validation of reconstruction algorithms. Multifrequency excitation will be investigated to improve depth discrimination through frequency-dependent penetration depths and sensitivities.

The second application examines microwave-enabled volumetric additive manufacturing of ceramic components. A high-power microwave beamforming array delivers localized energy into three-dimensional volumes, enabling processing of opaque, particle-laden resins. Coupled COMSOL models of electromagnetic propagation, microwave absorption, heat transfer, and ceramic sintering kinetics are used to predict temperature evolution, reaction progression, spatial resolution, and processing scalability. Future extensions will incorporate pulsed excitation, fluid flow, resin viscosity, convection, shrinkage, and solid mechanics.

Together, these examples demonstrate how the COMSOL software can integrate multiphysics modeling with sensing, manufacturing, and data inversion. This webinar will present two applications of coupled electromagnetic and thermal modeling in COMSOL Multiphysics: eddy-current thermometry in metal plates and microwave-assisted processing of ceramic-loaded resins. By connecting simulation with practical engineering systems, COMSOL-based modeling can accelerate technology development, reduce experimental iteration, and support reliable scale-up of next-generation electromagnetic technologies.

#3233. Seer Inc (SEER) Q3 2026 Earnings Call Transcript

Funding strain and slower purchasing are pushing Seer's late-stage deals later.

Need a quote from a Motley Fool analyst? Email [email protected]

Seer, Inc. (SEER -4.17%) reported a sequential revenue increase while lowering its full-year 2026 outlook due to persistent market headwinds. Management identified academic funding constraints and corporate uncertainty as primary factors delaying customer purchasing decisions. The company completed a strategic review by a Special Committee, resulting in its continued operation as an independent public entity. Operating expenses declined 23% year over year following cost-reduction measures in compensation and professional services. Management indicated that existing capital reserves are sufficient to reach cash flow breakeven under the current operating plan.

Operator: Good day and welcome to the Seer, Inc. Third Quarter 2026 Earnings Conference Call. [Operator Instructions] Please note, this event is being recorded. I would now like to turn the conference over to Marissa Bych of Gilmartin Group. Please go ahead.

Marissa Bych: Thank you. Earlier today, Seer released financial results for the quarter ended September 30, 2026. If you have not received this news release, or if you would like to be added to the company's distribution list, please send an email to [email protected]. In addition, during today's conference call, we will be referencing a slide presentation that can be accessed on the Events and Presentations section of Seer's Investor Relations website. Participating today from Seer is Omid Farokhzad, Chief Executive Officer and Chair of the Board, and Charles Endweiss, Treasurer, Principal Financial Officer, and Principal Accounting Officer.

Before we begin, I would like to remind you that management will make statements during this call that are forward-looking statements within the meaning of federal securities laws. These statements involve material risks and uncertainties that could cause actual results or events to materially differ from those anticipated. Additional information regarding these risks and uncertainties appears in the section titled Forward-Looking Statements in the press release we issued today. For a more complete list and description, please see the Risk Factors section of the company's quarterly report on Form 10-Q for the quarter ended September 30, 2026, and in its other filings with the Securities and Exchange Commission.

Except as required by law, Seer disclaims any intention or obligation to update or revise any financial projections or forward-looking statements, whether because of new information, future events, or otherwise. This conference call contains time-sensitive information and is accurate only as of the live broadcast today. With that, I would like to turn the call over to Omid.

Omid Farokhzad: Thank you, Marissa, and thank you all for joining us this afternoon. This quarter, our customers continue to demonstrate what Proteograph makes possible, from new biological discoveries in population-scale studies to emerging applications in AI. Established customers continue to purchase consumables, and new large biopharma customers adopted the Proteograph Product Suite for use in their own laboratories. These developments reinforce my conviction in the value of our technology and the business opportunity ahead for Seer. Our opportunity is to make deep unbiased proteomics a routine part of research programs that require a more complete understanding of biology. Proteograph substantially expands what researchers can learn from mass spectrometry while allowing them to use existing LC-MS infrastructure.

As this value becomes clearer across more applications, we have the opportunity to expand both our customer base and the use of the platform within each account. The business model connects directly to that use. Each additional sample processed with the Proteograph requires assay consumables. A successful study can lead to a larger cohort, follow-up research, or adoption by another team within the same institution. Technology Access Center, or STAC, and service providers give customers additional ways to access the technology. This allows us to serve researchers at different stages of adoption and build repeat revenue as their programs develop. We see that model at work in established accounts, including customers that have purchased consumables across multiple consecutive quarters.

Our commercial priority is to build on these relationships, help customers expand their research programs, and bring the same value to additional accounts. Revenue for the third quarter was $4 million compared with $3.1 million in the second quarter. Customer funding constraints and longer purchasing timelines continue to affect the pace of revenue conversion, and we're updating our full-year outlook to $13.5 million to $14.5 million. Charles will discuss the results and outlook in detail. We remain focused on converting funded opportunities and expanding repeat customer use. The activist campaign and subsequent acquisition proposals also led some customers to ask about the direction of Seer's future and the long-term support of their research programs.

We have spent time directly addressing those questions. As announced on October 29, the Special Committee has completed this review and Seer will remain an independent public company. This gives us a clear message for customers about our continued commitment to innovation, service, and support. I'm encouraged by the recovery we're seeing in our pipeline. Publications, preprints, and reviews describing research conducted using the Proteograph now total 116, up from 95 at our last quarterly update. I want to highlight the discoveries researchers are advancing, what this growth evidence means for the use of the Proteograph, and how it supports the commercial opportunity we're pursuing.

Turning to slide 3, let me turn to the scientific evidence from the PRECISE-SG100K cohort presented at the 2026 Human Proteome Organization World Congress, or HUPO. PRECISE-SG100K is Singapore's population health study of approximately 100,000 residents of Chinese, Malay, and Indian ancestry designed to understand how genetics, biology, lifestyle, and environment influence health and disease. Within this program, investigators selected our Proteograph workflow combined with Thermo Fisher's Orbitrap Astral mass spectrometry to deeply characterize the plasma proteome of 10,000 participants, complementing affinity-based measurements within the broader study. Professor John Chambers, Chief Scientific Officer of PRECISE and Lead Investigator of PRECISE-SG100K, presented preliminary findings.

Across 9,658 plasma samples, the Proteograph Astral workflow quantified approximately 8,800 protein groups across this study and approximately 88,000 peptides per sample. Performance was consistent across 126 processing batches with no reported sample failure. Population studies require both depth and reliable execution across thousands of samples, and these results demonstrate the ability of our workflow to deliver both. As subsequently reported by Thermo Fisher Scientific, the PRECISE investigators identified more than 4,200 proteins with significant cis-pQTL associations, which link nearby genetic variations with measured protein abundance. They also reported 2,762 genetic protein associations that had not been reported across the 12 reference studies used for comparison and connected proteins to 71 health-related traits.

When combined with disease genetics and other evidence, these relationships can help researchers investigate disease mechanism and prioritize potential therapeutic targets. The PRECISE-SG100K illustrates a central aspect of Seer's value proposition. Proteograph fundamentally expands the biology researchers can see with mass spectrometry. Published studies and customer presentations using matched plasma samples have repeatedly demonstrated that conventional mass spectrometry workflows without the Proteograph achieve approximately 10% to 15% of the protein coverage achieved when Proteograph is paired with a mass spectrometry. Used alongside advanced mass spectrometers, Proteograph substantially expands the biological information available for discovery.

Just as 10x Genomics enabled researchers to use DNA sequencing to resolve biology at the level of individual cells, Seer enables researchers to use mass spectrometry to explore a much deeper landscape of circulating proteins. By bringing thousands of additional proteins within reach of measurement, Proteograph opens new opportunities to uncover genetic protein relationships, investigate disease mechanisms, and identify potential therapeutic targets. This is the discovery capability Seer brings to population-scale research. The PRECISE team is now beginning to analyze the peptide-level data, creating opportunities to investigate protein variants and isoforms beyond the protein-level findings reported to date. For Seer, studies of this scale demonstrate both scientific value and the ability to support substantial sample processing programs.

Turning to slide 4, an independent study published in Clinical Proteomics provides another example of our differentiation. Researchers at CHA University in South Korea compared 7 plasma preparation approaches using accessible mass spectrometry instrumentation. Proteograph XT, together with the Orbitrap Exploris 480, delivered the greatest proteome coverage, identifying an average of approximately 6,060 proteins per sample and the lowest rate of missing protein measurements at 1.9%. These findings demonstrate that Proteograph enables deep proteomic coverage even in laboratories using earlier generations of mass spectrometers. Alongside this performance evidence, we have made important progress in protecting the technology behind it. Our intellectual property portfolio now includes more than 250 patent and patent applications, including 88 issued patents.

On November 5, we announced a significant development in our ITC action with Brigham Women's Hospital (sic) [ Brigham and Women's Hostpital ] against Nanomics. Nanomics stopped defending the investigation and the ITC's investigative staff subsequently recommended granting the full exclusion and cease and desist order we requested. The Commission's final determinations remains pending and is expected by year-end. This is meaningful progress in defending our foundational intellectual property. Our customers commit precious samples, time, and resources to scientific discovery, and we will vigorously protect the innovation they rely on. The downstream impact of the Proteograph-enabled discoveries is also illustrated by PrognomiQ's ProVue Lung, the blood-based lung cancer detection test developed from biomarkers discovered using our technology.

PrognomiQ commercially launched ProVue Lung in November 2025 as a laboratory-developed test, or an LDT, and has reported early results from its ongoing real-world clinical evaluation. In a recent conference presentation, PrognomiQ's Chief Technology Officer Bruce Wilcox described how the protein biomarkers from the original discovery study were independently replicated using both targeted mass spectrometry and immunoassays in a separate patient cohort. The findings supported translation into a multiplex immunoassay for the launch of ProVue Lung. We also reported that the program progressed from initial Proteograph-based discovery to a validated laboratory-developed test in 31 months with clinical deployment to Allegheny Health Network and Penn Highlands Healthcare.

This is a concrete example of how broader biological information at the discovery stage can support the development of a clinical assay. Turning to slide 5, AI is shaping biology, and the capabilities of a model depend on the data it learns from. Proteograph-enabled mass spectrometry produces information at the spectral, peptide, and protein levels. Researchers can use this data to investigate protein abundance, peptide-level differences, and signals that conventional identification-based analysis have yet to fully characterize. Professors Sang-Won Lee and Jaewoo Kang of Korea University presented preliminary findings for more than 5,500 plasma samples at the ASMS and HUPO conference this year.

Their work combines deep Proteograph-enabled plasma measurements with an ID-free AI proteomics approach that uses features from both identified and unidentified spectral signals. Preliminary results showed improved overall cancer classification performance compared with models using only identified peptide features. We believe AI can become an important driver of demand for deep unbiased proteomics. When researchers are searching for new biological relationships, the information available to a model shapes what it can discover. Proteograph allows them to explore thousands of proteins beyond predefined panels while retaining peptide-level information and identifying spectral signals that can be revisited as analytical methods advance. The Korea University work provides an early example of that opportunity.

As more organizations use AI to investigate biology, we see an opportunity to help them generate the deep proteomic datasets those efforts require. That scientific interest is now translating into commercial activity. Our priority is to translate that scientific value into sustained commercial growth. Under Tony Bazarko's leadership as our Chief Commercial Officer, we're concentrating customer engagement and resources on accounts with the potential to generate meaningful repeat revenue. Tony and I are also making AI-driven research an explicit commercial priority, focusing on organizations that need deep proteomic data and have funded programs that can translate into sample volume. Within existing accounts, we're working to expand successful studies into additional funded programs and introduce Proteograph to other research teams.

In new accounts, we're focusing on opportunities with a clear scientific use case, funding, and a defined path to sample processing. We're also in active discussion with public and private population-scale cohorts about how Proteograph can support their next studies. We're also focused on biopharma, where we have signed several new large pharmaceutical customers this year that purchased instruments and consumables for their studies. Pharmaceutical companies can use proteomics across multi-year research programs to investigate mechanisms of action, resistance biology, and biomarkers. Our objective is to help initial adoption develop into larger studies and broader use across research teams.

These priorities reflect how we intend to grow, expand sample volumes within established accounts, and develop additional customers whose research programs can support repeat use over time. We're aligning commercial activity with funded studies, anticipated sample volumes, and opportunities for account expansion. Those are the operating measures that connect our scientific differentiation to revenue. We also have the financial resources to pursue this opportunity thoughtfully. We ended the quarter with approximately $198 million in cash, cash equivalents, and investments. Our capital allocation approach combines investment in commercial adoption and product innovation, and disciplined spending and share repurchases. We believe our current share price does not reflect the value of our technology, customer relationships, and long-term business opportunity.

Through September 30, we had repurchased approximately 13.5 million shares at a volume-weighted average price of $1.85 per share using approximately $25 million of the combined $50 million authorized by our Board in May 2024 and February 2026. Approximately $25 million remained available under those authorizations. We review repurchases as an opportunity to increase continuing shareholders' ownership of the business at prices we believe are attractive, while preserving capital to execute our operating plan. Our confidence in our capital position reflects both our balance sheet and the changes we have made to our expense base.

Third quarter operating expenses were $16.5 million, approximately 23% below the prior year period, reflecting lower employee compensation, including stock-based compensation, and lower laboratory and professional service expenses. Our path to cash flow break even depends on growing revenue and improving gross margins while maintaining spending discipline. Based on those assumptions in our current operating plan, we believe our existing capital is sufficient to reach cash flow break even. We will continue to manage investment against commercial progress with a focus on building long-term value per share.

Before turning to the financials, I want to thank David Horn, who served on our leadership team for more than 6 years and helped guide Seer through an important period in the company's development. We're grateful for his contribution and wish him all the best. I would also like to welcome Charles Endweiss, who has been a senior member of our finance team for nearly 6 years and brings a deep understanding of our business. Charles has previously served as Vice President of Financial Planning and Analysis and assumed the roles of Treasurer, Principal Financial Officer, and Principal Accounting Officer on October 1. With that, I will turn the call over to Charles.

Charles Endweiss: Thank you, Omid. Slide 6. Total revenue for the third quarter of 2026 was $4.0 million compared with $3.1 million in the second quarter. The sequential increase was driven by higher product revenue from increased instrument shipments and new customer agreements. Product revenue was $2.8 million and consisted of Proteograph instrument and consumable kit sales. Service revenue was $1.1 million. Related party revenue was $0.1 million. Other revenue was approximately $67,000 and consisted of lease and shipping revenue. Gross profit was approximately $1.9 million, representing a gross margin of 47%, a decline of 130 basis points sequentially. We continue to expect quarterly variability in gross margin as the proportion of instrument, consumable, and service revenue fluctuates.

At scale, we continue to believe long-term gross margins can be in the range of 70% to 75%. Total operating expenses were $16.5 million, including $1.2 million of stock-based compensation, compared with $21.5 million, including $3.6 million of stock-based compensation, in the third quarter of 2025. Research and development expenses were $6.4 million compared with $10.8 million in the prior year period. The decrease reflected lower employee compensation, including stock-based compensation, as well as lower laboratory and professional service expenses. Selling, general, and administrative expenses were $10.1 million compared with $10.7 million in the prior year period. The decrease reflected lower employee compensation, including stock-based compensation, partially offset by higher professional service expenses.

Net loss was $13.7 million compared with $18.2 million in the third quarter of 2025. For the 9 months ended September 30, 2026, net cash used in operating activities was approximately $34.5 million. After approximately $311,000 of net purchases of property and equipment, free cash flow was approximately negative $34.8 million. During the third quarter, we repurchased approximately 61,000 Class A common shares at an average price of $1.64 per share. As Omid noted, we ended the quarter with approximately $198 million in cash, cash equivalents, and investments, and approximately $25 million remained available under our repurchase authorizations. Slide 7.

We are updating our full-year 2026 revenue guidance to $13.5 million to $14.5 million from our prior range of $16 million to $18 million. Two factors have affected the timing of customer purchasing decisions. Funding constraints in academic and government research have extended sales cycles and delayed the start of some studies. Separately, uncertainty surrounding Seer's future during the activist campaign and subsequent acquisition proposals caused some customers to seek additional assurances before committing to purchases. Together, these factors have extended the time required to convert opportunities into revenue, and several late-stage opportunities are now expected to close later than planned. Our revised outlook reflects those longer timelines.

Following the conclusion of the Special Committee's review, we are addressing customer questions directly and focusing our commercial resources on funded programs with a defined path to sample processing. With that, I turn the call back to Omid.

Omid Farokhzad: Thank you, Charles. I remain confident in Seer's future because of the value Proteograph creates for researchers and the opportunity to build lasting customer relationships around that value. The studies we discussed today show the platform enabling discoveries at a scale and depth that expand what researchers can learn about human biology. Repeat customer purchases give us a commercial foundation to build on, and our balance sheet gives us the resources to pursue the opportunity with discipline. Our focus is to expand adoption, grow sample volume within customer accounts, and convert that activity into sustained revenue growth.

I believe Seer is well positioned to play an important role in the next generation of biological research, and I'm committed to building long-term value for our shareholders. Thank you to our shareholders for your continued support, to our customers and collaborators for the work they're advancing with the Proteograph, and to our employees for your dedication to our mission. With that, we will open the call for questions. Operator?

Operator: [Operator Instructions] The first question today comes from Kyle Mikson with Canaccord.

Kyle Mikson: Just thinking about the guidance reduction here and maybe, like, as you, sort of, exit the year, enter '27, what can you do to mitigate these headwinds from the constrained academic funding environment and the spending among the broad, kind of, end markets here? You've got larger projects. I think you said several biopharma partners. I'm just curious if that's, like, enough to offset some challenges, like reinvigorate some growth, or do you intend on entering non-affected markets as well?

Omid Farokhzad: Kyle, thanks a million. So, I think it's important to break it up into tailwinds, headwinds, and what are we seeing. So you were spot on in that the headwinds have been the funding environment around academic, government. Biopharma spending has picked up, and we're seeing more and more customers doing sequential quarter-after-quarter consumable placements. Now, we also had a challenging start to the year with a lot of the, kind of, the background with the proxy contest, etc. That did create some challenges with some of our customers, Kyle, in terms of customers wondering if Seer was going to be around for long-term support, et cetera. So those added additional delay.

But then the tailwinds are that we are seeing more and more customers adopting the platform without the prior, for example, need to examine the utility of it. It used to be that a sales cycle involved doing these proof-of-concept studies before a customer would opt in to move ahead. We're not seeing that anymore. The body of literature out there, the proof points out there are robust enough that customers are interacting with our sales team going through the process and adopting the platform. And we're seeing more and more publications come out. We're at 116 now. We're going to enter 2027 with a run rate of 100 publications a year.

And these validations are basically currency of trust in our industry, as you know, Kyle, and they help. And then separately, we're seeing large population-scale studies get presented, like the PRECISE in -- at the HUPO just a month ago. And the data that is coming is exceptionally validating in terms of the value proposition. And then additionally, AI is an important driver for us as well because the foundational models need rich data, and the level of data that Seer provides is not matched with any alternative in terms of the proteomics space. You're looking at data across different dimensions: protein groups, peptides, spectral data.

The depth that Seer provides is unmatched, and so this is not just a mass spec, this is a unique capability that Seer brings forward in the era of AI biology if you want to add proteomic information to the function. So I look at, in aggregate, all of those headwinds and tailwinds, and I believe '27 is going to be a year of growth for us, and I am enthusiastic about it. We're not prepared to guide. We'll talk about that on the Q4 call, but I think it is going to be a good year for us, Kyle.

Kyle Mikson: Okay, and then in the clinical proteomics paper with the 7 head-to-head comparisons, Proteograph outperformed on, like, most of the metrics there. The workflow is the most expensive, though, required the largest volume of plasma input, and it looks like, I think it's the only workflow with automation. So maybe just talk about what you guys learned from that and the tradeoffs of cost and performance and other variables as you, sort of, look to scale over the long term.

Omid Farokhzad: Yes, Kyle, we -- I have a couple of thoughts on that. If you look at the overall cost of doing the proteomic studies of this type, you start off with the sample cost, processing cost, data analysis cost, data storage cost, etc. The lion's share of the overall cost is actually in the samples. In other words, the clinical samples, the human samples, they are in 1,000, 2,000, 3,000 plus. And so the relative cost of the consumable use is a small fraction of that. Now, that said, if you then compare Seer's price compared to the other options available to a customer, the value proposition is quite different.

Meaning, I think Seer, in terms of the depth of proteomics that it offers, in terms of the type of information that it provides, is quite differentiated and different from targeted approaches. I think they can coexist, but the value proposition is very different. So if you're interested in discovery, Seer provides a unique solution. Now, this misconception about Seer being expensive, I think progressively this is also being eliminated. We're now entering population-scale studies. These are studies of tens of thousands of samples. Those studies could not have been done if the cost of the reagents was not appropriate for it.

So not only is the value proposition, I think, quite attractive in terms of the exchange of price with the value that you get, but I also think that having scaled the organization to the way that we have advanced the platform that we have, we're also seeing some cost savings that we're passing that on to our customers. So I think you're going to see a reduction in price as well for the customer side. But the value proposition, I think, is the most important that I think is very much robust.

Operator: The next question comes from Kyle Boucher from TD Cowen.

Kyle Boucher: I wanted to talk a little bit about what you're seeing on the sales cycle side. I know you mentioned a number of times that they're elongated, but, I guess, how should we think about what, sort of, the average timeline is for the sales cycle at this point? And then on that, I think you also talked about going after some bigger customer opportunities, maybe accounts that will spend a little bit more. I guess, can you talk about your sales funnel in terms of maybe academic and government customers versus biopharma customers?

Omid Farokhzad: Yes, Kyle, thanks a lot. So the sales cycle continues to be long, but I think, Kyle, that has reduced in length. I would say today it's about 6 months. Before, I would say it was high single-digit number of months. The shortening of that from the high single-digit number to maybe 6 is a reflection of the fact that we're doing very small number of these proof-of-principle studies. I mean, I think customers are going from initial interaction to an acquisition or a STAC project. That's the first point. Second is, I'm super happy about the addition of Tony Bazarko to our executive team.

Tony is our Chief Commercial Officer, joined about 7 months ago, and then he brought Ryan Gossett as VP of Sales, someone who he had worked with in the past. And Ryan has been with us for about maybe 4 months or so. The 2 have been fantastic. They've been out seeing customers. The 2 of them in the last 7 months that Tony's been on the job, 4 that Ryan has been on the job, together, they have seen 50 distinct customers in person on their site globally.

And by the way, if a particular customer, like a large pharma, has multiple offices at different sites, different cities, I count that as 1, meaning these guys have actually seen more than 50 distinct customers over the last few months. The message that they're bringing to the headquarters is that there's a tremendous amount of appreciation for the kinds of studies that they're getting, and they're targeting progressively more and more biopharma customers. That is a priority for us. These are the customers with recurrent revenue, quarter-after-quarter revenue growth.

And then additionally, also looking at where the samples are, meaning we rather have -- we rather focus our commercial effort on large customers with recurring revenue quarter-after-quarter, and then customers that have the budget, customers that have the samples. We're now in multiple discussions of pharma and other types of customers that the initial discussions are at 10,000-plus samples. I expect to announce 1 of those over the course of the next few weeks that's going to be a 10,000-plus sample customer that -- with an initial order on a couple of thousand sample size. These are the kind of customers that Tony is targeting.

And I think it's a combination of the validation of the platform that is becoming more and more seen in the eyes of the customer that translates into these kinds of activities.

Kyle Boucher: Maybe just one more on pull-through. So I guess, can you just talk about what you're seeing from a pull-through perspective? I think in the past, you noted that it could take somewhere around 6 to 9 months for customers to reorder consumables after purchasing an instrument. So are you seeing consumables being reordered by customers who purchased instruments late 2025 into early this year?

Omid Farokhzad: Kyle, let me introduce you to Charles, and Charles is going to take that. I might add at the end of it, but Charles?

Charles Endweiss: Yes, Kyle. So the pull-through was relatively flat, sequentially quarter over quarter. Our established customers continued to purchase consumables, including accounts with purchases across multiple consecutive quarters. The purchasing remains project driven, so individual customers may order for a study and then there's a gap between when they reorder. Our priority is to build a broader base of repeat usage and higher utilization, and we're working to expand the number of active programs within each of these accounts.

#3231. When Electric Cars Were for Women

Early carmakers decided women wanted cars that were quiet, clean, and easy to start

Allison Marsh is a professor at the University of South Carolina and the codirector of the Ann Johnson Institute for Science, Technology & Society.

When automobiles were still a novelty, electric cars vied with those powered by steam and internal combustion.

At the turn of the last century, the automobile industry was still new and evolving rapidly. In 1898, there were about 50 carmakers in the United States. A decade later, that number had increased fivefold. In 1901, the companies produced 7,000 vehicles. By 1910, production had reached 181,000.

For several decades, electric cars vied with those powered by steam and internal combustion, and nobody was sure which technology would come out on top. Steam had the legacy of locomotive technology behind it but came with a risk of fire. Steam-powered vehicles could also become exceedingly hot, depending on the placement of the boiler and the steam piping. Both gasoline and electric cars faced logistical challenges: How far could you travel without refueling or charging? You could always throw an extra can of gasoline in the back of the car, but charging a battery involved more planning. The infrastructure for long-distance travel was not yet in place.

Before the invention of the electric starter in 1911, gasoline-powered engines had to be started with a hand crank; once running, they were loud and emitted noxious fumes. Fully electric vehicles, by contrast, were easy to start; you just turned on the main battery switch, often with a key, and there was no foul exhaust to deal with.

Electric carmakers looking for a way to differentiate their products decided that these attributes made their vehicles perfect for women. (Electric cars were also marketed to doctors so that they could make house calls in the middle of the night without waking the neighbors.) General Electric, which made car chargers based on mercury-arc rectifiers, was so captivated by the idea of women driving electric cars that the company created a series of advertisements featuring stylishly dressed women plugging in their cars and posing with their charging stations.

In ads for its electric car chargers, General Electric featured women using the equipment.miSci—Museum of Innovation and Science

A young woman named Fannie Goodnow was an early EV adopter. She owned a 1908 Bailey Victoria Phaeton, an open two-seater that really did look like a horseless carriage, and she used a GE mercury-arc rectifier to charge it.

Electrical engineer Peter Cooper Hewitt invented the mercury vapor lamp, which became the basis for the mercury-arc rectifier used in car-charging systems. Bettmann/Getty Images

Electrical engineer Peter Cooper Hewitt is generally credited with the invention of the mercury-arc rectifier. During the first decade of the 20th century, Hewitt received several U.S. patents for electric lamps and other apparatus for transmitting and using electric currents. U.S. patents 968,896 and 1,163,706, granted to Percy H. Thomas, advanced Hewitt’s designs. Thomas was chief electrician for the Cooper Hewitt Electric Co., which Hewitt had cofounded with George Westinghouse to manufacture and sell his lamps.

The mercury-arc rectifier functioned as a diode. In a car charger like the one Fannie Goodnow used, it converted alternating current from the power grid into direct current needed to charge the car’s battery. A small amount of liquid mercury contained in a glass tube would vaporize and glow as electricity passed through it. Coupled with the carbon anodes, the vapor allowed current to flow in only one direction. This unit took about 12 hours to charge a drained battery.

I couldn’t find any records as to why Fannie Goodnow opted for an electric car. But as a well-to-do woman living in the Boston area, she had more than a half dozen automobile producers to choose from. The one she chose was S.R. Bailey & Co. of Amesbury, Mass.

This early electric car charger used a mercury-arc rectifier to convert AC to DC.Heritage Museums & Gardens

According to Galen Handy, who maintains the Early Electric Vehicles website, Samuel Robinson Bailey started in the carriage and sleigh business as a teenager, winning a best-in-show prize at a carriage exhibition in Portland, Maine, in 1855. Bailey developed a reputation as an inventor and designed processes to streamline the manufacture of his vehicles. He went into business for himself in 1882. Just over a decade later, one of Bailey’s carriages won a gold medal at the 1893 World’s Columbian Exposition in Chicago.

Bailey’s son Edwin attended the exposition, where he likely would have seen a vision of the future: the Morrison electric wagon. This six-passenger, battery-powered vehicle ferried visitors and VIPs around the fairgrounds. It wasn’t long before automobiles began eating into the carriage business. In December 1906, with the carriage industry collapsing, S.R. Bailey & Co. announced it was getting into electric vehicles.

Bailey’s first model, the Victoria Phaeton, used an Edison alkaline battery. Thomas Edison had been working on a lighter, more reliable, and more powerful battery for the auto industry since the 1890s, and announced the achievement with great fanfare in 1903. Unfortunately for Bailey and other carmakers who deployed it, the battery leaked and wouldn’t hold a charge. Edison was forced to go back to the drawing board. By 1910, he had a better battery in production, but by then his friend Henry Ford had introduced the Model T, setting the stage for the internal combustion engine to take over the market.

While Edison toiled to improve his tech, Bailey pivoted to a battery from the Gould Storage Battery Co. of Depew, N.Y. Gould also supplied batteries for railroads, utilities, subways, elevators, and farms. Goodnow’s Victoria Phaeton used a 30-cell lead-acid battery housed in a wooden box that was suspended under the chassis. The standard battery had a range of 64 to 80 kilometers; a larger battery with 50 percent more capacity was available for an upcharge. With the standard battery, the Victoria Phaeton cost US $2,000 (about $73,000 today, or about the list price of an upscale EV like the Audi Q8 or BMW i5).

Fannie Goodnow’s electric car charger now resides at the Heritage Museums & Gardens in Sandwich, Mass. But her 1908 Bailey Victoria Phaeton has been lost to history. Shown here is a 1911 version of that model.Sarah Thornington/Heritage Museums & Gardens

Goodnow installed a mercury-arc rectifier charging station in the barn adjacent to her parents’ summer home in Hull, Mass. Bill Lillie of Vintage Electric Cars notes that the charging plug was of an unusual design. This is, of course, one of the banes of any early adopter: nonstandardized plugs and cables. The Electric Vehicle Association of America, which formed in 1910, tried to put forward a standard so that electric vehicles could be charged at any charging station. (Modern EV owners can no doubt relate.) But savvy electric car owners knew to carry spare plug adapters and cables when traveling.

When Edison’s improved battery was finally available, Bailey began using it in the Victoria Phaeton and then went on a publicity blitz. In September 1910, the carmaker sponsored a round-trip tour from New York to Boston, with a side trip up New Hampshire’s Mount Washington, totaling about 1,600 km. Sadly, the “This Car Climbed Mt. Washington” bumper sticker hadn’t yet become popular.

Thomas Edison supplied the batteries for an electric car made by S.R. Bailey & Co., which then went on a publicity road trip from New York to Boston. miSci—Museum of Innovation and Science

Although Thomas Edison posed for a photo with the new Bailey Victoria Phaeton that featured his new battery, he himself chose a Detroit Electric Victoria for his own use. (Edison was known to be a terrible driver, so someone else likely chauffeured him around.)

Unable to compete against the rising tide of Model Ts, S.R. Bailey sold its factory in 1915, having produced about 500 to 600 electric vehicles.

Although the vehicle Fannie Goodnow chose turned out to be just a blip in automotive history, I like to imagine her driving about town in a beautiful car that embodied all the quirks of early adoption. I hope her friends didn’t make fun of her for investing in electric just before internal combustion took off. I hope she didn’t get stranded without the proper charging cable. I do not know what happened to her or her Victoria Phaeton, but her charging station remained in situ until 2022, when it was donated to the Heritage Museums & Gardens in Sandwich, Mass. Now it stands ready to tell stories of technological change and adoption that continue to resonate today.

Part of a continuing series looking at historical artifacts that embrace the boundless potential of technology.

An abridged version of this article appears in the November 2026 print issue.

References For a detailed history of the development of the mercury-arc rectifier (or valve), see Deepak Tiku’s article in the March/April 2014 issue of IEEE Power & Energy Magazine.Harry Cooke Cushing Jr., a fellow of the American Institute of Electrical Engineers, wrote (and updated regularly over a number of years) The Electric Vehicle Hand-Book, which gave general instructions for the care and storage of batteries, including how to charge them with a mercury-arc rectifier. Discussion of the mercury-arc rectifier begins on page 156 of the 10th edition, published in 1922. (The American Institute of Electrical Engineers is one of the predecessor organizations of the IEEE.)

For a detailed history of the development of the mercury-arc rectifier (or valve), see Deepak Tiku’s article in the March/April 2014 issue of IEEE Power & Energy Magazine.

Harry Cooke Cushing Jr., a fellow of the American Institute of Electrical Engineers, wrote (and updated regularly over a number of years) The Electric Vehicle Hand-Book, which gave general instructions for the care and storage of batteries, including how to charge them with a mercury-arc rectifier. Discussion of the mercury-arc rectifier begins on page 156 of the 10th edition, published in 1922. (The American Institute of Electrical Engineers is one of the predecessor organizations of the IEEE.)

Allison Marsh is a professor in Women and Gender Studies at the University of South Carolina and codirector of the university’s Ann Johnson Institute for Science, Technology & Society. She combines her interests in engineering, history, and museum objects to write the Past Forward column, which tells the story of technology through historical artifacts. Marsh is currently working on a book on the history of women in electrical engineering.

The King of the Monsters is back, and bigger than ever. “Godzilla Minus Zero,” the sequel to 2023’s Oscar-winning “Godzilla Minus One,” stomped into U.S. theaters on November 6, and it's been attracting kaiju-hungry viewers ever since.

Picking up in 1949, two years after the events of the first film, the sequel continues the story of the Shikishima family in a shattered post-war Japan as they face a new threat from the towering kaiju.

The film was shot specifically for IMAX, the first Japanese production ever to do so. It’s playing in theaters right now, but how long before you can watch it from the comfort of your own couch?

Since it just hit theaters, “Godzilla Minus Zero” isn’t available on any of the best streaming services just yet. Here’s the good news, though: based on how its predecessor rolled out, we can make a solid guess about when you’ll be able to rent, buy, and stream it at home.

If you’re curious about when to start planning for a giant lizard-stomping movie night, we’ve got the answers right here. Keep reading to find out.

North American distributor GKIDS hasn’t announced a digital release date yet, but if “Godzilla Minus Zero” follows the typical pattern for a theatrical release, it should hit premium video-on-demand (PVOD) about a month after it opens, at which point you can rent or buy it on platforms like Amazon and Apple TV.

Counting forward from its November 6 release, that points to a digital debut sometime in December 2026.

Sign up to the weekly Tom's Streaming Guide to stay in the loop with the latest releases and top recommendations across your favorite streaming services. We’ve got you covered with a complete guide on what’s worth watching.

Physical media is a different story. It typically follows a few weeks after the digital release. “Godzilla Minus One” got a well-regarded 4K UHD and Blu-ray release, so its sequel is likely to get the same treatment.

That means a physical release for “Godzilla Minus Zero” around January 2027 seems like a reasonable bet, though nothing has been confirmed just yet. Since it was shot for IMAX, a 4K disc will be the closest most people get to that presentation at home.

As for streaming the movie with a subscription service, our strongest clue for a release date is how the first film was handled. “Godzilla Minus One” landed on Netflix in the U.S. about six months after its theatrical release, and with Netflix having become the streaming home for that movie, its sequel seems likely to follow suit.

If it sticks to the same roughly six-month timeline, “Godzilla Minus Zero” could reach Netflix sometime around May 2027. A ways off, yes, but good things are worth waiting for.

That said, nothing about the streaming date has been officially confirmed, so the exact platform and timing could still change. For now, the only way to see Godzilla’s latest rampage is on the biggest screen you can find. And you can still enjoy the other 30+ movies in the "Godzilla" franchise while waiting.

“Godzilla Minus Zero” is a direct sequel to 2023’s “Godzilla Minus One,” so you'll want to make sure you're caught up before watching this movie. It was set in the ashes of World War II and followed Kōichi Shikishima (Ryunosuke Kamiki), a former kamikaze pilot consumed by guilt after failing to act during an earlier Godzilla attack.

Back in Tokyo, he builds a family with Noriko (Minami Hamabe) and an orphaned child, only for a mutated Godzilla to rise from the sea and lay waste to the city. A group of civilian veterans ultimately got together to take the monster down and succeeded, so you'll want to watch that play out before diving into this movie.

“Minus Zero” picks the story back up in 1949, two years after those events. The Shikishima family has started to rebuild amid a Japan still struggling to recover, but the peace doesn’t last, and Godzilla returns to threaten the country once again.

With the memory of the last devastation still fresh, a disaster-response team scrambles to prepare for the renewed menace, and the Shikishimas are pulled right back into the fight for survival. And yes, it's just as epic in scale as the last movie, so you'll want to catch this one whether you see it at home or on the big screen.

Apple’s HomeView arrives this Friday (pre-order here), but leaks indicate there are already two major new features in the works that haven’t been announced. Here’s what to expect.

It’s been a busy product launch season for Apple, and the company isn’t done quite yet.

Two new Home products arrive in stores this Friday, November 13: Apple HomeView and the new Apple TV 4K.

Yet despite the HomeView still being days away from launch, leaks in Apple code have already revealed two unannounced features that are in the works.

Leaker pdfu discovered evidence in HomeView 27.2 software that Apple is preparing for the product to add security camera functionality.

Based on pdfu’s findings, much of the work has already been done for HomeView to integrate with HomeKit Secure Video.

However, Apple hasn’t announced any sort of security camera functionality, so there’s clearly still more work to be done and it’s always possible the feature is never enabled.

Additionally, pdfu found a key change in iOS 27.3’s beta that reveals support for third-party AI apps is coming to HomeView.

HomeView has a unique third-party app story. There’s no App Store, but the product can run CarPlay-compatible apps from your iPhone automatically. At launch, only audio and video apps will be supported.

But iOS 27.3’s beta code adds “conversational apps” as a third category of supported apps. That’s what AI chatbots like ChatGPT and Claude are classified as in CarPlay.

Nobody should buy a HomeView in the hope of these two features being added. But if you are interested in HomeView, it sounds like Apple has an ambitious set of software updates planned for its new product.

#3228. Guarding the Gates of Knowledge

AI can fake a plausible paper at the push of a button. Can detection tools and peer review keep up?

Harry Goldstein is Editor in Chief of IEEE Spectrum.

A recent scroll through social media got me thinking about trust. About half my feed was filled with AI slop that astute users would call out as being machine-generated, often to the embarrassment of the rube who unknowingly spread it and sometimes to the delight of the poster who shared it deliberately because they found it amusing or useful for sowing confusion.

Remember the good old days of GPT-3 when we could ask the chatbot anything and it would almost instantly and very confidently spit back a plausible but false answer? That’s when the word “hallucination” as applied to AI answers entered the lexicon. Six years and several versions of a few different chatbots later, I still can’t trust the answers I get, even though Claude or Gemini often do useful work for me. That’s the thing about current AI: Trust but verify. And verify you must.

Apply that maxim at scale to maintain the integrity of the scientific record and you get an idea of the challenge facing publishers of peer-reviewed scholarship. In “I Used AI to Fake a Scientific Paper,” freelance writer and doctor of applied mathematics Benjamin Skuse tells the story of the human gatekeepers trying to beat back the rising tide of AI slop by attempting to get his own AI-generated papers past IEEE’s defenses.

“He basically hit ‘run experiment’ and ‘write paper.’ And then he didn’t do a damn thing to it.” —Eliza Strickland

As features and AI beat editor Eliza Strickland told me, Skuse was surprised at just how effortless it was to generate a paper that was more or less plausible and more or less science. For one of his experiments, “he basically hit ‘run experiment’ and ‘write paper,’” she said. “And then he didn’t do a damn thing to it. He just launched it into the maw of the publishing engine.”

Skuse discovered that the combination of IEEE’s human-review processes and research-integrity checker programs are currently keeping pace in what amounts to a cat-and-mouse game against people using free tools. But the more advanced LLMs are no longer making the same dumb mistakes the free versions do. That leaves publishers locked in an arms race between increasingly plausible slop and the systems aimed at detecting it.

Scholarly publishers aren’t the only ones trying to hold the line against slop. So is that global depository of human-generated knowledge, Wikipedia. For this month’s Five Questions, Strickland interviewed Ellia Lebleu, a founding member of WikiProject AI Cleanup, a volunteer effort to detect and delete AI-generated material from the platform. Lebleu’s team is confronting the same problem as commercial publishers, but with fewer people and fewer tools.

“Wikipedia is known as a repository of human-generated information, and they want to hold on to that,” says Strickland. “Who knows how long they’ll be able to do that.”

If we can’t collectively assume that the scientific record is trustworthy or that basic facts about the world are accurate, then our understanding of what is real unspools into uncertainty. Perhaps that delights quantum scientists and the grifters who thrive in an information environment where there is no shared reality. But that uncertainty ultimately undermines trust in the institutions that exist to curate the corpus of human knowledge and to promote the advancement of science and technology for the benefit of humanity.

Or maybe in a world where AI is doing the science and writing the papers, it won’t matter whether or not humans trust the outputs. As Strickland put it, “Doesn’t it just feel crazy that we’ll have AI writing for other AIs at some point? We’ll just get left out of the loop.”

Harry Goldstein is Editor in Chief of IEEE Spectrum.
