#3227. Inovio (INO) Q3 2026 Earnings Call Transcript

Inovio's VOCERYQ launch plans and cash runway outlook are now in focus.

Need a quote from a Motley Fool analyst? Email [email protected]

Inovio Pharmaceuticals, Inc. (INO -3.97%) transitioned to a commercial-stage company following the FDA's accelerated approval of VOCERYQ for the treatment of adults with recurrent respiratory papillomatosis (RRP). Management stated that the company is now focused on executing its commercial launch strategy in the United States while preparing for international expansion and further regulatory filings in Europe. The company strengthened its financial position through a public equity offering that provided $80.5 million in net proceeds, extending the projected cash runway into late 2027. Leadership indicated that the approval validates the proprietary DNA medicine platform and provides a foundation for the development of its rare disease pipeline candidates.

Operator: Good afternoon, ladies and gentlemen, and welcome to the Inovio Pharmaceuticals Third Quarter 2026 Financial Results Conference Call. [Operator Instructions] This call is being recorded on Tuesday, November 10, 2026. And I would now like to turn the conference over to Jennie Willson. Thank you. Please go ahead.

Jennie Willson: Good afternoon, and thank you for joining the Inovio Third Quarter 2026 Financial Results Conference Call. Joining me on today's call are Dr. Jacqui Shea, President and Chief Executive Officer; Dr. Mike Sumner, Chief Medical Officer; Steven Egge, Chief Commercial Officer; and Peter Kies, Chief Financial Officer. Today's call will review our corporate and financial information for the quarter ended September 30, 2026, as well as provide a general business update. Following prepared remarks, we will conduct a question-and-answer segment.

Before we begin, I'd like to remind you that we will be making certain forward-looking statements as outlined in this slide, including, but not limited to, our ability to obtain and maintain regulatory approval of our product candidates, the design and timing of our planned confirmatory study, the potential benefits of VOCERYQ and its potential to become a product preferred by patients and their physicians, our commercial launch plans and strategy, including anticipated cash runway, cash burn and timing of product revenues, and our plans to expand VOCERYQ into additional indications and geographies to advance our broader pipeline. All of these statements are based on the beliefs and expectations of management as of today.

Actual events or results could differ materially. We refer you to the documents we file from time to time with the SEC, which, under the heading Risk Factors, identify important factors that could cause actual results to differ materially from those expressed verbally by the company or in this afternoon's press release. This call is being webcast live, and a link can be found on our website, ir.inovio.com, and a replay will be made available shortly after this call is concluded. I will now turn the call over to Inovio's President and CEO, Dr. Jacqui Shea.

Jacqueline Shea: Good afternoon, and thank you to everyone for joining. I'd like to start today's call by highlighting the recent FDA approval of VOCERYQ, formerly known as INO-3107, under the Accelerated Approval Program as a new nonsurgical treatment option to reduce the frequency of surgery in adults with recurrent respiratory papillomatosis, or RRP. In the press release it issued, the FDA stated that VOCERYQ was a groundbreaking therapy and that its approval represented a meaningful scientific breakthrough by offering patients a plasmid DNA-based immunotherapy that harnesses the body's own immune system to fight the underlying cause of RRP.

The accelerated approval for VOCERYQ and the broad indication included in its label for adults with RRP are an acknowledgment of the significant unmet need for nonsurgical treatment options for RRP and the potential therapeutic benefit that VOCERYQ can provide. We believe it has the potential to transform the treatment paradigm for this disease by delivering what we understand matters most to patients: reducing the need for surgery. This is a pivotal moment for RRP patients who have faced a relentless cycle of surgery for far too long with limited treatment options, and for Inovio, as we move forward into an exciting new chapter as a commercial-stage company.

Going forward, our primary focus will be maximizing the opportunity we see for VOCERYQ and executing our commercial launch with the goal of establishing it as the preferred first-line treatment for adults with RRP. To support those efforts, we recently completed an equity offering that provided approximately $80.5 million in net proceeds. These proceeds, together with our existing cash resources and subsequent warrant exercise proceeds, are expected to support operations into late fourth quarter 2027, past the launch of VOCERYQ, without taking potential expected product revenues into account. The approval of our first commercial product validates our platform and confirms our belief in the potential of our pipeline candidates to help patients suffering from other diseases.

While our initial focus is on the successful launch of VOCERYQ within our broad adult indication, we will also be looking to expand the potential of VOCERYQ to serve additional indications within the RRP marketplace, both here in the U.S. and internationally. We will also continue to prioritize partnerships to efficiently advance our clinical-stage candidates and look to establish new partnerships to advance promising earlier-stage candidates in our pipeline. This is truly a transformative time for Inovio and for DNA medicine, and we are excited about the significant opportunities ahead. I'll now turn it over to Mike Sumner, our Chief Medical Officer, to provide a few more details on the approval, product label and supporting clinical data. Mike?

Michael Sumner: Thank you, Jacqui. The approval of VOCERYQ is exciting on many fronts. It's Inovio's first approved product, the first FDA-approved plasmid DNA-based immunotherapy, and most importantly, an innovative and much-needed new treatment option for adults with RRP. I'd like to spend some time today providing a few highlights from the approval of VOCERYQ and its broad adult indication. VOCERYQ was evaluated in RRP-001, a multi-site clinical study designed to assess what matters most to patients, reduction in surgery. The study followed 32 adult patients who had 2 to 8 surgeries in the year prior to treatment. Patients had visible papillomas surgically removed before receiving their first dose of VOCERYQ. Patients then received 4 doses over a 9-week period.

The primary efficacy endpoint was a reduction in surgery following dosing initiation. In this trial, we counted all surgeries after the first dose against the efficacy endpoint. We also conducted study RRP-002, a retrospective assessment of treatment effect up to 3 years after initial dosing in patients who had participated in the 001 study. The full clinical data from these studies were published in 2025 in Nature Communications and in The Laryngoscope, the top journal for the specialists who treat RRP. An additional analysis of data was also recently published in The Laryngoscope, supporting the ability of VOCERYQ to generate an immune response that linked to durable clinical benefit over the second and third years following initial treatment.

These publications highlight the meaningful therapeutic benefit of VOCERYQ, with the vast majority of patients experiencing a 50% to 100% reduction in surgery in year 1, with durable responses and continued clinical improvement in year 2. The FDA's efficacy evaluation for Accelerated Approval focused specifically on the first year treatment effect for patients who required 3 or more surgeries in the 12 months prior to treatment. For those 26 patients, the median number of surgeries in the 12 months prior to the first dose was 4.5, which included the surgical debulking required immediately prior to treatment. FDA's efficacy analysis started at the end of the dosing window at week 9.

In the following 12 months, 27% of the patients achieved complete response, as defined by not requiring any surgeries to manage their disease. And as a reminder, this response was achieved without conducting any scoping or surgery during the dosing window. Patients going from needing 3 or more surgeries a year to needing 0 surgeries following treatment would not be expected as part of the natural history of the disease. In terms of safety, VOCERYQ was found in the clinical study to be well tolerated, with study participants experiencing mostly low-grade treatment-emergent adverse events such as injection site pain and fatigue, with the majority being grade 1.

This slide lists the most common adverse reactions occurring in greater than or equal to 5% of patients, as described in the prescribing information. Of note, because VOCERYQ is a drug device combination product composed of our plasmid DNA-based drug with delivery by our CELLECTRA device, this safety profile represents the combination product. For this approval, the safety data were further supported by data from prior clinical trials of VGX-3100, an HPV-16 and 18 related disease program, which included over 1,100 administrations and a placebo control. Delivery with our proprietary CELLECTRA device is well characterized and has also been shown in additional clinical studies to be well tolerated.

It is also important to point out here that reducing the need for surgery, both as part of or following treatment, is an important consideration for patients. Every surgery matters because every individual surgery comes with significant risk. Finally, I'd like to share a brief overview of our future confirmatory study. As VOCERYQ has received an Accelerated Approval, continued approval for this indication may be contingent on verification and description of clinical benefit in a confirmatory study. We expect to submit a draft protocol for this study before year-end with the goal of aligning with the FDA on a final protocol by mid-2027.

We have agreed with the agency that the study should enroll at least 50 adult and pediatric patients with RRP requiring 3 or more surgical interventions in the 12 months prior to treatment with VOCERYQ. Subject to further regulatory feedback, we expect the study to evaluate the number of surgical interventions required over at least 3 years following completion of treatment, and compare this to an appropriate external control group or scientifically justified threshold. We may also explore continued treatment in patients without a sustained complete response as part of the study. I will now turn it over to Steve Egge, our Chief Commercial Officer, for an overview of our commercial launch plans. Steve?

Steven Egge: Thank you, Mike. We're excited to launch VOCERYQ and are focused on ensuring eligible RRP patients can access treatment as quickly and efficiently as possible. Let's start by discussing the significant RRP market opportunity. Based on our ongoing analysis of claims data, we believe there's a prevalent population of at least 25,000 adult patients with RRP in the United States, with additional patients diagnosed each year. Most patients continue to be managed surgically, and every single surgery comes with a risk of permanent vocal cord and airway damage.

Key opinion leaders and the RRP Foundation stated in a position paper published in The Laryngoscope in January of this year that immunotherapy should be considered the first-line treatment for RRP, and that it should be started as soon as possible in the patient's disease journey to reduce the risk of permanent damage from repeated surgeries. This position paper also noted that should VOCERYQ be approved by the FDA, it would be recommended as first-line therapy. To date, only a small fraction of the prevalent population of patients have been treated with immunotherapy, indicating there is a significant market opportunity for a nonsurgical therapeutic treatment option designed to reduce the frequency of surgeries.

Our goal is to establish VOCERYQ as the preferred first-line treatment for adults with RRP by leveraging what we believe are the key differentiating strengths of the product. VOCERYQ targets the root cause of RRP to deliver compelling efficacy, reducing the need for surgery. Importantly, it provides this efficacy without requiring scoping and surgical removal of visible papilloma during the dosing window, which makes it a patient-centric approach to treatment. VOCERYQ also has a favorable tolerability profile, with the potential to minimize disruption to patient lives. And for physicians, providing treatment is simple and straightforward.

The device is designed to be easy to use and has a standard refrigeration requirement for drug storage that allows for flexibility in the location of administration. These strengths are what we believe can enable VOCERYQ to become the immunotherapy of choice for both patients and physicians. Looking at the patient journey in more detail, physicians and patients can discuss treatment with VOCERYQ as soon as a diagnosis has been established through the first biopsy or surgery. Once prescribed, the patient would undergo initial papilloma removal and then complete a 4-dose treatment series over 9 weeks. As we've noted in the label for VOCERYQ, there's no requirement to conduct scoping or surgery during the dosing window.

This patient-centric approach helps to eliminate or reduce surgeries both during and after treatment. Looking ahead, I'd like to outline our priorities to support a successful launch. First, we're working to ensure patients can access VOCERYQ as quickly as possible. Payers recognize the burden of recurrent surgery in RRP and the need for additional treatment options. We expect insurers that cover approximately 80% of patients in the U.S. to have policies in place for coverage within 9 months of approval based on our payer research to date.

In parallel, we plan to apply for a permanent J-code to help simplify reimbursement, support medical exception pathways and work closely with integrated delivery networks, or IDNs, and hospital systems to initiate product availability through pharmacy and therapeutics committee reviews. These committees decide which medications are added to the IDN or hospital's official drug list or formulary. Second, our commercial field teams will plan to engage targeted laryngologists and associated staff to educate on VOCERYQ and drive awareness and adoption. The focus will be communicating the unique value proposition of VOCERYQ.

To support adoption, as soon as providers are ready to start prescribing VOCERYQ, we will provide CELLECTRA devices, coupled with in-person training and implementation support, to ensure accounts can begin treating patients efficiently. Third, we aim to make the treatment process as seamless as possible for both patients and physicians. We're launching the VOCERYQ Support Program with a single point of contact to provide support around product ordering, patient benefit investigation and verification, co-pay support and our patient assistance program. Our goal is to minimize the administrative burden and make access to treatment simple for both health care providers and patients. We aim to have the VOCERYQ Support Program in place once product is available.

To drive awareness and adoption, our strategy is focused on efficiently reaching the physicians who treat the majority of patients with RRP. To do this, we plan to leverage highly experienced field teams through our field deployment partner, Syneos Health. Using a field deployment partner enables us to rapidly scale the team with highly experienced personnel as quickly as possible. As a rare disease, RRP is a concentrated market. About 400 laryngologists treat the vast majority of RRP patients. About 80% of these patients with RRP receive care in large IDNs or academic institutions, and there are about 100 of these institutions treating the majority of patients in this important segment.

The remaining 20% of RRP patients receive care in community hospitals and private group practices. Our field teams will plan to engage both of these important customer segments. And overall, our field footprint is designed to cover about 90% of RRP patient potential. Our field organization is expected to include 20 territories with key account managers, reimbursement specialists and dedicated payer support capabilities deployed across those territories. Our medical team has also commenced deployment of medical science liaisons to engage with KOLs in the field. With recruitment and deployment already underway, we believe this targeted model positions us to drive rapid awareness, adoption and patient access. We believe we've established the infrastructure needed to support a successful U.S. launch.

We expect our device and plasmid manufacturing network to be prepared to meet anticipated demand, with current inventory and capacity available to support the first year of launch through at least 2027. We currently expect VOCERYQ to be available to order and ship in approximately 60 days from the approval date, and expect full field deployment during the first quarter of 2027. Based on the combination of strong clinical data and broad adult indication, the significant unmet need and concentrated prescriber base, we're confident in the potential for a successful launch and longer-term commercial success.

I will now turn the call back to Jacqui to discuss how we plan to build on this approval and continue advancing our DNA medicines pipeline.

Jacqueline Shea: Thanks, Steve. The approval of VOCERYQ is a pivotal milestone for Inovio that we believe offers many exciting opportunities to drive progress across the Inovio pipeline. With VOCERYQ as our primary focus, we plan to initially invest in exploring opportunities to expand its ability to serve the RRP community, including pediatrics and continued treatment options for adults. One of the strengths of our platform is the ability to provide additional doses that can continue to amplify the targeted T cell response. We're also evaluating additional geographic markets, including the EU, U.K. and other international markets. And we plan to submit an application for conditional marketing authorization for VOCERYQ in Europe before the end of 2026.

As we look further ahead, we plan to leverage VOCERYQ's approval and the important validation of our DNA medicine platform to advance other promising candidates in the pipeline. Partnerships will continue to be important to advance our later-stage clinical candidates, and we are also seeking new partnerships to advance our next-generation DPROT candidates in rare disease. We believe these investigational protein replacement therapies have the potential to transform the treatment paradigm for rare diseases like hemophilia A, Fabry disease and hypophosphatasia. I'll now turn it over to our Chief Financial Officer, Peter Kies, for a financial update. Peter?

Peter Kies: Thanks, Jacqui. Today, I'd like to provide an overview of Inovio's financial results for the third quarter of 2026. With the upcoming launch of VOCERYQ, we are focused on supporting our commercial build-out. To support these efforts, we recently strengthened our balance sheet with an underwritten public equity offering that provided net proceeds of approximately $80.5 million after deducting underwriter discounts, commissions and offering expenses. These resources, along with the $48.4 million in cash, cash equivalents and short-term investments at the end of the third quarter of '26 and a further $10.9 million in proceeds from the exercise of warrants subsequent to September 30, 2026, are projected to support operations into late fourth quarter 2027, past the launch of VOCERYQ.

This projection includes an operational net cash burn estimate of approximately $21 million for the fourth quarter of 2026 as we ramp up our commercialization activities. These cash runway projections do not include the contribution of revenues from sales of VOCERYQ expected to commence in 2027 or any further capital-raising activities that we may undertake, and are based on current projections and assumptions. Turning to our results for the third quarter. Operating expenses decreased from $21.2 million in the third quarter of 2025 to $19.8 million in the third quarter of 2026.

Inovio's net loss for the third quarter of 2026 was $49.2 million or $0.50 per share basic and diluted compared to a net loss of $45.5 million or $0.87 per share basic and diluted for the third quarter of 2025. The increase in net loss was primarily driven by a $26.9 million non-cash loss on fair value adjustment related to our warrant liabilities for the third quarter of 2026 compared to a $22.5 million non-cash loss for the same period in 2025. As the fair value of the warrants fluctuate with our share price and other market inputs, this adjustment can result in significant variability in our reported net loss.

As a reminder, you can find our full financial statements in this afternoon's press release as well as in our quarterly report on Form 10-Q filed today with the SEC. And with that, I'll turn it back over to Jacqui.

Jacqueline Shea: Thanks, Peter. I'd now like to pause to open up the call to answer any questions you might have. Operator?

Operator: [Operator Instructions] And your first question comes from the line of Roger Song from Jefferies.

Peter Chen: Congrats on the quarter. This is Peter calling in for Roger. So just a couple from us. On the launch with PAPZIMEOS' strong early uptake, where do you see VOCERYQ positioned to win at the launch? And then on durability, what do you think explains the year 1 to year 2 improvement in surgery-free rates? And what gives you confidence that this is a true deepening of response?

Jacqueline Shea: Thanks. Great questions. To start off with the first one, I think what we're seeing with PAPZIMEOS in terms of the strong uptake that they've seen really indicates the high unmet need in this patient population. From our claims database analysis work, we estimate that there are about 25,000 patients in the U.S., adult patients in the U.S., with RRP. And to date, immunotherapy has only reached a fraction of those patients. So we think there's a strong opportunity for VOCERYQ. And we think with VOCERYQ's compelling efficacy, favorable tolerability profile and a patient-centric treatment approach that doesn't require scoping and surgeries during the treatment window, that we have the potential to become the preferred first-line therapy in this space.

And when we conduct market research, we found that the majority of patients, when given a choice, would prefer a therapy that doesn't require scoping and surgeries as part of the dosing window. So we're very confident in our product profile. I think you also asked a second part of your question in terms of durability. And I think there, what I can say is we saw a very solid durability into the second year, which was also maintained into the third year. And this was broadly across patients, regardless of the numbers of surgeries that they've had in the year prior, regardless of types of HPV. Mike, anything you'd like to add to that?

Michael Sumner: Yes. I mean, I'd sort of say this is also the focus of our recent publication in The Laryngoscope that I highlighted in my prepared remarks. And we were very fortunate with our patients. We had 3-year data going in. And with that durability data, we had a very complete picture of these patients. And I think any statistical analysis that we performed, it showed that the treatment effect was both statistically and clinically meaningful.

Operator: And your next question comes from the line of Ted Tenthoff from Piper Sandler.

Edward Tenthoff: Great. Can you remind me sort of what the plans are? I know you mentioned that you're planning on submitting the MAA by year-end. What are your partnering plans for VOCERYQ overseas? And I have a quick follow-up.

Jacqueline Shea: Thanks, Ted. So I'll take the partnering question and then maybe, Mike, you can provide some additional color on our plans to submit for conditional marketing authorization in Europe. So in terms of partnering plans in the U.S., our plan is obviously to bring VOCERYQ to market ourselves. We do believe that we would benefit from partnerships in ex U.S. territories, and we're actively seeking partnerships in those areas. And clearly, the upcoming submission of a conditional marketing authorization application in Europe is going to be supportive of those efforts. So Mike?

Michael Sumner: Yes. So I mean, we obviously had discussions with our rapporteurs ahead of filing the application, and they were very supportive of us putting in a conditional marketing application. I think also now that we obviously have that application in process, there's also other geographical areas that we can look at expanding VOCERYQ in the approvals.

Edward Tenthoff: And a quick follow-up, Mike, if I may. Are there countries where FDA approval grants approvals overseas? And would that be something where you could seek distribution partners? Have you thought about that as well?

Michael Sumner: Yes. We have looked at that. I think we struggle with a lot of the regions that will accept an FDA approval don't have necessarily the resources to be able to fund a product like VOCERYQ. So we're continually examining that as we look at our geographical expansion strategy.

Edward Tenthoff: That makes a lot of sense. And I'm just curious, with the approval of VOCERYQ, I know you guys have been developing the DPROT and the dMAb technology. Do you envision that, that approval and that validation could accelerate or actuate partnerships for some of the early-stage programs for long-term protein and/or antibody expression?

Jacqueline Shea: Yes, that's a great question. So yes, in one word, we do see the approval of VOCERYQ as validation of the platform and of our delivery device. And we do think it's going to generate interest in the other programs in our pipeline. We are incredibly excited by the potential of our DPROT candidates to address other rare diseases. We've published clinical proof-of-concept data in terms of being able to produce monoclonal antibodies within the body for over 96 weeks without generating any antidrug antibodies. So we're really excited by this potential. And Mike, maybe you want to comment on some of the work that we've been doing across those indications and recent conference presentations.

Michael Sumner: I'd also like to just add, I mean, obviously, from a regulatory point of view, we've talked before about the applicability of our nonclinical data across our platforms. And I think with the approval of VOCERYQ, that clearly strengthened our CMC knowledge and also the fact that we have the first approved electroporation device in the world, I believe. That really strengthens our ability to rapidly move into new areas. And just as recently as this last weekend, I was able to present at the Soft Bones Conference with nonclinical proof-of-concept data for our ability to secrete alkaline phosphatase in a mouse model as a potential future therapeutic for hypophosphatasia. And we've been at several hemophilia conferences earlier.

So we're excited about where this platform is going.

Jacqueline Shea: And if I can just add here, when you look across our pipeline, there are sort of really 2 key areas. The later-stage clinical candidates, including VOCERYQ, are really driving targeted T cell responses. The earlier preclinical candidates are really focused on protein replacements. And we see these as 2 key strengths of the platform, where DNA medicines really have advantages over other platforms.

Edward Tenthoff: Excellent. Well, congrats on the approval and looking forward to continued progress.

Operator: And your next question comes from the line of Yi Chen from H.C. Wainwright.

Yi Chen: Could you tell us how many physicians have been trained to administer VOCERYQ using the CELLECTRA device? And how many academic centers and community ENT practice do you plan to target during the initial period of the full field launch in the first quarter of next year?

Jacqueline Shea: Thanks, Yi. So Mike, I'll ask you to talk about our clinical experience with training physicians to date. And then Steve, maybe you can take the commercial question.

Michael Sumner: Yes. So in terms of familiarity with our device in the United States, we obviously had the original 8 clinical trial sites, which were some of our leading academic centers in the U.S. And as we were preparing for our confirmatory study, we had potentially 20 sites there. So there's good familiarity with the device. In terms of actually training, because of the ease of use of the device, training is actually accomplished in approximately 30 minutes. We have a field medical team ready to train, but that training really needs to be associated with the administration of the product. So we will wait for the availability of the product in the field to really commence that training.

Steven Egge: Yes. So in terms of -- I think you asked about the number of accounts that we'll be targeting. So as I mentioned in the prepared remarks, in the integrated delivery system kind of segment of the business, these large academic institutions, about 80% of RRP patients receive care. And most of them are concentrated in just about 100 accounts, and we will be in all 100 of those accounts once our full field team is deployed. The other 20% receive care in community hospitals and physician practices, and we will engage there. We haven't shared kind of the number of accounts that we'll be engaging.

But what I can tell you is that, that 20-person field territory team that we're deploying is designed to cover 90% of RRP patient potential. So it will definitely be a broad effort once we're fully deployed in the first quarter of 2027.

Operator: Thank you. There are no further questions at this time. I will now hand the call back to Ms. Jacqui Shea for any closing remarks.

Jacqueline Shea: With the approval of VOCERYQ as our first product, Inovio has become a commercial-stage company. This is a landmark moment of validation for our DNA medicine platform, and we are incredibly excited about the potential to help the many RRP patients who are searching for relief from the relentless cycle of surgery. VOCERYQ offers compelling efficacy within a patient-centric treatment regimen that does not require scoping and surgeries during dosing, combined with a favorable tolerability profile and ease of use. Our goal is for it to become the preferred first-line treatment option for RRP. We're focused on meeting the needs of patients and building long-term commercial success.

We see multiple catalysts ahead, including in the near term, our first sales and revenue. We look forward to providing updates on our launch progress and delivering on the promise of our DNA medicine platform for all our stakeholders. Thank you, and good afternoon, everyone.

Operator: Thank you. And this concludes today's call. Thank you for participating. You may all disconnect.

#3225. Gritt and MasTec bring bolt-on construction robots to solar sites

MasTec will put Gritt's robot arms on its US solar farms, months after Burns & McDonnell signed up.

Infrastructure builder MasTec will deploy Gritt’s AI robotic attachments on its utility-scale solar projects across several US states, after testing them on live sites. It follows a similar deal with Burns & McDonnell in August. No financial terms were disclosed.

MasTec, one of North America’s largest infrastructure builders, will use Gritt’s AI-powered robots on its solar farms, the two companies said on Tuesday. Neither disclosed financial terms.

Gritt makes robotic arms that bolt onto equipment crews already use, such as skid steers and forklifts, to lift and place solar panels. MasTec tested the systems on live sites, where they helped install “megawatts” of panels. The companies now plan a pipeline of projects across several US states.

“We’ve evaluated Gritt systems on active construction sites, and we see an opportunity to pair our teams’ expertise with technology that supports them in the field,” said Rob Turner, vice president of construction at MasTec Renewables.

It is Gritt’s second named partner in three months. Burns & McDonnell signed a similar deal in August after a year of trials, Solar Power World reported.

When Gritt raised $32M in July, it said it worked with three of the top 10 US power construction firms but did not name them. It said its robots let crews place 3,000 to 4,000 panels a day instead of about 800.

At the time, Gritt had only two systems in the field. Its website now lists more than seven job sites.

Construction firms are turning to robots as skilled workers retire. Procore agreed to buy drone maker DroneDeploy for $845M in July, and welding startup Path Robotics raised $300M on Tuesday.

#3224. IEEE Computer Society Chapter Offers Webinars With Industry Experts

Attendees in Region 4 learn about AI, cybersecurity, and more

Siva Rama Krishna Varma Bayyavarapu is an IEEE senior member and secretary of the IEEE Computer Society’s Central Indiana Chapter.

To help engineers keep up with emerging technologies such as AI, cloud computing, and sustainable infrastructure, and learn how they can be applied in practice, the IEEE Computer Society’s Central Indiana Chapter recently launched its Tech Talk Series.

The live webinar series connects IEEE members, undergrad and graduate students, and engineering professionals from IEEE Region 4 with industry practitioners. The monthly sessions have covered AI governance and security, agentic systems, and related topics. The sessions featured speakers from Apple, software company Tavant, and cybersecurity concern Zscaler.

Upcoming sessions and registration details are available on the IEEE Region 4 virtual events calendar.

Rather than presenting on emerging technologies only at a conceptual level, speakers discussed the design decisions behind specific tools and systems, how the systems are structured, and implementation challenges. They also shared lessons learned from using the tools in their daily work.

Sessions also include technical walkthroughs and practical examples.

The live format allows attendees to discuss and compare their approaches when evaluating and implementing new technologies with those used by other organizations.

The organizers chose to make the series virtual so that chapter members and other attendees could participate in technical discussions with engineers from major technology companies and eliminate the need to travel.

For young professionals, the sessions connect what they’ve learned in a classroom with the realities of the workplace.

Technical programs such as the Tech Talk Series give professionals and students access to expertise, help create connections across career levels, and make important engineering discussions available to a broader community.

Attendees learn how practitioners approach projects such as system architecture, reliability, security, governance, and product delivery. For experienced professionals, the talks offer a forum to examine new ways of designing, securing, and operating software systems, and compare technical approaches. They can ask questions relevant to systems being evaluated or deployed within their organization.

The most recent webinar, Feeding and Fencing AI Agents: Engineering Governed Agentic Systems on Real-Time Data, featured Gajendra Babu Thokala, a senior engineering leader at Apple in Seattle.

The IEEE senior member explained how teams can move beyond adding isolated AI features to applications and instead build governed AI-agent systems that use real-time business data to complete multistep business workflows.

Another recent session, Building AI Native Products: A Playbook for Agentic Systems, explored how products built around AI agents differ from traditional software. It also covered how agentic systems can help users complete multistep tasks and workflows. IEEE Senior Member Sandeep Shivam, a product and technology leader at Tavant in Dallas, led the webinar.

Those two sessions illustrate the series’ purpose: helping participants understand what a technology can do and what is required to use it responsibly.

Future sessions are being planned on areas including enterprise AI, software reliability, and responsible AI usage. In addition to speakers from technology companies, the chapter also plans to invite speakers from startups, universities, and research organizations.

Upcoming sessions are expected to cover cloud platforms, enterprise integrations, and the responsible development of AI systems.

Technical programs such as the Tech Talk Series give professionals and students access to expertise, help create connections across career levels, and make important engineering discussions available to a broader community.

Undergraduate and graduate students are invited to participate to gain exposure to technical decision-making and challenges encountered in professional engineering environments.

Siva Rama Krishna Varma Bayyavarapu is an IEEE senior member and the secretary of the IEEE Computer Society Central Indiana Chapter. He is also the chair of the IEEE Central Indiana Student Activities Committee.

This flying home security camera has been in the works for a while

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

After years in the works, Ring's flying home security camera drone is finally taking flight. The Ring Drone Cam, as it's called, has gone through several iterations since the company first introduced it as the Ring Always Home cam three years ago.

Now that Ring is ready to ship the device, it gave us a sneak preview in advance. Here's my initial impressions of the Ring Drone Cam, as well as how much it'll cost, and when you can get one for your home.

A post shared by Tom's Guide (@tomsguide)

Unlike the Always Home Cam, which had a large protuberance on its underside, the Ring Drone Cam looks somewhat like the DJI Neo; it has a small rectangular body with four encaged rotors. Weighing 265 grams (5.8 ounces), it's lighter than most phones. While the demo unit I saw was white, the actual product will be a light gray. The Drone Cam docks and recharges in a square base station.

The drone has a 2K camera with two LEDs on either side, which it uses to light up your home as it's patrolling at night.

When activated, the Drone Cam lifts up out of its base, rises to about 4-5 feet in the air, and then proceeds at a stately pace as it moves throughout your home. Even though it's small, you'll definitely notice its presence, as its rotors make a very loud, high-pitched whine.

Knowing how my dog reacts to a vacuum cleaner, I can only imagine his response to this thing flying around the house. Don't even ask what my cats might think.

The Drone Cam navigates your home using a combination of an Alexa Home map (similar to what you'll see on one of Amazon's smart displays) and the setup process, whereby you hold the drone and carry it through your house, taking it on a trip of where you'd like to go. Ring says the Drone Cam can cover multiple stories of your home.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

Unlike previous, unreleased versions, the Drone Cam relies on the cloud for navigation, using Amazon's AI Pilot to get around and interpret what the drone is seeing. If the drone loses its connection, it's designed to immediately land — which is why it's important that you make sure its flight path doesn't go over any delicate objects.

The Ring Drone Cam can be programmed to make regular patrols of your house, or to respond to a particular event — such as a window or a door sensor tripping, or a water leak detector going off. Using the Amazon Alexa Home map, it can fly to the location of the event, and give you a live view of what's happening.

Remember the Amazon Astro? Ring took its parent company's home robot and redesigned the internals to make it a security robot for small businesses and enterprise customers.

Now called the Ring Rover Cam, it's meant to patrol warehouses and stores, and alert you if it detects an intruder. Like the Astro, it has a telescoping camera, but Ring also added a light on the back, which lets you see where the robot is at a glance, and flashes red and screams out a siren when there's an unwanted guest.

The Ring Rover Cam will cost $999, and will ship on December 16.

I am more than a bit skeptical about having a camera drone flying through my house. For starters, my pets get nervous enough around vacuum cleaners; I can only imagine how they'd react to a high-pitched drone flying about. And, the idea of a drone autonomously roaming around, potentially recording everything, feels a bit dystopian.

And, if you want the Ring Drone Camera to be able to access every corner of your house, you'll also have to make sure you leave every door wide open before you leave. And, the drone moves so slowly that if it's set up on one side of your house, by the time it responds to, say, a window breaking on the other side, the potential intruder could be long gone.

I can see some utility in it — I don't have, nor do I want, security cameras in every corner of my house, so I can see it being handy if a sensor is tripped in my basement. But, I'm still not sold on the concept; maybe trying it out will change my mind.

What do you think? Would you want a drone security camera for the inside of your house? Take our poll, and let me know in the comments.

#3222. Apple TV launches new sign language accessibility feature

Apple today launched a neat new accessibility feature for the Apple TV streaming service. Users will now have the option to watch with a sign language interpretation for some of Apple’s original movies.

The feature is launching this Friday with the debut of the new film Being Heumann, as well as F1: The Movie. Support for more titles will follow later.

Alongside those two films, Apple said that sign language options will be available for Greyhound and Way of the Warrior Kid later this year, with more to come.

To access the new functionality, you need to be using the Apple TV app on iPhone, iPad or Mac running 27.2 or later. The feature will also be available on some versions of the Apple TV app on other platforms.

By default, the Sign Language controls are hidden. If you want to use the feature, firstly go to the Settings app -> TV app, and enable the Sign Language display.

Then, on eligible titles, a new Sign Language button will appear in the player controls. You can simply toggle to enable, and choose from American Sign Language or British Sign Language modes.

When enabled, a signing interpreter then appears in the corner of the frame, synced with the video playback.

When browsing the catalog, sign language availability will also be shown next to the usual subtitle and audio language information. Users will also be able to search “with ASL” or “with BSL” to find compatible titles.

#3221. OpenAI lets businesses claim ChatGPT profiles and launch their own agents

Brands get a blue check, mention counts and a chat agent, which OpenAI also sells as an ad.

A mock-up from OpenAI of a verified business profile in ChatGPT, with a button to chat with the shop’s Business Agent.

OpenAI launched Businesses in ChatGPT in beta, letting businesses claim verified profiles, update their details and see aggregated data on how often ChatGPT mentions them. US ecommerce and online-service firms can also launch Business Agents, which OpenAI also sells as ads.

OpenAI is letting businesses claim their profiles in ChatGPT and launch AI agents that talk to customers on their behalf, the company said on Tuesday. The beta, called Businesses in ChatGPT, is aimed at the 1.2 billion people OpenAI says use ChatGPT each week.

Through a tool called Business Hub, verified companies get a blue check and can update their details, prices and stock. They can also see how often ChatGPT mentions them, how many people click through to their website and common topics in those conversations. OpenAI says it does not share users’ chats with businesses.

Eligible US ecommerce and online-service firms can also launch a Business Agent. When a business shows up in a ChatGPT answer, users can open its profile and chat with its agent, which answers using the company’s product details. The chat is labelled and kept apart from ChatGPT’s own answers.

The same agent can be sold as an ad. Businesses can sponsor it as the landing spot for ChatGPT Ads, building on Sponsored Agents, which OpenAI began testing in September. OpenAI says paying does not change how often ChatGPT recommends a business, Digiday reported.

Agents must say they are AI, keep prices accurate and avoid pressure tactics. Purchases and sharing personal data need the user’s explicit approval. For now, buyers are sent to the brand’s own website, though OpenAI is building agent payments with Visa.

The move deepens OpenAI’s push into advertising, which passed a $1B annual run rate in August and now has 100,000 advertisers. It could also squeeze startups such as Peec AI, which sell brands estimates of how visible they are in ChatGPT.

#3220. Aura Ink 10 review: A digital photo frame that looks (almost) like a real picture

Keep exploring and earning more as a member.

Unlock and manage exclusive Tom’s Guide member rewards.

Join the Tom's Guide Club for quick access. Enter your email below and we'll send confirmation, and sign you up to our newsletter.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The Aura Ink 10 is a second-generation ePaper photo frame that’s smaller and less expensive than the original, and can display a few more colors. If you’re looking for a digital photo frame you can hang on your wall without any wires showing, this is the one to get, though it is more expensive than most other frames, and overall it's less vibrant than a traditional digital photo frame.

Why you can trust Tom's Guide Our writers and editors spend hours analyzing and reviewing products, services, and apps to help find what's best for you. Find out more about how we test, analyze, and rate.

A year ago, Aura introduced the Aura Ink, the first ePaper photo frame; this device, while not as vibrant as a traditional digital photo frame, had the advantage of letting you hang it on a wall — no power cord required — for up to three months at a time without needing to be recharged.

The company is back with the Aura Ink 10, the first in the second generation of ePaper style photo frames. This frame can show more colors, and at $349, is also less expensive, albeit still well above some of the best digital photo frames. So, is the premium worth it?

The Aura Ink 10 went on sale on November 10, 2026, for $349 at Aura's website. It’s offered in just one size, and with just one matte color (black). The original only came with a white matte; I wish the company offered both options.

The frame itself is very thin, at a little less than an inch, and comes with both a stand for placing it on a table, as well as pins so you can mount it on a wall. Three buttons sit inconspicuously on the back edge of the frame, and let you switch photos and get the frame ready to go. Overall, it’s a very subtle design, and it’s unlikely that anyone would recognize it as a digital frame at a glance.

The Aura Ink 10 uses an E Ink Spectra 6 display, which can produce nine colors (black, white, red, yellow, blue, green, off-white, mustard yellow and orange), up from six on the original Aura Ink. That means it can show more nuances in pictures, though don’t expect true-to-life fidelity that you would get from a traditional LCD picture frame. The 10-inch frame also has the same resolution as the 13-inch model, which means greater pixel density.

To see the difference in Aura Ink generations, I placed the 10-inch Ink next to the 13-inch Ink, and then displayed the same photos on each.

The 10 inch model tended to show photos a little darker, but with better transitions between light and dark areas. For example, in an image of a girl jumping off a sand dune, there was less obvious pixelation from the sun-drenched stretches of the beach to shaded areas.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

In another photo of a girl in front of a blue and white wall, the blues of the wall were a bit deeper, but shadows were more pronounced, making it more difficult to make out features in her face and neck area.

The Aura Ink 10 has very gentle lighting that only turns on if it senses someone in front of the frame. Again, it’s not something you’d notice unless you see it turn on, but it helps bring a little more vibrancy to the photo.

Aura says the Ink 10 will last up to three months on a charge, assuming it changes photos just once per day. Once it runs low, you simply have to plug it into a USB-C for a little bit.

Aura also updated the manner in which the frame refreshes; on the original model, the screen kind of flashes randomly as the photo changes. On the Ink 10, there’s a wave-like pattern that starts in one corner, and ripples across the screen. It’s more intentional, and doesn’t make it look like the frame is shorting out.

One thing that Aura does well is make it easy to add photos to its devices. For starters, you can sync your iCloud or Google Photos albums in the Aura app. And, to help narrow things down, the Aura app can filter photos by person, so that you can more easily find photos of particular individuals; unfortunately, there’s no pet filter. If you want to skip the app entirely, you can also either email or text photos to the display. Handy!

As someone who tests smart home devices for a living, I suspect my house, which has smart displays everywhere, is a bit different than most. So while I appreciate traditional digital photo frames — the Alexa Photo Frame is one of my favorites, for its innovative use of AI — it’s nice to have some tech that doesn’t look like tech.

Yes, there are some tradeoffs to an ePaper photo display like the Aura Ink 10. You’re not going to get colors that really fly off the screen, and you’re going to pay a premium over other photo frames. But, in a digital-everything world, I appreciate its subtleness.

#3218. Why a Mathematician Is Chasing Eclipses With Algorithms and Cameras

With custom-built gear, his team seeks to solve a long-standing solar mystery

Advanced image-processing software developed by Miloslav Druckmüller combines scores of individual images, captured during a total solar eclipse and painstakingly calibrated. The techniques reveal fine details in the sun’s corona, which is white in this image. The tiny pink shapes seen along portions of the edge of the blacked-out solar disk are prominences, which are extensions of relatively cool plasma that can jut out hundreds of thousands of kilometers into space.

The sun hangs low over the plains of Castile and León, in the north-central region of Spain. But from a slope of the mountain Pico Trigaza, it appears that a few puffy white clouds have started to block the sun. That’s vexing.

A group of researchers, some wearing cardboard eclipse glasses, is clustered around sets of portable telescopes and cameras connected to laptops. All this gear is scattered on tabletops perched on the mountainside. On the computer screens, the sun’s disk looks like a deep orange crescent that is slowly waning. That’s because the moon began to crawl across it about half an hour ago. In 25 minutes, it will obscure the sun completely, producing an eerie and wondrous phenomenon—a total solar eclipse.

In the late-summer, late-afternoon heat, the researchers watch anxiously as those fluffy clouds linger around the sun. From an abandoned hut on the slope a few meters above, where the researchers have set up camp, one of the grad students emerges and nods toward the cloud formation. “Do you think it will dissolve?” he blurts out.

“It will.” Miloslav Druckmüller glances calmly at his group of doctoral candidates, now making final checks of the equipment in preparation for totality. Here in Spain, on this 12th day of August, Druckmüller is getting ready for his 19th solar eclipse. He knows from long experience that weather can turn quickly when the moon’s shadow suddenly pushes the temperature down. Plus, there’s no sense in riling up the grad students any more than they already are.

Miloslav Druckmüller led the design and construction of a unique optical instrument that incorporates eight astrocameras. Each is equipped with a spectral filter for sensing and recording specific emission spectra from the solar corona. Each of those spectra, in turn, is associated with a particular ionic species of iron atoms. Because the temperature needed to ionize iron varies depending on the ionic species, analyzing the locations and relative abundance of these ionic species offers valuable insights into the distribution of heat in the corona.Václav Široký

During totality, the moon blocks the overwhelming glare of the solar disk, revealing delicate structures in the sun’s outer atmosphere, the corona. Using custom-built telescope systems and image-processing techniques that Druckmüller has spent decades developing, the researchers aim to gain insights into the processes in this enigmatic region that is otherwise hard to study. In addition to imaging the visible coronal light, the team will try to track the dispersal of superhot ions of iron into interplanetary space, which could give rare insights into the pattern of heat emanating from the corona.

And they’ll have 107 seconds to do all that.

Druckmüller is a professor of mathematics and image processing at the Brno University of Technology in the Czech Republic and a leading figure in the Solar Wind Sherpas, an international team that studies the sun’s corona during total eclipses. In the solar eclipse world, he is nothing short of a legend, albeit a reluctant one.

An image from Miloslav Druckmüller’s first solar-eclipse expedition, to Hungary, vividly shows Baily’s Beads. These elongated white lights along a piece of the left edge of the blacked-out solar disk are caused by beams of sunlight shining through gaps in the irregular lunar surface during the eclipse. The pink shapes are solar prominences, which are jets of plasma extending out into space and held in place by the sun’s intense magnetic field.

He photographed his first solar eclipse in 1999, in what he thought would be a one-off lark. During that eclipse, the moon’s deep shadow missed Druckmüller’s native Czechia by just a few tens of kilometers, so he chased it to Hungary with a 30-year-old Soviet MTO 1,000-millimeter lens. All he remembers from that day is the rush of adrenaline he felt while trying to find the sun in the sky with the lens’s minuscule field of view and keep it in focus for the two minutes of the eclipse.

He insists that he has never enjoyed any of the eclipses he has photographed. “In fact, I have never properly seen any of those eclipses. You are just watching the screens, making sure that it’s all doing what it’s supposed to do. There are so many things that can go wrong and you can’t redo it.”

A composite sequence of photographs shows the 12 August 2026 solar eclipse as seen from a slope of the mountain Pico Trigaza in Spain.

Despite Druckmüller’s outward tranquility on this Spanish hillside, the stakes are high. Just 45 minutes ago, his group heard from their colleagues in Iceland, where viewing conditions had promised to be better than in Spain. But a vast low-pressure system had clouded the entire sky, leaving all three Iceland teams without a view.

On the Pico Trigaza mountain in Spain, two postgraduate researchers used a laser to get a rough, initial alignment for the tracking mount of an optical instrument. The alignment was necessary to precisely compensate for the Earth’s motion.

The corona has been a mystery for centuries. Though dimmer—by a factor of a million—than the sun’s visible surface, the corona is nevertheless extremely hot: about a million degrees Celsius compared to 5,500 degrees on the surface. Because the sun’s nuclear fusion engine churns at the star’s heart, it might seem that temperatures should fall farther from the core.

To observe the faint corona in visible light, researchers must block the sun’s ferocious glare. Specialized telescopes called coronagraphs do this with an opaque disk called an occulter. But because light bends around the occulter’s edges in an effect called diffraction, it must block an area much larger than that of the solar disk to prevent light from spilling over and ruining the images. But doing so means obstructing the inner part of the corona, which harbors the most important processes that underpin the puzzling phenomena of the sun’s upper atmosphere.

That’s why total eclipses matter so much to solar physicists. By sheer chance, the moon is exactly the right size and at just the right distance to completely cover the sun during a total solar eclipse. Because the moon is so far away from Earth, the view is not marred by diffraction, and the corona reveals itself nearly all the way down to the sun’s surface.

As astrocameras recorded spectral data about the sun’s corona, a laptop computer [on table, at left] displayed the phase of the eclipse.

Space probes can image the solar surface in other wavelengths, but those views have limitations, too. Spacecraft such as NASA’s Solar Dynamics Observatory do see the innermost parts of the corona in extreme ultraviolet light, explains Shadia Habbal, a solar physicist at the University of Hawaii and leader of the Solar Wind Sherpas project. “But it cuts off very quickly, so you don’t see its extension into space as well as we can see it in the visible emission lines” during an eclipse. “That’s the biggest advantage,” she says, of solar eclipse photography.

The European Proba-3 mission, launched in 2024, simulates total solar eclipses by flying two spacecraft in a formation 150 meters apart with one acting as an occulter and the other as the telescope. The instruments aboard that satellite, however, have limitations compared to the equipment used by the Solar Wind Sherpas team.

When Druckmüller developed the film from his 1999 eclipse expedition, the photographs didn’t do justice to the event’s eerie beauty. He spent countless evenings applying his expertise in numerical image processing in an attempt to re-create in his photographs the sights he witnessed in that Hungarian corn field.

It took two years, but eventually he succeeded. Where before there were dull views of the blackened lunar disk surrounded by the blunt wisps of the corona, Druckmüller revealed the subtlest details of the magnetic field lines stretching from the sun far into space. As his photographs circulated among solar physicists, invitations to eclipse expeditions began to arrive.

Solar researchers Miloslav Druckmüller and Shadia Habbal have been collaborating for two decades and 15 eclipses.

Habbal learned about the images from a Ph.D. student who had seen them at a conference presentation that didn’t credit Druckmüller. When Habbal’s team later published the images in a paper, they misattributed them to another researcher. Druckmüller found out through an astrophysicist friend. “I wrote her a rather disappointed email and she responded within 10 minutes,” Druckmüller recalls. “She really didn’t have a clue.”

The error was corrected, and within weeks, Habbal and Druckmüller began a collaboration that grew into a friendship. “Milos’s processing brings out details that nobody has seen before, and they tell you a lot about very tiny features in the corona that you don’t see otherwise,” says Habbal.

Capturing the corona’s delicate structures means finding a way to show its brightest and faintest features in the same image. “During the solar eclipse, the contrast between the darkest and brightest parts of the corona is enormous, possibly one to a million,” Druckmüller explains. “But a computer monitor only allows you to display a contrast ratio of one to about 800.” (Some modern monitors, particularly OLED ones, can deliver higher contrast ratios.)

The human eye can adjust to this enormous range of brightness, allowing an observer to see both the bright corona and the faint stars and planets that briefly emerge in the darkened sky. To bring those details together in a photograph, Druckmüller uses custom image-processing algorithms to combine exposures that capture different parts of that range.

Researchers Martin Šebek and Peter Urgoš make fine adjustments to the focus and alignment of the astrocameras on a key optical instrument before the 12 August solar eclipse.

To create a single image, Druckmüller’s teams need to take 200 individual frames during the eclipse at exposure times ranging from 0.001 second to two seconds. The data must then be calibrated against a vast number of reference images to filter out noise and imperfections. Flat fields, which depict a uniform light background, help correct for defects caused by telescope optics, dust spots, and variations in pixel sensitivity. Dark frames, taken with light blocked from the sensor, help correct for artifacts created by the camera’s image sensor itself. “It takes the computer more than two days to process one image,” Druckmüller says. Including the calibration data, a single finished image requires about 3,000 input frames.

Since 2008, teams directed by Habbal and Druckmüller have traveled to every total solar eclipse, spreading out across multiple locations to hedge against bad weather. About half of the teams return with usable data. For the others, it’s just a short and stressful voyage. For the 12 August eclipse, three groups deployed to Iceland and two to Spain.

The teams seek sites close to the center of the band of totality, where the moon blocks the sun for longest. In Spain, the 12 August band of totality cut across the north of the country; the center line of the shadow passed within 11 kilometers of Pico Trigaza, promising Druckmüller and his colleagues a precious 107 seconds of totality.

But duration is only part of the calculation. Totality on Pico Trigaza will commence 51 minutes before sunset, with the sun just 8 degrees above the horizon. That low, the rays must pass through a much thicker layer of the atmosphere than when the sun is higher in the sky, increasing the light distortion that complicates photography. At the researchers’ camp on Pico Trigaza, 1,600 meters above sea level, the thinner air should help a bit.

An abandoned hut on the mountain Pico Trigaza in Spain was spruced up so that it could serve as a home base for the research team recording the 12 August solar eclipse.

“Iceland would have been a much better place for us than Spain because the sun was higher up, some 25 degrees above the horizon,” Druckmüller says wistfully. But Iceland’s notoriously unpredictable weather made Spain an essential backup.

If you pack a van with thousands of dollars’ worth of cameras and optical gear and then set out on a 2,351-kilometer journey, you shouldn’t be surprised if you finish the trip with a few striking photographs [top]. The sleeping arrangements for the grad students at the Pico Trigaza hut [bottom] were spartan, but the views were first-rate.Top: Martin Šebek; Bottom: Václav Široký

On the mountain, locals have spruced up a rustic, long-unused hut for the researchers, running power cables from a nearby telecommunication outpost and bringing in a water tank. Five Ph.D. students drove more than 2,000 kilometers from Brno and have spent nearly a week preparing the equipment. Druckmüller and his wife joined them two days before the eclipse. They cook on a small propane grill and sleep in sleeping bags on yoga mats. “We have plenty of space here to set up our telescopes, beautiful views, and a roof over our heads,” Druckmüller says with a grin. “It’s perfect.”

But even the best equipment and a carefully chosen site count for nothing if the clouds roll in. “So much work goes into the preparations and then, if you end up with nothing, you just feel terrible sadness,” says Jana Hoderová, an assistant professor of mathematics at Brno University of Technology and one of Druckmüller’s key collaborators.

As the moon continues to slide in front of the solar disk, the pesky cumulus cloud that kept everybody on edge begins to dissolve. It’s 10 minutes to totality. The relief is palpable.

The countdown on the computers that control the cameras has begun. The screens are now showing only a tiny orange sliver, and the evening is becoming perceptibly less bright.

Twenty astrophotography cameras, most of them drawing power from a car battery that was also buffering the cameras from any grid instabilities, are pointed at the sun. Alongside equipment capturing the corona’s visible light, the team has built an assembly of eight cameras to detect light emitted by various iron ions that arise in the corona.

Among the optical gear assembled at Pico Trigaza to capture the 12 August solar eclipse was a unique instrument designed to record the distributions of iron ions in the corona [at left]. Václav Široký

Those instruments looking for iron ions have been put together with resourcefulness and thrift. A colleague of Druckmüller’s laser-cut the aluminum plates holding the carefully aligned lenses in exchange “for two bottles of whisky.” The brackets and attachments were 3D-printed at Brno University of Technology. The lenses, produced for the defunct camera maker Contax, were bought at steep discounts on eBay. By far the most expensive elements are interference filters that isolate the wavelengths emitted by the iron ions.

Around the blackened solar disk rises the magnificent golden halo of the corona. In the hush on the mountainside, it seems that even the birds have gone still.

“That’s something nobody else in the world can do,” Druckmüller says with visible satisfaction. The unique technology, codeveloped with Habbal’s Hawaii team, has already enabled researchers to map the distribution of temperatures across the entire corona and to discover previously unseen structures, dubbed “smoke rings,” in the coronal plasma. The photographs also revealed the boundary region where the solar plasma becomes so thin that its ions stop colliding.

The optical assembly designed to record the distributions of iron ions in the corona is outfitted with astrocameras, each of which captures spectra from a different ionic species. To do that, each astrocamera is equipped with a spectral filter whose bandwidth is so narrow—one nanometer—that the filter appears as a mirror.Martin Fornůsek

“Iron is the most abundant of the heavy elements that we see in the solar corona,” says Habbal. “And because the corona is so hot, the iron atoms lose electrons and get ionized. The larger the loss, the higher the temperature.”

For example, a temperature of around 1.6 million °C is necessary to produce an iron ion that has lost 12 electrons. But only 1.4 million °C is needed to strip an iron atom of 11 electrons. Once it’s in a particular electrical state, the ion retains its specific ionization, even as it travels outward with the solar wind. Each of those ions, whether +11 or +12, emits a different wavelength of light, allowing the researchers to map not just temperatures within the corona, but also how those iron ions spread into interplanetary space and distribute heat. Habbal and her colleagues had long been trying to image those iron ions during solar eclipses. But it wasn’t until Druckmüller entered the picture that they were able to develop the gear and the mathematical techniques to do it.

With just a minute to go to totality, the researchers begin removing protective filters from the lenses. It’s 50 minutes to sunset, and the waning sun has just begun to light up the clouds above the horizon with the first tinge of orange. Then, suddenly, the evening begins a rapid and premature descent into darkness. Along the edge of the fantastically thin solar crescent, the brilliant orange points known as Baily’s Beads flash and disappear—the last fragments of photospheric light visible through deep lunar valleys. As totality begins, observers remove their glasses. The hot air cools. The graduate students remain quietly and intently focused on their gear.

Druckmüller looks up from his camera toward the darkened plains. Around the blackened solar disk rises the magnificent golden halo of the corona. In the hush on the mountainside, it seems that even the birds have gone still. The sky is ablaze with fiery colors all along the horizon where the deep lunar shadow drops off. Venus burns brilliantly in the southwest, a sharp white pinpoint in the darkened sky. The sound of camera shutters suddenly fills the air. Then, as quickly as it fell, the darkness begins to recede, bid farewell with another handful of golden Baily’s Beads.

The crowd erupts in cheers. The Ph.D. students throw themselves at each other and hug like they mean it.

“The students did most of the work this time, so I actually allowed myself to really look at it,” Druckmüller says. “It was beautiful. Pico Trigaza may not have been the best for science photography, but from the aesthetic point of view, it was extraordinary.”

The 2026 solar-eclipse team at Pico Trigaza in Spain included [from left] Magdalena Šrotířová, Peter Urgoš, Martin Fornůsek, Miloslav Druckmüller, Václav Široký, and Martin Šebek.Václav Široký

But for Druckmüller, this is just the beginning. While other eclipse chasers will race to release their images, he will take his time. He expects to publish the first visible-light images of the corona in about two weeks. Processing the iron-ion images, and uncovering whatever insights they may hold, will take months—maybe even a whole year.

“Probably until the next eclipse in 2027” in North Africa, Druckmüller says.

Who knows? Maybe he’ll even enjoy that one, too.

Tereza Pultarova is a London-based journalist specializing in aerospace and defense technologies. She is a native of the Czech Republic.

I enjoyed this piece very, very much, and I truly hope this team continues its work.

Those are some pretty impressive photos! It also seems like the iron ion filtering is pretty unique. I love seeing cases where people build something they want to see in the world with minimal outside support. Seems like it would be a solid return on more public money to seek out and support scrappy projects like this one.

#3217. iPadOS 27.3 adds new iPad setting I instantly turned on

iPadOS 27.3 is currently available in beta, and it introduces a new iPad setting for app windowing that I instantly turned on. Here are the details.

I use the iPad Pro as my primary computer, and for the most part have found Apple’s software changes in iPadOS 26 and 27 to be great upgrades.

But with the powerful new windowing capabilities, there have definitely been some quirks that need refining. One of them involves resizing windows with the traffic light controls in the top-left corner.

For example, in iPadOS 27 the controls move locations and even disappear depending on the size of the window. It can be pretty frustrating.

I need to just get better about learning keyboard shortcuts for window controls. But in the meantime, iPadOS 27.3 adds a new optional setting that I instantly turned on and have been loving.

Inside Settings ⇾ Multitasking & Gestures, if you have ‘Windowed Apps’ enabled you’ll see a new option below it: ‘Double-tap Top of Window to Zoom’

If you use your iPad mostly with touch input, or simply haven’t used keyboard shortcuts enough to remember them, this new setting is a great way to quickly resize windows.

When the setting is enabled, two taps (or a double-click with the trackpad) will zoom the window to take up the full screen. Then you can double-tap again to revert it to its previous size.

I generally keep my app windows in specific size setups, but regularly find myself wanting to go fullscreen temporarily. The new setting provides a convenient way to do that quickly without needing the traffic light controls or my keyboard, and is a welcome refinement to iPadOS windowing.

Will you enable this new iPadOS 27.3 setting? Why or why not? Let us know in the comments.

#3215. Use Your Year-End Review to Reach for a Promotion

Maintaining a document of your successes throughout the year gives you a starting point

Brian Jenney is the owner of Parsity, a program that helps engineers through hands-on training.

This article is crossposted from IEEE Spectrum’s careers newsletter. Sign up now to get insider tips, expert advice, and practical strategies, written in partnership with tech career development company Parsity and delivered to your inbox for free!

When I landed my first job as a software engineer, I had a simple plan: Work hard and somebody would notice. Eventually a manager would tap me on the shoulder and hand me a promotion (probably with a nice little speech).

That plan stalled my career for about five years.

I switched jobs twice, kept my head down, read a stack of programming books, and sometimes pulled 12-hour days. I was never promoted. At my third job, out of frustration, I started interviewing at other companies and almost immediately got an offer for a senior engineer role.

So I went back to my job and quit. My team was blindsided. I liked my manager and the people I worked with, and they came back with a counteroffer. Then someone from HR asked me, “Why didn’t you just ask us?”

I took the counteroffer and stayed. Three jobs in, I finally got promoted, and all it took was asking (in the most dramatic way possible).

Today, I would take a different approach.

Year-end review discussions are a great time to push for a promotion. But at most companies, raises and promotions are largely settled before the formal review conversation happens. If the year-end review is the first time your manager hears you want a promotion, you’re usually too late.

Now is a great time to start the conversation.

Engineers tend to believe good work speaks for itself. It rarely does. Your manager is juggling a team, a roadmap, and their own boss. They see a fraction of what you do, and the work they don’t see might as well not exist when raises get decided.

Perception is reality, so you have to shape it. That means learning to brag a little.

A “brag document” is a running list of what you accomplished, when, and why it mattered. Add to it every two weeks or once a month, and write each entry so your manager’s manager would understand it.

Engineers tend to write things like “migrated the billing service.” A better entry reads “migrated the billing service, which cut failed payments by 30 percent and unblocked the Q3 pricing launch.” If there’s no number, name who benefited and how.

Include the work people forget to count, too: handling incidents, mentoring new hires, interviewing candidates, and writing the docs everyone else relies on. If you helped your team adopt AI tools this year, write that down. (It counts as leadership, whether or not anyone called it that.)

The document does two jobs. It gives you ammunition when you make your case, and it gives your manager something to ctrl + c then ctrl + v when they argue for you in meetings you’ll never attend.

Bragging builds the case. Asking forces action.

If your goal is a promotion or a raise, you might ask: “What would it take for me to get to [the next level] in the next year?”

A good manager will give you an outline that can turn into a plan. Push for specifics until you have deliverables you can work toward, then send a short recap email so the plan exists somewhere besides your manager’s memory. (Managers change jobs too.)

Sometimes the answer will still be “not this year,” and the reason may have nothing to do with you.

Budgets get frozen, promotion slots get capped, and decisions get made above your manager’s head where even a manager who wants to help can’t.

Don’t read too much into that. But be honest with yourself, too. Most of the time, a no means there’s something you aren’t doing yet. Find out what it is instead of guessing for five years like I did.

Asking costs you one slightly awkward conversation. Sitting back and waiting to be noticed can cost you years.

Don’t try this at home: To better understand the risk AI slop poses to scientific publishing today, IEEE Spectrum contributor Benjamin Skuse put IEEE’s research integrity checks to the test by submitting two entirely AI-generated papers. “Science has a spam problem. And the spam filter is getting clogged up…”

Policy change doesn’t just come down to paid lobbyists—lawmakers want to hear from working experts, too. One engineer shares what he learned from his first two visits to Capitol Hill.

Could community colleges help fill the coming talent shortage in the U.S. semiconductor industry? Alternatives to four-year university degrees are a promising option for the technicians who will be needed to run new fabs.

Brian Jenney is the owner of Parsity, an online education platform that helps people break into AI and modern software roles through project-based learning and one-on-one mentorship with senior developers. Parsity helps career changers transition into software by focusing on practical skills, real-world systems, and the kind of experience companies actually look for.Outside Parsity, Brian works a senior software engineer in the SF Bay Area.Brian is also a father of three, and when he’s not working with students or building programs, you might catch him running around Lake Merritt in Oakland, California.
