#3189. Intercorp Financial (IFS) Q3 2026 Earnings Call Transcript

Consumer lending surged despite El Nino provisions weighing on profit.

Need a quote from a Motley Fool analyst? Email [email protected]

Intercorp Financial Services Inc. (IFS +1.38%) reported third-quarter results characterized by growth in higher-yielding loan segments and the continued scaling of its digital payments ecosystem. Management maintained its full-year profitability guidance while taking a proactive approach to risk management through extraordinary provisioning for climate-related contingencies. The company reported a recovery in net interest margins, driven by a shift toward consumer and small business lending and a reduction in funding costs. Operations were supported by a resilient macroeconomic environment in Peru, where private investment and domestic demand reached multiyear highs. The company continues to prioritize its digital transformation, reporting high penetration across its banking, insurance, and wealth management platforms.

Operator: Good morning, and welcome to the Intercorp Financial Services' Third Quarter 2026 Conference Call. [Operator Instructions] Please be advised that today's conference call is being recorded. [Operator Instructions] It is now my pleasure to turn the call over to Mr. Ivan Peill of InspIR Group. Sir, you may begin.

Ivan Peill: Thank you, and good morning, everyone. On today's call, Intercorp Financial Services will discuss its third quarter 2026 earnings. We are very pleased to have with us Mr. Luis Felipe Castellanos, Chief Executive Officer, Intercorp Financial Services; Ms. Michela Casassa, Chief Financial Officer, Intercorp Financial Services; Mr. Carlos Tori, Chief Executive Officer, Interbank; Mr. Gonzalo Basadre, Chief Executive Officer, Interseguro; and Mr. Bruno Ferreccio, Chief Executive Officer, Inteligo. They will be discussing the results that were distributed by the company yesterday. There is also a webcast video presentation to accompany the discussion during this call. If you didn't receive a copy of the presentation or the earnings report, they are now available on the company's website, ifs.com.pe.

Otherwise, if you need any assistance today, please call InspIR Group in New York on (646) 940-8843. I would like to remind you that today's call is for investors and analysts only. Therefore, questions from the media will not be taken. Please be advised that forward-looking statements may be made during this conference call. These do not account for future economic circumstances, industry conditions, the company's future performance or financial results. As such, statements made are based on several assumptions and factors that could change, causing actual results to materially differ from the current expectations. For a complete note on forward-looking statements, please refer to the earnings presentation and report issued yesterday.

It is now my pleasure to turn the call over to Mr. Luis Felipe Castellanos, Chief Executive Officer of Intercorp Financial Services, for his opening remarks. Mr. Castellanos, please go ahead, sir.

Luis Castellanos López-Torres: Thank you. Good morning, and thank you all for joining us on our third quarter 2026 earnings call. Let me start with the macro environment. In the first half of 2026, private investment grew 15%, its fastest growth since 2012, and domestic demand grew almost 6%, which is the highest since 2013. Exports have reached new historical records, and all of this has come with a prudent fiscal deficit and debt-to-GDP ratio. Business confidence is also at its highest level in recent years. On the political front, we see the executive pushing forward its investment agenda, which is consistent with expectations for a stronger private investment and should help bring Peru back to its medium-term growth potential.

All in all, we are optimistic about what lies ahead for Peru, and we believe the coming years should be positive. In the short-term, we are especially focused on the El Nino event, which we are now assuming that will be an extraordinary magnitude. We expect that impact to be temporary, mainly affecting primary sectors such as agriculture and fishing and -- extending into the first half of 2027. Depending on the strength of the rains, infrastructure primarily in certain regions of the North will be affected. Even so, we continue to expect GDP growth of around 3% next year. We believe the country is well-positioned to return to its medium-term growth path once these effects fade.

In this context, IFS net income was PEN 457 million with an ROE of 14%. These results mainly reflect the provisions that were booked in anticipation of El Nino at Interbank and to a lower extent at SIP, in line with our prudent approach to risk management. Excluding these provisions, net income would have been PEN 543 million with an ROE of close to 17%. As mentioned, we see the impact of El Nino as short-term, while our medium-term view has actually improved. We see our medium-term ROE target to be above 20% now. At Interbank, the underlying business continued to show positive trends. Excluding El Nino provisions, risk-adjusted NIM expanded to 3.9% from 3.5% last quarter.

Loan growth accelerated in consumer and in small businesses, both higher-yielding segments, which is contributing to the NIM expansion. Asset quality is also performing very well with a positive trend. Year-to-date cost of risk, excluding El Nino provisions, is 1.8% and NPLs is at 2%, reflecting the quality of our portfolio and our risk management capabilities. As a result, we believe the bank is better positioned as we enter this El Nino period as compared to the previous ones. We continue to strengthen our payments ecosystem through Izipay and PLIN. These platforms are important levers to deepen our relationships, increase engagement, and support the growth of low-cost funding.

Interseguro maintained strong momentum in its core business while preserving its leadership in annuities. The business continues to leverage synergies with Inteligo and Interbank to advance more integrated solutions for our customers. Inteligo continued to grow at double-digit rate, reaching a new record in assets under management, supported by healthy client engagement and strong advisory model. The investment portfolio had more moderate quarter, but this does not change the trend of its core business. Overall, this quarter shows that we remain on-track in terms of results and profitability, supported by a diversified platform, clear growth opportunities across businesses and a disciplined execution of our model. El Nino event should be a short-term effect.

Our strategy remains focused on profitable growth with the customer at the center of our decisions and continued investments in the capabilities that support long-term value creation, including digital solutions, data analytics, cybersecurity, and GenAI. Looking ahead, we believe IFS is well-positioned to continue growing with discipline while sustaining profitability and strengthening our leadership in Peru over the long term. Now let me pass it on to Michela, who will walk you through this quarter results in more detail. Thank you.

Michela Ramat: Thank you, Luis Felipe. Good morning, and welcome again, everybody, to Intercorp Financial Services' Third Quarter 2026 Earnings Call. I would like to begin with our key messages for the quarter. First, Peru remains resilient ahead of El Nino. Even after incorporating a stronger El Nino, the Central Bank projects GDP growth of 3% for 2027. Second, core earnings maintained a positive growth trajectory. Excluding El Nino-related provisions, net income was PEN 544 million with an ROE of around 17%. Third, accelerating momentum in higher-yielding loans, which grew 21% year-over-year and 10% in the quarter alone. Fourth, NIM recovery on a better asset mix.

NIM expanded 20 basis points to 5.1% and risk-adjusted NIM, excluding El Nino provisions, improved 40 basis points quarter-over-quarter to 3.9%. Finally, insurance and wealth management continued to deliver strong growth with written premiums up 30% in the first 9 months and assets under management up 13% year-over-year. Let's start with our first key message, which is that Peru remains resilient ahead of El Nino. On Slide 4, let me update you on the macro environment. The economy is regaining speed. GDP is tracking around 3.4% in the third quarter based on data through August, up from 2.6% in the previous quarter. Nonprimary sectors continue to support growth.

The Central Bank now expects GDP to grow 3.2% this year and 3% in 2027, below its previous estimates of 3.4% and 3.2%, as it incorporates a stronger El Nino. Growth remains supported by commerce, services, and construction, with exports at record levels. Looking ahead to 2027, we expect a more challenging first half as El Nino would weigh on activity during the summer months. However, we anticipate a significant recovery in the second half, supported by reconstruction spending and the fiscal response. The impact will not be the same everywhere.

The North, the most exposed region, would contract in the first half and rebound in the second, while other regions would be less affected, limiting the impact on overall annual growth. Inflation reached 5.3% in October, remaining above the Central Bank's target range. Core inflation is lower at 4.6%. And excluding transportation, which was affected by fuel prices increases, it would be close to 2%, consistent with the target range. That said, the reference rate has remained at 4.25% over the past year and a rate increase over the next 6 months cannot be ruled out. Overall, Peru continues to stand out for the strength of its macroeconomic fundamentals. Public debt remains among the lowest in Latin America.

Country risk is one of the lowest in the region, and financing conditions remain favorable across the yield curve, supporting a constructive medium-term outlook. On Slide 5. For a bank, what matters is whether this macro recovery translates into credit demand, and we are beginning to see clear signs that it does. Business confidence rose to 69, its highest level in recent years, while consumer confidence reached 50 points. This improving sentiment is translating into stronger spending in investment decisions. In fact, the Central Bank expects domestic demand to grow 6.2% this year and private investment 14%, one of its strongest expansions in more than a decade, with private investment remaining resilient at 8.5% in 2027.

Supporting this outlook is a robust investment pipeline for 2026-2030, totaling USD 124 billion. Mining represents 52% of the total and infrastructure, another 28%, led by projects such as Tia Maria, Trapiche, Pampa de Pongo, Anillo Vial Periferico, de la Sierra Tramo 4. Beyond their direct impact, these projects should continue supporting employment, business activity and financing needs across sectors. We can already see this momentum in the financial system. As of September, loans grew 11.8% year-over-year with retail expanding 13.8%. We are seeing a similar trend in our own portfolio, which reinforces our view that renewed confidence is translating into stronger credit demand. On Slide 6, before turning to the results, let me spend a moment on El Nino.

ENFEN's October update raised the probability of an extraordinary cost at El Nino in the first quarter of 2027 to 55% from 9% in June. So we are facing the possibility of an extraordinary event, and therefore, we decided to provision in line with this scenario. Around 11% of our loan portfolio is flagged as potentially exposed with about 8% through direct exposure to agriculture and fishing, which we consider very low risk, and about 3% through consumer and small business loans in the affected zones, which we consider medium risk. The 8% is made up entirely of commercial clients with direct exposure and all of them already have sent clauses that allow them to refinance or defer payments.

So we do not expect the agriculture and fishing exposure to generate provisions for the bank. On the 3%, retail clients do not have these clauses, which is why we see it as medium risk, but we are ready to support them through rescheduling programs allowed by the superintendency. This quarter, Interbank set aside PEN 185 million in total provisions for El Nino, comprising PEN 81 million of already held under expert criteria and PEN 104 million of additional provisions. SIP recorded PEN 37 million as well, of which 50% or PEN 18.5 million was recognized by IFS. Including our share of SIP, the after-tax impact on IFS net income was PEN 86 million.

This provisioning reflects the scenario we see today, which assumes a stronger El Nino than previously expected, but we will reassess as the event evolves. We are already acting by tracking the exposed portfolio on a daily basis, tightening underwriting standards in the affected areas and supporting our employees in those areas. Once the event has passed, we will be there to support recovery in the affected regions. On the government side, the Ministry of Economy has announced a broad support package that includes additional fiscal funding, cash transfers to affected families, state-backed loan guarantees for SMEs and accelerated public work programs.

Together with reconstruction spending, these measures should help mitigate the economic impact of El Nino and support a stronger recovery in the second half of 2027. Let's now turn to our second key message, which is that core earnings maintained a positive growth trajectory. On Slide 8, in the context of what we just discussed, our core earnings are on the right track. Excluding El Nino-related provisions, net income was PEN 544 million, up 19% year-over-year with an ROE of 16.6%. Compared to last quarter, net income was down 7%, mainly because investment results at Inteligo and Interseguro normalized after a strong second quarter.

Once we include the El Nino provisions at Interbank and SIP, reported net income was PEN 457 million with an ROE of 14%. Overall, setting El Nino aside, the underlying trends remain solid year-over-year and the bank is leading the way. At the bank, the net income, excluding El Nino was PEN 439 million, up 10% from last year and 9% from last quarter, with an ROE of 16.4%. This was driven by higher loan income and lower funding costs, which are also behind the NIM recovery. At Interseguro, net income was PEN 97 million with an ROE above 30%.

That's below an exceptionally strong second quarter, but 2.6x what we reported a year ago when the results included a credit loss provision on financial investments. At Inteligo, net income was PEN 38 million with an ROE of 13.5% as investments return normalized after a very good first half of the year. Importantly, the recurring part of the business is on-track, and fees and assets under management continue to grow. On Slide 9. Looking at the first 9 months of the year, net income excluding El Nino was PEN 1,731 million, up 17% year-over-year with an ROE of 18.1%. Including El Nino, reported net income was PEN 1,644 million, up 11% year-over-year with an ROE of 17.2%.

The important point is that even after absorbing El Nino, we remain in line with our full year ROE guidance of around 17%. On Slide 10, revenues grew 8% year-over-year to PEN 2.1 billion and flat versus the previous quarter. At the bank, the trend is encouraging. Revenues were up 4% in the quarter and 8% year-over-year with NIM recovering to 5.1%, in line with our strategy to grow in higher-yielding loans. We also benefited from lower funding costs, partly offset by lower FX results. At Interseguro and Inteligo, revenues declined versus the previous quarter by 3% and 30%, respectively, due to investment results, which were very strong in the previous quarter.

The underlying trend is moving in the right direction as revenues grew 12% year-over-year at Interseguro, driven by the insurance result and 8% at Inteligo. On Slide 11. Expenses for the first 9 months grew 10% year-over-year, and our cost-to-income ratio was 37.8% compared with around 37% a year ago. The main driver was technology, up 15% versus last year as we continue to invest in cybersecurity, infrastructure, and data and analytics. Personnel expenses are up 14%, reflecting the expansion of Interseguro sales force and key talent that we are adding across the platform. Now let's turn to our third key message, which makes us most optimistic about the coming quarters. On Slide 13.

Our higher-yielding loans, consumer and small businesses are accelerating, growing 21% year-over-year and 10% in the quarter, almost doubling the pace of the previous quarter. In consumer loans, the recovery we anticipated in our last two calls is now materializing. Excess liquidity is normalizing and activity is coming back, supported by better confidence. As a result, consumer loans are up 18% year-over-year and 10% in the quarter, outperforming the market and gaining 20 basis points of market share versus last quarter. In September, cash loan disbursements grew 44% year-over-year and credit card turnover 21%. And so far, we have not seen a pause due to El Nino.

In small businesses, growth continues at an accelerated pace with loans up 34% year-over-year and disbursements up 63% in September. Our business banking app, which brings together Interbank and Izipay, the acquiring business, strengthens our value proposition, and we still see room to continue gaining share. Together, these segments now represent 23% of the performing loan book, which supports NIM recovery. That said, these segments are also the most sensitive to El Nino. So we want to be very clear that we are growing conservatively. We are focusing our growth on zones that we do not expect to be affected by El Nino and on low-risk clients and we have already tightened origination in the exposed areas. On Slide 14.

Our performing loan book grew at a double-digit pace or 10% year-over-year, up from 6% last quarter. In the quarter alone, it grew 4% with good momentum in both retail and commercial. What we like about this growth is that it is broad-based and led by segments with attractive risk-adjusted returns. Starting with retail, we are growing more than 9% year-over-year. Consumer, as previously mentioned, is leading with 18%, and mortgages continue to grow steadily at 8%. The good news is that now mass market is the fastest-growing segment at more than 10%, while the affluent segment is growing as well, but at a more moderate pace. In commercial, we are growing 11%, led by small businesses at 34%.

And I would also highlight midsized companies, which are growing more than 14%. Deepening our relationships and complementing our value proposition with Izipay is helping us grow both in small businesses and midsized companies. Turning to our fourth key message, a NIM recovery on a better asset mix. On Slide 16. The NIM story is positive, and it is driven by lower funding costs and a better asset mix with a higher weight of loans that should keep building in the coming quarters. NIM increased 20 basis points to 5.1% with contributions from both assets and funding. On the asset side, the return on interest-earning assets rose 20 basis points to 7.7%.

Importantly, this came mainly from loan yields, which rose to 9.7%. This marks a change in trend driven by the shift towards consumer and small business loans, which now represent 23% of the performing loan book. At the same time, our asset mix is improving with loans now representing close to 70% of the interest-earning assets. Excluding El Nino provisions, risk-adjusted NIM was 3.9%, which is 40 basis points above last quarter, reflecting our strategy to grow in higher-yielding loans. Including El Nino provisions, it was 3.4%. Looking ahead, we expect the shift in mix towards higher-yielding loans to become a larger driver of NIM together with lower funding costs.

Given the possibility that the Central Bank raises rates, it is worth sharing our sensitivity. For every 100 basis points increase in the soles reference rate, we estimate a negative impact of around 7 basis points on NIM. On Slide 17. Excluding El Nino, cost of risk was 1.9%, below the 2.1% of both last quarter and a year ago. Including it, cost of risk was 2.7%, so El Nino explains the entire increase. The underlying indicators all improved. Delinquencies are declining mainly due to better payment behavior of customers, in line with stronger economic activity. Our recent vintages are also performing well across the portfolio, even with the growth we mentioned in higher-yielding loans.

In retail, excluding El Nino, cost of risk was 3.4%, slightly above the 3.3% of last quarter. That increase reflects the growth of the portfolio. Commercial remained very low at 0.5%, which, together with an NPL ratio of 1.3% shows the portfolio is performing well. El Nino provisions were booked based on expert judgment as we decided to provision for the scenario we see today. We will reassess as the event evolves. Excluding El Nino, we would expect a slight increase in line with portfolio growth in higher-yielding segments while continuing to improve risk-adjusted returns. On Slide 18. The improvement in funding is the other half of the NIM story.

Cost of funds fell 10 basis points in the quarter and 20 basis points from a year ago. This is a result of the mix, which is moving in the right direction as low funding costs increased to 39% of total funding, reflecting our focus on the payments ecosystem, primary banking and transactional deposits. Retail and commercial deposits now represent 85% of funding and the loan-to-deposit ratio is at 93%. On Slide 19, our payments ecosystem connects directly with the funding trends we just discussed. More transactional activity brings more low-cost deposits and creates cross-selling opportunities. In payments, flow from the Interbank Izipay relationships grew 58% year-over-year and Interbank's share of Izipay flows increased to 48%.

In small business, deposits grew 30% alongside 34% growth in loans. Engagement continues to rise. PLIN transactions are up 43% year-over-year and 86% of our retail customers are now digital, which is the engine behind our lower cost of funds. PLIN also keeps expanding its use cases. PLIN TC or PLIN credit cards, which lets customers send money using their credit card line, has already surpassed 100,000 active customers. On WhatsApp, we cut transactions time by 1/3 and transactions per user increased by 17%, reflecting stronger customer engagement and higher recurrence. We are also making the app more useful and safer with tools like Modo Calle, which helps reduce fraud from phone theft.

Clients are noticing with retail NPS reaching 64 points. We are growing while improving the customer experience, which makes that growth sustainable. Let's now turn to our fifth key message on insurance and wealth management, where growth remains healthy. On Slide 21. At Interseguro, the key metric is the contractual service margin, or CSM, which represents the stock of future profits from our long-term insurance business. It reached PEN 1.2 billion, up 8% year-over-year, driven by annuities and individual life, and short-term insurance grew 10% year-over-year. Investment results were PEN 278 million, a 6.6% return, well above last year's 4%, when we recorded credit loss charges on financial investments.

Compared with last quarter, the return is broadly stable, excluding inflation effects. The 7.1% return in the second quarter would have been 6.7%, very much in line with this quarter. Overall, the business is performing well as expected. On Slide 22. At Inteligo, assets under management, including deposits, reached USD 10.1 billion, up 13% year-over-year, supported by market performance and net inflows from clients. Fee income reached PEN 53 million, up 5% year-over-year and 3% in the quarter. This is the recurring part of the business, and it continues to grow alongside assets under management. Overall, Wealth Management continues to deliver resilient growth, supported by a strong advisory model and healthy demand for investment solutions. On Slide 23.

We are bringing the same digital approach to insurance and wealth management. At Interseguro, direct digital sales grew 25% year-over-year to PEN 40 million and 74% of client interactions are now self-service, improving both customer experience and cost to serve. At Interfondos, we are turning the app into a digital adviser. Digital users went from 30% to 42% of customers in a year, supported by accelerated app adoption, which added more than 11,000 new clients versus the same quarter last year. Digital transactions now represent 64% of platform activity, up from 55% last year, while physical transactions continue to decline. Our renewed website and richer content also strengthened our digital ecosystem.

Now let me move to the final part of the presentation, where we bring everything together. On Slide 25. Let me bring together what we have discussed on growth. Our growth is broad-based with retail loans up 9% year-over-year and commercial loans up 11%. Within the bank, our focus is on consumer and small businesses, and this is where growth is accelerating with consumer loans, excluding payroll deductible loans up 18% and small business loans up 34% year-over-year. Beyond the bank, long-term insurance and wealth management keep growing with the CSM of insurance up 8% and assets under management up 13% year-over-year. On Slide 26.

I'd like to close with our 9-month operating trends and how they compare with what we commented at the beginning of the year. On profitability, ROE for the first 9 months is 18.1%, excluding El Nino, or 17.2% on a reported basis. We continue to expect a full year ROE of around 17%, even after absorbing El Nino provisions. On loans, growth is 10% year-over-year, a little bit above the high single-digit growth we expect for the full year. The acceleration in higher-yielding segments gives us confidence. On efficiency, our cost-to-income ratio is around 37%, within our guidance range even as we continue to invest for growth. Let me close the presentation with our key takeaways.

First, Peru remains resilient ahead of El Nino. Second, core earnings maintained a positive growth trajectory. Third, we are accelerating and we have a momentum in higher-yielding loans. Fourth, NIM recovery on a better asset mix. Finally, insurance and wealth management continued to deliver strong growth. Thank you very much. Now we are ready and welcome any questions you might have.

Operator: [Operator Instructions] The first audio question will come from Ernesto Gabilondo with Bank of America.

Ernesto María Gabilondo Márquez: My first question will be on El Nino. So you mentioned that total exposure to El Nino represents roughly 11% of your total loan book. So just wondering how much additional provisions would you require in the fourth quarter and maybe in the first quarter of next year? Luis Castellanos López-Torres: Ernesto, thanks very much. Yes, you're right. The other 3% potentially exposed is more in consumer and SMEs, also mentioned by Michela. So with the information that we have now, that's the level of provisions that we consider we will have. As Michela mentioned, we need to continue monitoring because news continue to change. But if we do have an extraordinary El Nino, as has been mentioned and analyzed during the last couple of months by the analysts, this is what we should have. Ernesto María Gabilondo Márquez: Okay. You will have to evaluate how is El Nino evolving. I just want to double-check these figures.

Luis Castellanos López-Torres: That's correct. PEN 185 million of provisions allocated to El Nino and Interbank, and around PEN 37 million allocated to SIP, which, as you know, has also a consumer book.

Ernesto María Gabilondo Márquez: Perfect. Luis Castellanos López-Torres: Okay. I'm going to pass it on to Michela or Carlos for a deeper view on the cost of risk, particularly. But we're not changing our view that we will be around 17% for this year.

And as mentioned before, the trajectory of the profitability of IFS will be continuous recovery based on how fast we can rebuild what we've already seen during the second half of this year, the consumer book and the SMEs proportion of loans weighting more over the overall portfolio and maintaining the profitability of the other businesses as we have been doing during the last month. But now, maybe let me pass it on to Carlos or Michela, so they can -- to Michela, so she can walk you a little bit more in detail on the cost of risk evolution and expectations.

Michela Ramat: Thank you, Luis Felipe. Good morning, Ernesto. Let me just comment, Ernesto, that cost of risk throughout the year, excluding, of course, these extraordinary provisions for El Nino has been, I mean, below our expectations. We had 2.1% in the last quarter, and it would have been 1.9% this quarter without El Nino. So basically, what we have been looking at quarter-by-quarter is a better performance of the portfolio than expected given the strong macro backdrop that we have. We commented in the past quarter that as long as the higher-yielding loans continue to represent a higher proportion of the total book, we should start to see that cost of risk to increase.

And we never gave a guidance in terms of cost of risk, but we said we should be getting closer to 2.5% and in the medium term, maybe even above that, okay? So basically, we should see, excluding El Nino, a cost of risk that gradually increases to those levels during next quarter and most likely 2027. But the positive surprise has been also this quarter that taking aside El Nino phenomenon, no cost of risk did not increase but it was even 20 basis points better than the previous quarter, which is good news because it means that we are, let's say, facing El Nino, which -- with a much healthier credit portfolio.

Ernesto María Gabilondo Márquez: No, no, perfectly understood in terms of the cost of risk without El Nino, but just to forecast our estimates in the model, cost of risk, including the provisions for El Nino was around 2.7% in this quarter. Michela Ramat: I couldn't tell you a number, Ernesto, at this point because we need to see what happens in the fourth quarter both without El Nino and with El Nino.

Luis Castellanos López-Torres: I guess if you just add those PEN 185 million to your base number, you will kind of have a good proxy of what the number could be, Ernesto.

Michela Ramat: Thank you, Luis Felipe. Yuri, talking about funding, as you see from the slide, cost of funds was down 10 basis points in the quarter, but also cost of deposits was 10 basis points below the previous quarter. There are a number of reasons, but I would say that the main one is what Luis Felipe mentioned. We continue to grow faster on the low-cost funding elements on the funding base, which comes from retail deposits, transactional deposits, but also small business and midsized companies deposits, which are nonremunerated. So those components are growing double digit and faster than the rest of the funding base.

There was also a small impact because of the -- what you mentioned, the double carry of the bond that -- starting the full October, we don't have. That also helped. But I guess the more medium-term trend is what I mentioned about the strategy. Now of course, going forward, we have some pressure on cost of funds because of what is happening with rates. So we are trying to balance those two forces. Now talking about capital. You described the situation perfectly. And one of the things that kind of changed in the OCI is the non-realized losses that the previous quarter were non-realized gains on the portfolio of sovereign bonds that we have at the bank, okay?

Now just to remind you about our internal policy for both core equity tier 1 and total capital ratio. There are new regulatory limits that go fully in place December 2026 that for Interbank are around 9% core equity tier 1 minimum capital ratio and around 14.2% total capital ratio, okay? So with the levels that you see, we are okay, we are comfortable and we are above our internal buffers. It is important to mention also that with this new regulation in place from the superintendency, there is a much broader differentiation, if you want, in terms of the capital requirements for the different banks in the system.

And that I think is important because as the systemic buffer is different among banks, you will also see minimum regulatory requirements, which are very different between us and the other top banks in the country, okay? In our case, we are in the first bucket of that buffer, which is 50 basis points. But in the case of other banks, that goes up to 150 basis points to 200 basis points. So I think it's important to consider that you will start to see different total capital ratios in the system, but also because the minimum regulatory requirements have a difference of around 150 basis points, okay? So now in any case, we are growing faster than expected.

So we continue to assess our plan -- our medium-term plan in terms of funding. We have more space in the core equity tier 1. As you can see, we are a little bit tighter in the total capital ratio. So we are, of course, in any case, looking at our strategy for 2027.

Luis Castellanos López-Torres: And just to round up, you're right, we completed our approved buyback program, I think, at the beginning of last year or at some point last year. So we completed that program. We have purchased equivalent to around $200 million of IFS shares equivalent. And...

Carlos Tori Grande: Sorry, Luis. I just wanted to complement Michela on the funding part. She explained like the reason for the growth. But what's behind it is the strategy with Izipay and PLIN. As we grow the flows from Izipay, that brings funding, and same with PLIN, we're growing 40%, 50% per year on PLIN transactions, and that translates in more funding. So that's kind of the -- when we speak about the strategy is working, I think that's where it starts. And then obviously, the NPS and everything that we're building in our app helps with the funding.

Yuri Fernandes: No. Great. Super clear answers. If I may, just a final follow-up on the buybacks. You completed the program. Any plans of opening new programs on buybacks?

Luis Castellanos López-Torres: Yes. That's being reviewed right now. Yuri, as you know, we have a positive view on the potential evolution of the shares. So management is ready to recommend that, but we have to balance growth, liquidity to capital as well. So that has not been defined yet, but it's an alternative that we will definitely evaluate at the right time.

Yuri Fernandes: And liquidity, right? Sometimes people ask about the share liquidity as well.

Luis Castellanos López-Torres: Liquidity -- the good thing is that liquidity has improved significantly even after the buybacks. We used to trade, like, as I call it, by appointment. And today, we see like $10 million to $15 million of average daily trading volume in NYSE. So that has come back a long way during the last, I'd say, 3 years.

Operator: The next question will come from Carlos Gomez with HSBC.

Carlos Gomez-Lopez: I have two. And like Yuri, I want to move beyond El Nino. So the first one refers to PLIN. It's obvious that as a platform, it is running behind its competitor today. I mean, this can change in the future. What can you do to make PLIN more competitive in the market? And where do you see this kind of business going forward? And second, more generally, as a management team, you have a public profile, you write in the newspapers. We have a new administration. We have the prospect of stability in government over the next 5 years. What is it that we should be looking for?

What -- are you excited about in terms of changes that we can see with this administration? And what could worry you if it doesn't happen?

Luis Castellanos López-Torres: Sure. For your strategic question, I would like to pass it on to Carlos, who I'm sure can give you a little bit more detail on exactly how we see this.

Carlos Tori Grande: Thank you, Luis Felipe. Hello, Carlos. So on PLIN, the first thing that's important to understand is when you talk about the competitor, I'm assuming you're speaking about Yape. And it's very important to understand that we're not comparing apples-to-apples, right? PLIN is a brand and it's, let's call it, a highway through which payments go through. It's not an app. It's not a separate app. It's not a transaction. So when we talk about PLIN vis-a-vis Yape, most of the things that we do at Interbank, PLIN helps all the other things that we do at Interbank.

For example, the micro loans that Michela mentioned through PLIN TC, that's not something that you're going to see when we speak about PLIN. It's something that you see at the Interbank app, right? When we pay services, you see it in Interbank. When we do digital loans, we see it in Interbank. So what PLIN has helped us with is a lot of engagement and growth in terms of transactions and the -- how deep our relationship with our clients are, but you don't see everything when we talk about PLIN. In terms of transactions, Yape has grown a lot, and they are definitely larger than PLIN.

But our growth over the last couple of years has been 40% in the last 12 months and almost 100% the year before. So we continue to grow. We continue to have deposits coming from this strategy, and we're looking to accelerate constantly. Probably, what's coming in from the Central Bank with TAPP, which is somewhat similar to Pix, is going to be an accelerator, not necessarily for PLIN, but for Interbank and new customers coming in and more transactions. For example, anything we do through TAPP will not be PLIN, but will be Interbank, it's the same customer. So I would say we are very bullish in terms of the next few quarters in terms of payments.

We are waiting -- TAPP should come in line in the first and second quarter of next year and should accelerate. So that's a little bit of how we look at it, the way how we profit from PLIN and how much we invest in growing those transactions.

Luis Castellanos López-Torres: Does that answer your question, Carlos?

Carlos Gomez-Lopez: No, and well, perhaps to follow-up. I mean, obviously PLIN, you do together with the other banks. Are there any new initiatives or new way of doing the business going forward that is different from what you are doing today, or the way it is working with your partners is fine at the moment?

Carlos Tori Grande: So there's a lot of things that we are doing in our app, for example, security for our clients. We're doing Modo Calle. But that's just Interbank, it's not PLIN. I would look at PLIN sort of when you talk about Visa or Mastercard or Amex, it's a rail, okay, through which you do the transaction. So most of the innovation and the strategy and relationship goes through what we do in our app, and there's separation from that. So transactions are running smoother. We've got steps to the transactions, and we're building additional things to that engagement, not necessarily on PLIN, okay?

And then one thing that I forgot to mention, and it's very important, there's a lot of growth coming in from SIP. So SIP is the other subsidiary for IFS, which has a different value proposition, which also uses PLIN, so they can send and receive money from PLIN customers, but that's where probably most of the quick growth will come over the next couple of quarters. So I don't see many new things coming on PLIN because at the end of the day, it is just a transaction rail.

There are a lot of things that we're building in our app that is better for our customers and obviously improves the value proposition and helps us to grow at Interbank.

Luis Castellanos López-Torres: Thank you, Carlos. Just to add, like, probably based on what Carlos was mentioning, it's more like apples-to-apples view will be Yape to SIP than Yape to PLIN. So we can go deeper over that in a different moment. In terms of our views of the political scenario, again, as mentioned before, we're positive. I think that, first, it's a government that has market-friendly view orientation. They're fostering investments, trying to recoup Peru's growth potential as fast as possible and reduce the poverty levels, understanding that there's lots of investments that need to be done, both from the public and the private sector.

And that growth is the way to go around the economy in order to reduce the gaps that the social landscape of Peru has. So that's kind of the overall understanding. We have a constructive view on the way Congress is working now with two chambers. I think that's positive. That brings stability towards what we've seen compared to what we've seen in the last years. So that's also a positive. We do expect this government to remain in place for the next 5 years with Keiko Fujimori to remain in place over the next 5 years given the landscape now. And again, we were hoping for some stability. It's tough when you have so many changes coming in.

So this stability has resulted in increased business and consumer confidence, which translates into a positive view towards more investments and unlocking Peru's growth potential because we have many industries that have significant potential. We can discuss mining. We can discuss energy. We can discuss all the infrastructure that is required. There's always risks, obviously, but we are on the positive side. We're optimistic about what's to come. There's lots of work to do. There's some reforms that need to pass. But overall, our sentiment as expressed before, but also shown in the indicators of the business confidence and consumer confidence I mentioned, is positive.

So I think we are on the right track with lots of work to do for both the public and the private sector.

Operator: [Operator Instructions] Our next question will come from Andres Soto with Santander.

Andres Soto: I have just one question. When I look at your loan book composition, consumer and SME loans now represent 23% of the total portfolio. This has been an important driver for your NIM expansion recently, 20 bps this quarter, if I'm not wrong. But you had mentioned in this call that you are tightening your underwriting to linear exposed regions and expect an impact in terms of loan growth in 2027. How much could this more cautious origination affect the pace of portfolio shift and NIM expansion? And what is -- what are your expectations, generally speaking, regarding NIM also considering the potential for higher rates in 2027?

Luis Castellanos López-Torres: Yes. Okay. Thank you very much for your question. Just to sum up, I mentioned in the previous question, I mentioned consumer and business confidence. But yesterday, Peru had a significant vote of confidence from investors as well, the sovereign placed bonds, $4.5 billion with a demand, like, 5x to 7x that. So that's another view on the confidence that the government is raising towards what we can do in the future. In terms of the specific question about loan growth, NIM expansion and what we see in SMEs and consumer, let me pass it on to Carlos.

Carlos Tori Grande: Thank you, Felipe. Hello, Andres, thank you for your question. Yes, we're at 23%. As Michela said a little bit earlier and we've been saying, we want to go above 25% in higher-yielding loans. We have been growing over the last 2 or 3 months at the rates that we were aiming at. And being able to focus on regions that won't be affected or higher credit ratings. So we should continue with the performance that we've had in terms of growth. It shouldn't affect, El Nino shouldn't affect. Obviously, we need to be very careful in how our models work and how our leads are developed and stuff like that.

But we've been doing that fairly well over the last couple of months, and that shouldn't change in the next few years. So our -- in the next few months, our expectation is for NIM to continue to expand and our growth to be as we have shown in the last couple of months. So short answer is, yes, we can continue to grow at this rate.

Luis Castellanos López-Torres: Andre, just a matter of perspective. This is on the backdrop of very solid economic performance of Peru. In the -- last time, we've had a strong El Nino, extraordinary El Nino close to recession. This time, we do expect Peru will continue to grow at around 3% despite El Nino. So that situation is very different. So we are being cautious, but we do see many avenues of potential growth.

Carlos Tori Grande: Thank you, Felipe. Just to complement, sorry, Andres, we're going into El Nino with a very strong portfolio, with very low cost of risk over the last couple of quarters. So a very good portfolio as well, and that helps compared to previous El Nino. So it's a strong backdrop for the country, but also for Interbank in specific. So yes, that will help as well.

Andres Soto: Absolutely. Two follow-ups there. The first one. Based on this scenario, do you think a double-digit loan growth in 2027 is doable given the strong macro backdrop? And the second, once you reach this 25% participation of SME and consumer loans, do you have any idea of what is the NIM that the Interbank or IFS should have?

Luis Castellanos López-Torres: Yes. On your first question, this is not guidance, but the answer is yes, it's doable over strong GDP. We've always said the system should go up between 2x and 3x. So -- and Interbank has always, like, been focused and proven with results that we scratch market share overall. And then on the second part, maybe let me pass it on to Michela, so she can give you a little bit more on that.

Michela Ramat: Thank you, Luis Felipe. And just on the same line of not giving guidance yet, I will not be able to give you an exact NIM number, Andres. But you have seen the first results of the NIM expansion this quarter. So as we have, like, the full year effect during 2027 of what we are building in the portfolio now, and we continue to outgrow, if you want the rest of the credit loan book with the higher-yielding loans, we should continue to see an expansion of NIM even if we don't expect a lot of contribution from cost of funds given the trends of increase in interest rates, okay?

But given yield on loans and the overall return on the interest-earning assets, we should continue to see a NIM expansion. And even if we will also see an increase in cost of risk because of the loan needs, we should also see an expansion of risk-adjusted NIM.

Operator: As there are no further audio questions, I would like to pass the call over to Mr. Peill for any webcast questions.

Ivan Peill: Thank you, operator. No questions have been submitted via the webcast. So I'd like to turn the call back over to you.

Operator: Thank you, sir. And we will conclude the question-and-answer session today. We'll pass the call back over to Ms. Casassa for closing remarks.

Michela Ramat: Okay. Thank you very much. Thank you, everybody, for joining our call. We continue to be positive on the backdrop of El Nino and the macro scenario, and we will see you again in the last quarter conference call in February. Thank you very much.

Operator: This concludes today's conference call. You may now disconnect.

#3188. CleanupBuddy 2.0 expands beyond the keyboard with new display cleaning features

Developer Gui Rambo updated CleanupBuddy today, expanding its ability to prevent accidental inputs while cleaning your Mac from the keyboard to the touchscreen. Here are the details.

If you’re not familiar with CleanupBuddy, this is a nice little app that locks the keyboard to prevent accidental inputs while the user cleans it up.

Once they’re done cleaning, users can press and hold both Cmd keys to unlock the keyboard, then proceed to grease it up again.

The app also features a fun little animated character that reacts to your cleaning sessions with playful (and sometimes snarky) comments.

Today, CleanupBuddy was updated to version 2.0, with options to dim the display and ignore touch inputs, making it useful for users of both the new touchscreen MacBook Pro and Macs with traditional displays.

You can use the new “Lock Touch Screen” option to block touch input while cleaning a supported touch screen. On Macs without a touch screen, the “Dim Display” option can still be used to darken the display for easier cleaning.

Today’s update also tweaks the in-app character, which now uses on-device Apple Intelligence to generate personalized comments before and after cleaning sessions, based on stats such as time spent cleaning, key presses, and mouse clicks.

Rambo explains that these stats are collected only during cleaning sessions and stored locally on the Mac, and that users can independently turn off both cleanup stats and Apple Intelligence integration in the app’s settings.

Other tweaks in today’s update include temporarily disabling Sticky Keys and its Shift-key shortcut during cleaning sessions, as well as improving the readability of the “Start Cleanup” button when using Liquid Glass.

CleanupBuddy 2.0 is available for $2.99 and is compatible with macOS 14 and later, while the new personalized messages require macOS 26 or later, with Apple Intelligence enabled and its models ready to use.

To learn more about CleanupBuddy, follow this link.

#3187. Nvidia board hires ex-prosecutor Joon Kim to investigate Jensen Huang

The Nvidia board running the inquiry has no chair and no compliance chief, and its lead director once ran the company’s law firm. Three of Huang’s relatives work there.

NVIDIA founder and CEO Jensen Huang during his GTC 2026 keynote at the SAP Center in San Jose, 16 March 2026

Nvidia’s independent directors have hired the law firm Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz to investigate chief executive Jensen Huang. The board retained Joon H. Kim, a former acting US Attorney in Manhattan, and his firm to run it. The board announced the choice on Tuesday, CNBC reported.

“The independent members of the NVIDIA Board have retained former acting U.S. Attorney of the Southern District of New York Joon H. Kim and his firm Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz to conduct a thorough and independent investigation as was announced on Sunday,” the board said in a statement.

The board opened its own inquiry after Huang admitted an affair with Alice Huang, a former executive at the chip buyer Megaspeed. US intelligence agencies have concluded she was a spy for China, which has rejected the claims. Huang would not take part in choosing counsel and would keep leading the company, a spokesman had said, according to the Times.

The Nvidia board has a combined 161 years of service, Kalley Huang and Don Clark reported for The New York Times. Huang, Tench Coxe and Harvey Jones have sat on it since 1993, according to Nvidia’s proxy statement.

Sequoia Capital and Sutter Hill Ventures led a $2m round in Nvidia in 1993. Their investors, Mark Stevens and Coxe, then joined the board. Stevens left in 2006 and returned in 2008, the proxy shows. Brooke Seawell, a former Synopsys finance chief, joined in 1997. Jones and Seawell held Nvidia shares worth a combined $1.86bn as of June, the Times reported.

Before the hire, people familiar with the inquiry told the Financial Times it would probably be led by Stephen Neal, the lead independent director. Neal ran the law firm Cooley from 2001 to 2008 and is still its senior counsel. Cooley set up Nvidia in 1993 and has been its main outside counsel since, CNBC reported, citing the firm. Neal did not respond to CNBC.

Average director tenure is almost 15 years, nearly twice the S&P 500 norm, Semafor reported. No director is a current or former S&P 500 chief executive, and none has national security experience. None of the directors responded to the Times.

Nvidia has a lead independent director instead of a board chair. The proxy says this gives each member “an equal voice”. Huang told Bloomberg’s Emily Chang that he skipped the chairman role so the chief executive could be held accountable, Bloomberg reported.

“Unlike many CEOs, I’m completely fireable,” Huang said.

Nvidia’s code of conduct tells staff and directors to avoid any activity that conflicts with the company’s interests, the proxy says. That includes anything that looks like a conflict. The company does not have a chief compliance officer, the filing confirms. Nvidia has said a committee of its finance, operations and human resources heads checks that staff follow its policies, Fortune reported.

Nvidia’s annual report does not name Huang as a key person. It says the company depends heavily on its longstanding executive team.

“Failure to ensure effective succession planning, transfer of knowledge, and smooth transitions involving executives and key employees could hinder our strategic planning, execution, and long-term success,” the filing says.

Huang is Nvidia’s co-founder, chief executive and president. He has 33 direct reports this week, according to internal records reviewed by CNBC. He told CNBC in September 2025 that he had as many as 60. The proxy says the senior managers who work directly with him give the board a pool of candidates for promotion.

Huang owned 3.58% of Nvidia in March, the proxy shows, and he has no special voting rights, the Financial Times reported. He told Bloomberg he hoped the next chief executive already worked at Nvidia. In January, he said a chief executive who does not do the job “is let go”, the Times reported. He added a second thought.

“There will never be one like me, and the reason for that is because I was raised by the company,” Huang said.

Three relatives work at Nvidia. His son Spencer is a director of product management in robotics, and his daughter Madison is a senior director of product marketing, according to the Times. His son-in-law, Nico Caprez, works on business development, the Times reported. Fortune gives his title as vice president of global AI infrastructure growth.

Nvidia paid Madison about $1.23m and Spencer about $1.32m in its 2026 financial year, the proxy shows. Neither is an executive officer, shares a household with Huang or reports directly to him. Their pay was set under the company’s normal practices without Huang’s involvement, the filing says.

Nvidia reports its third-quarter results on 17 November. A day later, House committee chairs expect Huang at a closed-door briefing on Megaspeed.

#3185. iFixit tears down touchscreen MacBook Pro, reveals light-up Apple logo details

iFixit published its teardown of the new MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display today, revealing interesting details about how Apple brought back its illuminated logo on the lid. Watch it below.

iFixit’s teardown of the new MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display is now live, and it explores not only how the new illuminated Apple logo works, but also its tandem OLED and how Apple managed to trim its weight down to 3 pounds (1.38 kg) from 3.4 pounds (1.55 kg) on the standard 14-inch model.

The teardown opens with a close look at the tandem OLED, which stacks two light-emitting layers to deliver higher brightness than conventional single-layer OLED displays.

Under a microscope, iFixit found that the blue subpixels are larger than the red and green ones, which they say should help reduce strain on the materials and potentially extend the display’s lifespan.

Most of the teardown process is quite familiar from past models, though iFixit noted that replacing the USB-C ports or fans still requires removing the entire logic board, despite both components being independently replaceable.

iFixit noted that the headphone jack also requires logic board removal, while the HDMI port, SDXC port, RAM, and storage remain soldered to the board.

As with past teardowns, iFixit also tested what happens when swapping logic boards between two MacBooks.

While last year’s M5 MacBook Pro failed to complete Touch ID calibration through Apple’s Repair Assistant, iFixit noted that the new model successfully recognized the battery, display, and Touch ID sensor after a logic board swap, with True Tone, brightness controls, and the touchscreen all working as expected.

iFixit was also able to enroll a fingerprint with the donor board installed from another MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display.

As for the illuminated Apple logo, iFixit had a bit of a rough time getting to it, destroying the OLED panel in the process and even asking whether anyone had managed to remove it intact.

Once inside, iFixit found that the Apple logo is illuminated by a strip of four LEDs, which work in conjunction with a reflective layer and a diffuser to distribute the light evenly.

The Apple logo itself, in turn, has a two-way mirror coating that gives it a shiny, reflective appearance when the LEDs are off, while allowing light to pass through when they’re on.

When it comes to weight, Apple shaved 92 grams off the chassis and 101 grams off the display assembly, despite adding touch and an illuminated logo. The battery is just 2 grams lighter, while the slightly smaller trackpad saves another 8 grams.

Finally, iFixit gave the new MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display a repairability score of 5 out of 10. That was one point higher than last year’s M5 MacBook Pro, but one point below the cheaper MacBook Neo.

#3184. AI firms sign Macron’s Paris Call, but safety group says it lacks teeth

OpenAI, Anthropic and Microsoft promise shutdown switches and outside testing, but there are no shared risk limits.

The Paris Call meeting at the Élysée Palace on 9 November, with leaders and AI executives joining by video

OpenAI, Anthropic, Microsoft and Mistral are among ten AI companies that have signed a new declaration on the safety of advanced AI models. The Paris Call for AI Safety and Security was agreed on Monday at a meeting hosted by French President Emmanuel Macron.

L’intelligence artificielle avance très vite. On l’a déjà vu : cela implique des risques réels pour notre sécurité collective.

Notre travail pour developper nos technologies doit aussi être celui de l’anticipation et de la maîtrise de ses risques.

J’ai réuni à Paris et en visio une cinquantaine d’acteurs : chefs d’État et de gouvernement, dirigeants des plus grands laboratoires d’IA, chercheurs et experts.

Le constat est partagé. Il faut agir ensemble. Nous avons obtenu des engagements de tous autour de trois priorités : mieux évaluer de façon indépendante et publique les risques des modèles les plus avancés, mieux partager les alertes en cas d’incident grave et responsabiliser les acteurs qui développent des modèles.

Notre ambition est claire : faire de l’IA un progrès pour tous, avec une sécurité garantie par l’engagement de chacun.

— Emmanuel Macron (@EmmanuelMacron) November 9, 2026

The announcement came on the opening day of the Paris Peace Forum, where AI was one of the main topics of discussion.

Six countries signed the declaration: France, Canada, Finland, Norway, the Netherlands and Bahrain. The other participating companies are Hugging Face, Cohere, Black Forest Labs, Domyn, Sakana AI and Synthesia. Yoshua Bengio’s AI safety organisation LawZero is among the research groups supporting it.

Around 50 people joined the discussions by video, including OpenAI chief executive Sam Altman, Anthropic chief executive Dario Amodei and Microsoft president Brad Smith.

US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent also took part, although the US is not among the signatories. Google, Meta and China have not signed the declaration either.

Macron said AI was advancing rapidly and posed “real risks to our collective security”, calling for governments and companies to work together to address them.

The signatories have committed to developing fail-safe mechanisms that can shut down their AI models, including during training and internal use. They will also provide clearer information about what their systems can and cannot do, and allow qualified independent experts to test them where appropriate.

The declaration also calls for a shared approach to assessing and managing the risks of frontier AI. This would cover malicious uses, including cyberattacks and weapons development, as well as the possibility of AI systems acting independently or moving beyond human control. Non-sensitive test results would be published in a common format.

Governments and companies will also share early warnings about serious incidents, while whistleblowers will have access to secure channels for reporting concerns.

The commitments have drawn criticism from French AI safety organisation CeSIA, which signed the declaration but argues that it leaves important gaps.

It sets no common risk thresholds for deciding whether a model should be developed or released, and does not guarantee that independent testers or governments will have access to the systems they need to assess.

CeSIA also wants governments to have the authority to suspend a model when its risks become too high. It argues that developers need clearer obligations and a timetable for meeting them.

“These decisions must rest with public authorities,” said Charbel-Raphaël Ségerie, CeSIA’s executive director.

The Paris Call follows an initiative launched by Norway and Finland in September to bring frontier AI under greater oversight, which France later joined. It also builds on earlier global safety commitments made by AI companies in Seoul and discussions at the G7 summit hosted by France in Evian.

The declaration remains open to other signatories, but it sets no deadlines. The shared testing framework it proposes has yet to be developed.

On Tuesday, the forum turned to another concern for Macron: the effects of AI on children. Speaking at a summit on children in the AI era, the French president called for AI tools to undergo checks before being made available to young users.

“We will push for pre-certification of all artificial intelligence solutions,” he said.

Macron compared the idea to the safety checks required for children’s toys, arguing that parents would not give a child an untested toy and that AI tools should be held to the same standard.

He also warned that the effects of AI on young people’s mental health were already becoming apparent, as more children and teenagers turn to chatbots that can influence their emotions and how they see the world. A charter on safer AI for children was due to be signed later on Tuesday.

President Emmanuel Macron also received a report, titled “Protect without preventing”, from a government-appointed panel of experts examining generative AI and human vulnerability.

#3181. Why Securitize Stock Surged Today

More real-world assets are moving onchain.

Shares of Securitize (SECZ +22.38%) spiked 22% on Tuesday after the tokenization platform announced an intriguing acquisition.

Securitize's revenue rose 13% year over year to $18.6 million in the third quarter.

The financial technology provider helps convert ownership of real-world assets into digital tokens stored on a blockchain, bringing greater access and transparency to previously illiquid markets.

Average tokenized assets on Securitize's platform jumped 39% to $5 billion.

"That growth came from tier one asset managers bringing real products onchain including new ones from Ark Invest, BlackRock, and Neuberger, and to me it's the clearest sign yet that institutions are past the experimenting stage," CEO Carlos Domingo said.

Still, investors should note that Securitize has not yet achieved sustained profitability. The company's adjusted earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation, and amortization (EBITDA) checked in at a loss of $2 million.

Securitize also struck a deal to acquire River One to enter the $6 trillion asset-backed finance market. River One specializes in connecting the $321 billion global stablecoin market with the traditional lending industry.

The deal is projected to close in the fourth quarter.

"Credit is one of the most exciting emerging asset classes for blockchain-based financial markets, and acquiring River One represents an important step in expanding our business into this space," Domingo said.

#3180. Speech Processing Pioneer Bishnu Saroop Atal Dies at 93

IEEE also bids farewell to innovators in space, power, and telecom

Bishnu Saroop Atal received the 2013 IEEE Jack S. Kilby Signal Processing Medal for “fundamental and pioneering contributions to speech coding.”

Bishnu Saroop AtalAcoustics and signal processing pioneerLife Fellow, 93; died 19 August

Atal was an acoustics and signal processing researcher at Bell Labs in Murray Hill, N.J., and later at AT&T’s Shannon Laboratory, in Florham Park, N.J. His pioneering work on voice-coding techniques became the foundation for efficient, high-quality voice transmission over cellular networks. He received the 2013 IEEE Jack S. Kilby Signal Processing Medal for “fundamental and pioneering contributions to speech coding.”

He joined Bell Labs in 1961 as a communications researcher, and his early work there focused on speaker identification technology. During the 1960s he helped develop linear predictive coding, a powerful method for analyzing and compressing speech. LPC is now the most widely used method for encoding speech at a low bit rate.

Atal developed increasingly sophisticated low-bit-rate speech-coding techniques. They included multipulse LPC, which improved the quality of compressed speech.

He also worked with his colleague Manfred R. Schroeder to develop code-excited linear prediction, a method for producing high-quality speech at very low bit rates. CELP became a foundational technique in modern speech coding, letting digital communications systems carry voice using less bandwidth. The extra efficiency expanded cellular capacity, allowing wireless networks to handle more simultaneous calls.

Later in his career, he led the acoustics and speech research departments at Bell.

The company named him a Fellow in 1994. When AT&T Bell Laboratories split into separate research organizations in 1996, Atal continued his career at the AT&T Florham Park headquarters, and he was named a Fellow the following year.

He retired in 2002 and became an affiliate professor of electrical engineering at the University of Washington, in Seattle. There he continued his research in speech processing, speech recognition, and high-dimensional computing.

Atal was elected to the National Academy of Engineering in 1987 and the National Academy of Sciences in 1993. He received numerous awards including the 2018 International Speech Communication Association Medal for Scientific Achievement and a 2003 medal from the Franklin Institute.

He received a bachelor’s degree in physics in 1952 from the University of Lucknow, in India, and a master’s degree in 1955 in electrical engineering from the Indian Institute of Science, in Bengaluru. While working full time at Bell he earned a Ph.D. in EE in 1968 from the Polytechnic Institute of Brooklyn (now New York University’s Tandon engineering school), in New York City.

Darryl Palmer Jr.Chair of the IEEE Central Illinois SectionSenior member, 55; died 30 August

Palmer was a dedicated IEEE volunteer, serving as chair of the Central Illinois Section and as the government relations chair of Region 4. He was a member of the IEEE Industrial Electronics Society and its industrial activity committee. He also served as associate editor of the IEEE Transactions on Industrial Informatics.

In 1986, at age 16, Palmer completed a summer internship at NASA’s Glenn Research Center, in Cleveland. He helped develop FoilSim, an interactive educational software program that introduces aerodynamic engineering to preuniversity students.

While studying computer science at Cleveland State University in 1996, he joined the university’s Allen-Bradley PLC lab as a research assistant. He designed hardware and software systems for the Glenn Research Center to collect and process thermal wave imaging data. He also designed software for General Motors’ North American robotic and welding division.

In 1999 he completed a second internship at the research center and helped develop EngineSim, an educational software program that models jet engine design and testing.

For his work, NASA recognized him with a Space Act Award.

In 2000 he earned his bachelor’s degree in computer science and became a software engineer at the Danfoss Drives manufacturing facility in Loves Park, Ill. He worked on embedded control systems for variable-frequency drives and high-power equipment. He also developed sensorless control technology for beam pumps used in the oil and gas industry.

In 2014 Palmer and his wife, Alexandra “Sasha” Goodwin, founded Janus Choice, a health technology platform that matches hospital patients with post-acute care facilities. He served as its CEO until the company closed in 2020.

From 2018 to 2023, he was a lead software engineer at Adept Coalescence, a startup in Rockford, Ill., focused on developing front-end software for control systems. He then worked in Peoria, Ill., as a control systems team lead at Caterpillar, a manufacturer of construction and mining equipment.

Henry Leopold RichterTelecommunications engineerLife senior member, 99; died 12 August

Richter was a spacecraft engineer at NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory, in Pasadena, Calif., before starting his own public safety communications consultancy.

He earned a bachelor’s degree and a Ph.D. at Caltech in 1952 and 1956, respectively. In 1955 he joined JPL as an engineer and supervisor of its new circuit elements group. Later, he was assigned to NASA’s Explorer program as project manager for satellite design, serving as a liaison between the organization’s satellite instrumentation group and its operations and data groups. Since 1958 the program has launched more than 90 missions for physics, geophysics, and astrophysics research.

As NASA prepared to launch Explorer 1 in January 1958, Richter worked with the San Gabriel Valley Radio Club in Los Angeles to set up stations across the United States to track the satellite.

He eventually was named JPL section chief and was responsible for scientific instruments on the lunar Ranger, Surveyor, and Mariner programs. He also helped develop NASA’s Deep Space Network, an international tracking and communications system.

Richter left NASA to become vice president and technical director of Xerox Electro-Optical Systems, in Pasadena, Calif.

In the mid-1970s, he joined the Los Angeles County Sheriff’s Department as a communications engineer, overseeing the department’s microwave and mobile radio networks.

He later ran a telecommunications consulting practice for more than 20 years. His clients included federal, state, and local government agencies, school districts, universities, and organizations. His work covered strategic technology planning and the design and implementation of public safety radio, microwave, CCTV, and paging systems.

He wrote several books including America’s Leap Into Space: My Time at JPL and the First Explorer Satellites (2015), a personal account of his experience working on the Explorer 1 and America’s space program.

In 2019 the Radio Club of America presented him with its Lifetime Achievement Award for “significant achievements and a major body of work that has advanced the art and science of wireless technology.”

Raymond L. GiordanoFormer RCA engineerLife member, 91; died 19 July

Giordano was an electrical engineer who designed integrated circuits and defense electronics at companies including Harris, Intersil, and RCA.

After earning his bachelor’s degree in electrical engineering in 1956 from the Newark College of Engineering (now the New Jersey Institute of Technology), Giordano joined RCA in Moorestown, N.J., as an engineer. He helped develop a video formatter for the company’s missile and surface radar division, and he taught in-house engineering courses, eventually attaining the rank of senior technical staff member.

Later he developed technologies for General Electric (which acquired RCA in 1986), Intersil, and Harris. He designed the circuitry for Kodak’s Cameo cameras and one of its laser printers.

Giordano was awarded several patents for his designs including a smoke detector chip for Siemens, a speed control chip for Ford, an engine control system for Delco Remy, and a control component for Chrysler.

He earned a master’s degree in EE in 1964 from the University of Pennsylvania, in Philadelphia.

Delano D. WilsonPresident of Power TechnologiesLife Fellow, 92; died 26 May

Wilson was president and CEO of Power Technologies, a consulting firm in Schenectady, N.Y., that specialized in electric power systems.

He was a director of R&D at General Electric in Schenectady until he joined Power Technologies in 1974 as a principal engineer. He developed utility systems and software for the company.

Wilson authored six books and 65 technical papers, and he held two patents.

Outside of his engineering work, he served on the boards of several hospitals, YMCAs, Rotary clubs, and chambers of commerce.

After returning to his hometown of Great Falls, Mont., in 1995, he volunteered as a court-appointed advocate, a trained community volunteer appointed by a judge to represent the interests of children in foster care.

Daniel I. Amey Jr.Electronic packaging engineerLife Fellow, 84; died 12 March

Amey was an electronic packaging engineer, working at several companies including General Dynamics, Sperry Univac, and E.I. du Pont de Nemours (now DuPont). His research interests included connectors, chip packages, and high-frequency materials.

He began his career in 1963 as an engineer in the General Dynamics electronics division, where he designed military electronic hardware including analog and digital support equipment for aerospace applications.

In 1967 he joined Sperry Univac in Blue Bell, Pa. From 1972 to 1981 he was engineering manager of packaging techniques, responsible for interconnection hardware for small and medium computer systems. His work focused on large-scale integration packages, hybrid circuits, connectors, and printed wiring board processes.

He left the company to serve as director of electronics technology at Thomas & Betts of Raritan, N.J. He led research and development of packaging and interconnection products there.

In 1986 he became a director of Elco, an electrical component manufacturer in Huntingdon, Pa., where he was responsible for the design and development of connector and packaging hardware.

In 1988 he joined E.I. du Pont de Nemours as director of its electronics and communications technology group in Research Triangle Park, N.C. He worked on packaging technology development, high-frequency materials characterization, and applications engineering. He retired from there as a research fellow.

Amey wrote or cowrote more than 70 technical papers and held more than 14 patents. He developed courses on electronic packaging and printed wiring technology for education companies McGraw-Hill and Cobblestone (formerly the Center for Professional Advancement).

He received the International Microelectronics Assembly and Packaging Society’s 2004 Wagnon Technical Achievement Award and the Electronic Industries Association’s 1984 Distinguished Engineering Contribution Award.

After receiving a bachelor’s degree in electrical engineering and a master’s degree in engineering science from Pennsylvania State University, he earned an MBA from Lehigh University, in Bethlehem, Pa.

Amanda Davis is a freelance writer based in San Diego.

#3179. Zendesk moves to pay-per-result AI pricing with its new Outcome AI Platform

Customers will pay when AI resolves an issue, and a new directory helps AI assistants find official support.

Zendesk is changing how businesses pay for its AI, charging them for problems solved rather than for the number of people using the software. The customer service company announced the change on Tuesday at its AI Summit in San Francisco, as part of a new Outcome AI Platform.

Under the new plans, customers set an ‘Outcome Budget’ and pay for each eligible issue the AI resolves or task it completes. Zendesk checks each result for quality and completeness, so customers can see what counts towards their budget. As a result, businesses can start small and spend more as the AI takes on more work.

Zendesk has backed this model before. Earlier this year, it argued alongside Sierra that AI agents should be paid per result, not per seat, and OpenAI has started trying a similar approach with some customers.

Tapan Patel, a research director at IDC, said the change reflects how business buyers now want to pay for AI. Linking cost to verified results, he added, makes it clearer what customers get for their money.

The platform is also built for a world where people send their own AI assistants to deal with companies. To help with that, Zendesk is launching the Open Service Directory, a public list where brands can register their official support channels. AI assistants can then use it to find verified help, even for brands that do not use Zendesk.

Brands control what they share and when a human must step in. The directory does not access private customer data or take any action itself. Early members include Betterment, ElevenLabs and Telekom Payment.

Meanwhile, a tool called Zendesk Bridge lets businesses connect AI agents and apps of their choice, such as ChatGPT, to Zendesk’s systems. Setting up a connection starts with a name, which is kept for audit logs, and a plain description of what the outside agent should and should not do.

Administrators then choose exactly what each agent may do, such as reading, creating, answering, updating or merging tickets. An assistant called Admin Copilot suggests which tools to switch on, based on the description.

Every action then passes through Bridge, which checks permissions and company rules and asks for human approval where needed. An observability page shows how many requests came from AI agents and how many from people, which ones were blocked and why. It also includes a kill switch. Bridge is in early access, and the directory is launching soon.

“People don’t think about which channels, systems, or departments they need to navigate to interact with a business,” said Zendesk chief executive Tom Eggemeier.

Other new tools, now generally available, help teams build and improve their AI agents. AI Agent Launchpad studies past customer conversations and suggests where AI could take over. In Zendesk’s demo for a scooter rental firm, it proposes a step-by-step process for rides that will not end, using a connected billing system such as Stripe.

Similarly, Agentic Analytics lets managers ask questions about their data in plain language, such as how many tickets are still open. They can then see whether changes are cutting repeat contacts.

The launch reflects changing habits, according to a Zendesk survey. It found that 52% of consumers are comfortable relying on personal AI assistants for everyday tasks. Even so, 84% said human help should always be available.

The announcement follows Zendesk’s purchase of Forethought, its biggest deal in two decades, as it builds out its AI agents.
